This research focuses on laying out the principles of quantum dynamical systems that incorporate noncommutative geometry. Our work also reveals that certain finite-dimensional Lie algebras guarantee ergodicity within a specific class of quantum dynamical systems. Additionally, we've developed a method to create quantum dynamical systems that are topologically mixing when equipped with a specific topology, along with a strategy for constructing their fundamental invariant, the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy. Our results demonstrate the uniqueness of these quantum dynamical systems under the principles outlined in this research, in addition to showing the relationship between their underlying Lie algebras and the spectrum of their associated operators, along with a new definition of the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy that incorporates geometric noncommutative geometry and proves that its measure is finitely representable when equipped with a specific topology. Our research also introduces a new set of operators defined by Lie algebras, such as the Heisenberg, abelian, and solvable Lie algebras, along with their respective cross-spectra, including the standard matrix representation of the GNS construction, along with a new set of simple and direct formulae for computing the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy of these quantum dynamical systems. This research focuses on enhancing the performance of underwater fiber communications using digital signal processing techniques, specifically with a decision-feedback equalizer. Real-world underwater transmissions are hindered by numerous distortions including nonlinear effects, weather conditions, and the unique properties of seawater. These constraints introduce significant chromatic and polarization-mode dispersion, lead to frequency-splittings and multi-path distortions in underwater transmissions. As a result, underwater fiber communications pose a significant technical challenge for engineers. To address this issue, we employed a combination of field trials and laboratory experiments to gather insights and data. Our findings showed that underwater transmissions are prone to burst errors caused by the diverse and ever-changing environmental conditions. To tackle this problem, we developed an innovative error-mitigation technique that complements the decision-feedback equalizer. By gathering and analyzing data from over 20 weeks of continuous underwater transmissions in two different locations, we demonstrated that our proposed method can significantly enhance the performance of the decision-feedback equalizer, correcting up to 90% of burst errors and achieving error rates below 10^-3 in 10-Gbps transmissions. Our research provides valuable insights and actionable recommendations for engineers working on underwater communications projects and offers a framework for designing and evaluating the effectiveness of error-mitigation strategies in underwater transmissions. To further address the limitations of underwater transmissions, we also explored the feasibility of employing multiple wavelength-diversity receivers and our analysis indicated that using this approach can provide up to 5-dB improvement in signal reception. However, this technique is still in its infancy and more research is needed to fully utilize its benefits. To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first to investigate error-mitigation techniques in underwater transmissions in such a comprehensive and in-depth manner. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) are consistently achieving high accuracy rates in various time series prediction tasks. TCNs utilize a technique called causal convolution that offers both efficiency and effectiveness; however, this technique has a significant drawback; when using broad filtering windows, it can lead to premature optimization at non-kernel timesteps. To mitigate this issue, a relatively straightforward yet highly successful approach called trimming in time has been proposed but lacks a systematic analysis. In contrast, another proposed method called Trimmed Convolutional Network (TCN) involved an intricate trimming strategy that is both difficult to execute in practice due to its high computational requirements and challenging to interpret due to its complex structure. In contrast to these methods, our proposed Triming In Time (PIT) framework provides a trimming strategy that is both mathematically justifiable and computationally feasible. PIT involves a novel factor called PIT-factor that offers a clear and intuitive explanation of the model's behavior at each individual timestep. Through a thorough examination of both convolutional network structures, we discovered that the PIT-factor is directly correlated with the model's ability to learn data at different timesteps and found that it follows a uniform distribution. Building on this discovery, we created a trimming strategy that is both data-independent and ensures that the model's optimization is performed at the most informative timesteps. To validate the PIT framework, we conducted an exhaustive examination of both synthetic and real-world datasets that included results from both TCNs and PITs. The code for the proposed PIT framework can be found at https://github.com/author-name/PIT. The proposed PIT framework offers a trimming strategy that is both computationally efficient and free from bias, providing a clear and intuitive explanation of the model's behavior at each individual timestep. This research focuses on enhancing the traditional Poisson autoregressive (PAR) model, commonly used to forecast time series with count data, where past observations are used for prediction. In contrast to linear autoregressive models, the PAR model incorporates the relationship between adjacent observations. However, the PAR model is limited to modeling by assuming a constant relationship between consecutive time series readings. This study proposes a new Temporally Varying Poisson Autoregressive (TVPAR) model that learns and adapts to changes in the time series by utilizing and forecasting based on varying relationships between consecutive readings. Unlike the PAR model, the TVPAR model is capable of detecting and adjusting to changes in the time series by fitting parameters for each observation period. This new model offers improved forecasting performance, especially in scenarios with rapid data variations, in comparison to the PAR model. Experimental evaluation of the TVPAR model showed significant improvement in forecasting accuracy (+35%) in scenarios with rapid data variations in comparison to the PAR model. This improvement in TVPAR model was verified across different dataset sizes. TVPAR model achieved comparable forecasting performance (+5%) to the PAR model in scenarios with slow data variations. TVPAR model is suitable for forecasting real-world applications with rapid data variations such as network intrusion detection, financial transaction data, and weather forecasting. This research introduces TVPAR model in comparison to PAR model and three alternative models including Generalized Linear Model, Seasonal ARIMA with Hyperbolic Distribution and Seasonal ARIMA with Inverse Hyperbolic Tangent Function. TVPAR model is found to deliver the best forecasting performance in comparison to the baseline model. This research provides theoretical justification for TVPAR model by deriving its maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) and asymptotic distribution. This research is relevant to statistics and machine learning communities by addressing the limitation of PAR model and delivering the superior forecasting performance. This research is applicable across various real-world applications with rapid data variations such as network intrusion detection, financial transaction data, and weather forecasting. We introduce Neural Description Fields, a novel framework that leverages object
descriptions as input and enables SE(3) symmetry in object representations. This
framework addresses the challenge of creating robust object representations when
considering real-world image datasets, which are often characterized by significant
variations in lighting and clutter, and diverse scenes with multiple objects per
image. To achieve SE(3) symmetry, Neural Description Fields define a potential field
that maps a description to a potential function over SE(3) translations and
orientations. This potential function is then used to create a potential-based
loss function that is employed in a 3D convolutional neural network. By using
descriptions as input, NDFFs bypass the need for explicit 3D supervision, enabling
robust object representations even with minimal annotation. Notably, our approach
encompasses multiple objects per image by defining an object prior that encourages
replications of objects in a scene to be registered as separate instances.
Experimental results demonstrate that Neural Description Fields produce state-of-the-
art performance on benchmark datasets, including instances with heavy clutter, and
outperform non-symmetric baselines even with extensive annotation, showcasing the
critical role of SE(3) symmetry in object representation. The code is available at

We present new observations of Tonantzintla 2, a globular cluster in the Milky Way's bulge, taken as part of the CAPOS (Carrasco Area Photometric survey) initiative. Located approximately 9.8 kpc from the Sun and 7.8 kpc from the Galactic center, Tonantzintla 2 has been the subject of several studies in the past. Our data, obtained with the APOGEE-2 spectroscopic survey, includes nearly 50 members with high confidence and provides a detailed analysis of the cluster's chemical composition, as well as its kinematics and astrophysical characteristics. Our studies reveal that detailed information about critical edge behavior can be determined through critical exponents and specific heat exponents at both general and special (such as symmetric or asymmetric) temperature conditions. Our key findings show that certain edge critical properties fit into clear O(N) universality categories, confirming many established predictions. However, our main contribution comes from identifying previously unknown edge critical behaviors at certain half-lines or on branches that don't belong to any established O(N) category, particularly in cases where temperature symmetry is broken. These discoveries are illustrated through explicit examples in the Ising model on a cylindrical graph and near a wall, demonstrating edge critical behaviors that don't fit into any standard O(N) category when temperature conditions are asymmetric. Our theoretical investigations provide a clear understanding of edge critical phenomena across all possible situations and offer a framework that can be applied to other phase transitions as well. This new classification system should be applied across all possible situations to ensure a comprehensive understanding of edge critical phenomena. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of the TAP free energy for a broad class of Bethe tree graphs, thereby extending a previous result by Mézard and Montanari that relied on a more complex proof. The vast majority of galaxy research relies on one-dimensional spectra, yet two-dimensional photometry offers a distinct and valuable perspective. By utilizing photometric techniques to measure galaxy distances from their peaks in luminosity curves, our team has made significant breakthroughs in developing methods to derive physical properties directly from these measurements. Specifically, we have developed novel approaches to determine the dust mass, dust temperature, and gas density in a one-dimensional framework. These methods have been applied to numerous galaxy samples, including those at different redshifts, allowing for extensive aerosol-related studies. Furthermore, we have investigated the fundamental relationships between these physical properties and others such as stellar mass, star formation rate, and cosmic age. Our research has produced several significant observations, including: certain star-forming galaxies at high redshifts exhibiting unusually low dust mass; a positive correlation between dust mass and gas density as well as a linear relationship between gas density and stellar mass; an inverse correlation between dust temperature and stellar mass as well as a positive correlation with the Eddington ratio; a threshold in gas density for star formation; and an expected correlation between dust temperature and the Eddington ratio. These discoveries have significant implications on our understanding of galaxy evolution and the interplay between matter and the cosmos. The knowledge gained from these studies has also been used to create a new multi-dimensional diagnostic tool to investigate galaxy evolution, the so-called "zoom-zoom diagram". This diagram allows for the examination of galaxy populations based on multiple properties such as dust mass, gas density, and stellar mass, providing a more comprehensive view of galaxy evolution and helping to identify potential areas of research. The zoom-zoom diagram can be utilized for any physical quantity with a known relationship, making it an adaptable tool for a wide range of aerosol-related research. The breakthroughs presented in this thesis have demonstrated the value of combining one-dimensional and two-dimensional galaxy observations, and it is expected that this approach will become a standard method in galaxy research and a powerful resource for future galaxy surveys. The innovative analysis of galaxy data using photometric techniques in conjunction with spectroscopic information has paved the way for novel research and methodological advancements, and it is anticipated that this approach will contribute significantly to the success of upcoming galaxy surveys. Accurate pose estimation in 3D from 2D images is a fundamental challenge, largely hindered by a major issue: there are an unbounded number of possible 3D configurations that can project onto a single 2D image. This problem is compounded by relying solely on features extracted via convolutional neural networks, which can be both unreliable and inefficient. Existing deep learning methods that attempt to resolve this issue typically fall into two categories: those that extract more sophisticated features, and those that employ correspondence information to reduce the number of possible poses. Notably, none of these methods have explored the integration of both approaches. This paper proposes a novel framework called DeepHMap++, which combines two cutting-edge techniques: a deep learning-based feature extraction method, and a merged projection clustering algorithm using correspondence information. By leveraging both domain expertise and data, this framework delivers superior performance, as evidenced by DeepHMap++ outperforming the existing state-of-the-art method by a significant margin on the HPB dataset and demonstrating robust pose estimation on the PASCAL3D dataset for the first time. We have designed a novel acoustic lens made of a rigid material with a curved surface, which significantly increases the effective sensing area of extended detectors in photoacoustic imaging. The acoustic lens curves around the detector, refracting sound waves and focusing them on specific points. As a result, it can utilize the entire area of the detector, extending beyond the limited area defined by the active elements. We have theoretically and experimentally demonstrated that the acoustic lens can double the effective sensing area of a flat detector. When used with a 16-element flat detector, it equates to using a virtual detector with 256 sensitive elements. Experiments conducted on phantom and human breast tissue have shown that the acoustic lens-enhanced system can produce high-contrast images with clearly defined structures in both cases. It has been observed that the resolution of the system is primarily limited by the size of the active elements and the depth of focusing rather than the area of the detector. This paper tackles the challenging issue of low-level vision tasks in a collaborative framework, focusing on a specific problem: demosaicing, deblurring, and denoising a single raw image from an arbitrary camera. Historically, vision researchers have worked on these problems separately, under the assumption that they are independent given certain conditions. However, in reality, camera sensors capture images that are affected by both blur and noise, and are arranged in a mosaic pattern. As a result, demosaicing, deblurring, and denoising these images requires a collaborative approach. To address this, we propose an innovative framework that can handle these tasks simultaneously. Instead of treating them in isolation, the framework is designed such that its components - a demosaicing module, a deblurring module, and a denoising module - are highly interdependent and learn from each other during training. Notably, the demosaicing module is informed by the deblurring and denoising modules to produce a plausible mosaic pattern. The deblurring module, in turn, utilizes the demosaicing module's output, and the denoising module utilizes the deblurring module's output to restore the image. The proposed framework is shown to yield high-quality results on real-world raw images in comparison to state-of-the-art methods that process demosaiced images. The experimental evaluations also demonstrate its superiority in terms of speed and model complexity. The framework's effectiveness is further validated across diverse cameras and scenes. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyangwang/collaborative-raw-image-processing. The model achieves the current best PSNR of 32.42 on the RAWSKETCH dataset, and can be found at the MM2021 workshop on Low-Level and Cross-Domain Vision https://zhengyangwang.github.io/mm2021-workshop/. The framework's potential for handling multiple raw images is also explored, and the findings indicate that it is a promising direction for further research. The proposed method wins the MM2021 workshop on Low-Level and Cross-Domain Vision Best Paper Award. The model has been integrated into the Adobe Lightroom RAW demosaicing plugin, and is available for public download at https://github.com/zhengyangwang/lightroom-plugin. The model has been optimized for NVIDIA A100 and NVIDIA T4 GPUs, and is available at https://github.com/zhengyangwang/tensorflow-gpu-optimization. We investigate a class of $\mathcal{N}=2$ superconformal field theories in four dimensions, specifically within the Type IIB effective field theory framework, with non-trivial NS-NS fluxes. Our analysis focuses on the interplay between these fluxes and relevant $\theta$-terms in the effective field theory, with the aim of identifying symmetries that could potentially be broken in string theory. By extending the $\theta$-terms to include additional symmetries, we demonstrate the presence of additional relevant deformations, which could be related to the appearance of non-trivial B-field fluxes. These additional deformations correspond to deformed S-duality and the non-geometric $\tau$-shift symmetries, with the potential for them to be realized in six-dimensional superconformal field theories, leading to the breakdown of the duality between the NS-NS and R-R fluxes. This implies that an infinite number of $\theta$-terms could be added, each corresponding to a distinct, non-trivial B-field flux, with this phenomenon being a fundamental aspect of Type IIB string theory. This discovery has significant implications for the study of superconformal field theories in six dimensions, with potential connections to systems displaying non-trivial B-field fluxes and, in certain cases, extended EFTs that are distinguishable through global symmetries alone. Ultimately, this theory cannot be replicated through an analytical continuation of four-dimensional, $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal field theories in Type IIB, due to the presence of these additional, non-trivial deformations. As a result, one can construct a new class of six-dimensional, $\mathcal{N}=2$ superconformal field theories that exhibit a breakdown of the duality between the NS-NS and R-R fluxes, with this theory then being used to solve a previously unresolved issue in the Type IIB holographic duality, providing a new solution for an exact, non-trivial fixed point in the $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal field theory in six dimensions. This solution is found to be consistent with an existing, exactly solved three-dimensional, $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal field theory, with both theories being an instance of a universal symmetry-breaking scenario in Type IIB string theory. This universal symmetry-breaking scenario has far-reaching implications, with the potential for the breaking of any global symmetry present in Type IIB string theory

Our model builds upon the standard DenseUnet architecture and enhances two key components:
it modifies the contraction path to capture localized image features and introduces a
simple yet effective Dense Focus Attention mechanism in the expansion path, which is
subsequently applied to the contraction path.
By incorporating a pre-trained model, our DDAUnet also addresses the challenge of
esophageal tumor segmentation from CT scans, which is characterized by disordered
slice orders and varying tumor lengths.

This research focuses on nested Named Entity Recognition, where entities within other entities are annotated, but cannot assume independence. In contrast to other NLP tasks that isolate individual components for analysis, NER considers entities as interconnected parts of a whole. Based on this understanding, we propose treating entities in a nested context as a unified structure for comprehensive analysis. Within this framework, we suggest enhancing model performance by allowing models to access the context beyond a single entity at a time and incorporating the relationships between all entities in a single context. Our model, which embodies these principles, combines a bidirectional transformer for contextual understanding with a single-layer transformer that analyzes the entity structure as a whole. Our results show that this approach achieves top performance in the 2010 CONLL-NER shared task, surpassing existing state-of-the-art models by a significant margin without relying on sophisticated techniques like multi-task learning or the integration of external knowledge. Our analysis of nested entities reveals that only a small proportion hold other entities as their partial; the majority of the NER annotations in this category are incorrect, as do those of the 2012 CONLL-NER shared task. In addition to improving NER, our model excels in other structure-based tasks, such as dependency parsing and part-of-speech tagging, without being optimized for these tasks, indicating that it effectively captures fundamental language properties. In contrast to other high-performing models with complex architectures, our model is relatively simple and easy to train, making it a strong candidate for large-scale, multi-task learning in a variety of NLP applications. In addition to achieving top performance in NER, our model is also a fundamental building block for constructing more complex linguistic structures, as evidenced by its superior performance in other structure-based tasks like dependency parsing and part-of-speech tagging, even without being optimized for these tasks. Our analysis of nested entities reveals that only a small proportion hold other entities as their partial; the majority of the NER annotations in this category are incorrect, as do those of the 2012 CONLL-NER shared task. In addition to improving NER, our model excels in other structure-based tasks, such as dependency parsing and part-of-speech tagging and SEMEVAL 2007 Task 10, also known as "Insertion/Deletion" NER, which involves identifying newly created or removed entities from existing NER corpora. Our model's ability to analyze complex structures and capture fundamental language properties makes it a strong candidate for large-scale, multi-task learning in a variety of NLP applications

We provide a method to enumerate bitangents to a surface of degree four using a non-degenerate configuration of nine points. This approach is based on a connection between the problem and the study of tropical curves, along with their GRH-related asymptotic counts, as they pass from a genus of 8 to a genus of 1. Our proof of the rationality of the space of such curves, for any genus within this range, is a key component of our proof of the enumerative property of the tropical counting. This property enables us to derive the formulas found by Ionica and Leroy in the genus 1 case and generalizes them for any genus between 1 and 8. Our results also include an alternative proof of the 2^d property of the space of genus g tropical curves in the plane of degree d, as genus varies between 1 and (d-3). Lastly, we describe how to compute the number of bitangents in real space using a method we call real signed tallying, in contrast to the standard approach of using the Torelli theorem and Majcen's results. This enables us to verify the conjecture of Ionica and Leroy that this number is odd for any genus between 1 and 8. This method can likely be applied to a broader range of enumerative problems related to plane curves and might be useful in solving other conjectures related to such curves. It relies on a previously unknown family of genus-minimizing tropical curves and a previously unknown application of the A1-invariant property to define and compute local counts. This enables us to define and compute the real signed tally of such curves, assigning a value of either +1 or -1 to each curve based on a previously undefined but computable local real signed tally. This value depends on the orientation of the tropical map and, when summed over all possible configurations, yields the usual enumerative property. This value is either +1 or -1 for each possible genus between 1 and 8 and, interestingly, matches the number of bitangents to a surface of degree four for each of these genus values. This property makes it likely that this value will be +1 for any genus between 1 and 8 but, due to the highly non-trivial nature of these results, it cannot be formally proven by this method for any genus outside the scope of our computations. These results are based on a previously unknown application of the Gross-Zagier type formula and a previously undefined but computable local real signed tally

Human-generated descriptions are utilized to train and evaluate image description systems but rely heavily on automated methods. This study supplements existing datasets with human-provided descriptions, enabling evaluation and tuning of such systems. Two experiments were conducted to assess the performance of an automatic description system compared to human standards. Firstly, ranking automated descriptions against human references in ranking order revealed a significant gap in consistency. To address this, we collected additional data to focus on quality rather than order, resulting in improved but still noticeable discrepancies. These findings provide insight into the current limitations of automatic image description systems and suggest potential directions for enhancement. Moreover, we introduce the ViMPR dataset, a set of human-issued quality scores for descriptions, along with the description data collection called ViMPD, both available for community use. Systems tested in this study include Contrastive Learning-based Visual Description (CLVD) and BERT-based Visual Description (BVD). According to our results, there is room for improvement in generating accurate and consistent descriptions, with a particular shortcoming in the use of pre-trained models for both evaluation and training. Additionally, we observed a notable discrepancy between human-generated data used for training and validation sets, highlighting the value of diverse data sources. To build on these findings, future research could explore methods to directly train automatic description systems using minimal human input, in a data-efficient yet effective manner. Furthermore, we emphasize the significance of incorporating human standards in the development of visual understanding systems to ensure they align with human expectations and provide sound foundations for further exploration and innovation. In this research, we take an initial step in examining the performance of automatic description systems against human-generated data, with numerous avenues for exploration and discovery waiting to be uncovered. As such, we invite the community to engage with these findings, contribute to this research, and explore the emerging landscape of visual description in the presence of human standard information. Finally, we outline several path forward for future research in this area. Two specific research paths are currently being explored by our team. Firstly, we aim to investigate alternative methods for collecting high-quality human reference data, in order to further address the limitations uncovered in this research. Secondly, we are currently exploring the integration of visual description systems with other visual understanding systems, in order to establish a baseline for multimodal visual understanding. Additionally, we are open to receiving input and guidance from the community on this research. Anyone with research advice or guidance on this topic is welcome to contact us. System codes and data collections presented in this research are available at https://github.com/abhishekkr

Our research involves determining the fundamental crystal structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$ using a combination of first-principles simulations and Monte Carlo methods, starting from a hypothetical oxygen face-centered cubic configuration. We employed accurate first-principles calculations to analyze the Ta$_2$O$_5$ polymorphs, considering 13 possible structures derived from this starting point, and assessed their stability across high-pressure and high-temperature conditions. These simulations revealed that Ta$_2$O$_5$ forms an orthorhombic structure under normal pressure and room temperature, which contradicts the experimental findings reported in the Ta$_2$O$_5$ phase diagram, indicating a need for revision of this diagram. To resolve this discrepancy, we conducted Monte Carlo simulations to explore the Ta$_2$O$_5$ potential energy landscape at normal pressure and room temperature, resulting in a structure identical to the simulated and experimental orthorhombic structures obtained under higher pressure and temperature conditions respectively. Additionally, we identified a Ta$_2$O$_5$ metastable phase with a GdFeO$_3$-type structure, which has a high energy gap but remains stable under extreme conditions of high pressure and low temperature, and we provide a comparison with a recently reported Ta$_2$O$_5$ metastable phase, suggesting a possibility of its connection to the recently discovered Ta$_2$O$_5$ phase, known as $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$. Furthermore, we investigated the electronic and optical properties of both the fundamental and metastable Ta$_2$O$_5$ structures, and the results show that the energy gaps of these structures are in the range of 3 eV to 5 eV, and their refractive indices are similar to those reported for other oxide materials. The calculated absorption spectra of Ta$_2$O$_5$ also show a similarity to those of other oxide materials, and the results of our time-dependent density functional simulations indicate that Ta$_2$O$_5$ has a high absorption capacity in the ultraviolet range, and it starts absorbing in the visible range, and it exhibits a high reflectivity in the infrared range, and it has a high density of states at the Fermi level, and it exhibits superconducting behavior when doped with sulfur. Our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the Ta$_2$O$_5$ material, and it offers a solution to the discrepancy in the Ta$_2$O$_5$ phase diagram,

The spread of misinformation news across the United States has been analyzed using a complex network of geographic regions, built from a dataset of 150,000 Reddit news comments. Our research focuses on the large-scale arrangement of these areas and its impact on misinformation dissemination. We discovered a long-lasting pattern called the "BGA" (The Big Geographic Arrangement), present in both winter and summer, which consists of east coast and west coast regions that exchange misinformation at varying speeds. We found that this exchange accelerates the spread of misinformation in the summer by up to 20%. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the BGA is more pronounced when misinformation is shared between adjacent regions during the winter, and when it is shared within the same coast during the summer. Our results also reveal that the BGA is more evident for news propagated by social connections (friend-to-friend) in the winter, and for news propagated through online searches in the summer. We offer theoretical explanations suggesting that these patterns are caused by seasonal changes in population movements and temperature, seasonal fluctuations in online activity, and the timing of holidays. Our research provides valuable insights into the complex spread of misinformation across the United States, highlighting the significance of considering the underlying geographic structure and seasonal factors. Building on our findings, we offer a framework for studying information dissemination in other geographic networks. Our data and analysis methods can be applied to investigate information diffusion in social networks in various contexts. Our discoveries are relevant to the development of strategies for containing the spread of misinformation in online communities and could be adapted for use in other information diffusion applications. Our work on the BGA raises several research questions that could be explored through further analysis of online data, combined with field studies and experiments that examine information dissemination in the real world. Our results demonstrate the value of collaborative research between computer scientists and social scientists, with a focus on network analysis and data-driven approaches. Teaching robots through demonstration and feedback is crucial for their effective learning in complex tasks, but the process is often hindered due to the limited amount of training data available. One significant challenge is that robots struggle to accurately interpret the instructor's intended mappings between actions and consequences, which is a critical step in understanding the demonstrated task. In an attempt to address this issue, this research involves instructing humans to demonstrate various manipulations to a robot in a straightforward manner, with the goal of uncovering the underlying relationships between action sounds and action consequences. Twenty different manipulation tasks were carried out with this approach, resulting in a dataset of 1440 sound-consequence pairs that can be used by other researchers in their own studies. In addition, a statistical analysis of the data revealed that the sounds produced by the instructors are relatively consistent and are not significantly linked to the visual aspects of the manipulation. In contrast, the consequences of the manipulation have a more substantial impact on the sounds made during the task. In light of these findings, a basic model was developed that attempts to predict the consequences of a manipulation task based solely on the sounds made during the task, with positive outcomes. In a more advanced model, a significant increase in predictive accuracy was achieved by incorporating a more complex relationship between the sounds and the consequences, resulting in an ability to accurately map sounds to consequences and vice versa. This research provides valuable insights into the acoustic patterns of human instructors and the potential for a more detailed analysis of demonstration data, along with the development of more sophisticated learning algorithms that take into consideration the instructor's intended mappings between actions and consequences. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, with numerous applications where humans interact with computers via text or speech. Evaluating these systems is complex due to their natural language-based human-computer interface, which encompasses multiple aspects, including understanding, reasoning, and responsiveness. Current assessment methods are limited to specific criteria, such as system accuracy or user satisfaction, but a comprehensive evaluation framework is desperately needed to guide the development of next-generation conversational systems. To address this critical issue, our project involves creating an automated evaluation platform that can simulate human interactions with a system in various contexts and environments. We introduce an original task called Neural Machine Rendering (NMR), where a neural machine translation system is expected to generate target-language descriptions for novel source-language descriptions that were not seen during training. Current machine translation models are not designed to handle this task because they are typically trained on paired data and cannot effectively utilize unlabelled target-language text that is available in many real-world scenarios. In such cases, having access to a large translation archive that contains multiple target-language renderings for each source-language sentence can be beneficial. We investigate two variants of the NMR task: a simple one and a more complex one that is influenced by neural machine translation. We propose a method to adapt neural machine translation systems to render target-language descriptions and evaluate our approach on a large-scale NMR dataset that contains 20K pairs of source-target language sentences. Our results show that, even without any target-language data during training, a neural machine translation system can generate more accurate descriptions than a neural machine translation system that is trained on paired data. We also find that using a large translation archive that contains target-language sentences improves the performance of our system by 15% on the test set. In addition, we discover that our system that is trained on an archive performs 10% better than a system that is trained on paired data alone. We release our code and data at https://github.com/seyed-gh/Neural-Machine-Rendering. One of the key observations from our research is the potential to enhance machine translation systems using monolingual data in a cross-lingual framework. This idea can be applied to other machine learning tasks as well. One possible application of this idea is to improve machine translation systems in low-resource scenarios by leveraging data from more resourceful languages. Another possible application is to use this method for generating novel descriptions for novel situations. This is an area that calls for further research and we hope that our work will inspire other researchers to explore it. One possible direction for future research is to train a system that can effectively utilize both paired data and a translation archive. Hawking's 1974 proposal, modified conformal cyclic cosmology, sees the universe's evolution through periods of contraction and expansion. We've applied this model to explain Solar System irregularities and certain features in the Cosmic Microwave Background. Our research suggests that the Hawking proposal eliminates black hole formation during Big Bang cosmology, while conformal cyclic cosmology links black hole creation to universal contraction phases. We've identified four such instances: the early universe, the plasma era, the cosmic web era, and the present day. Each contraction phase resulted in black hole formation, which then evaporated as the universe expanded. We propose that these black holes gave off information used to map the universe, recorded in the CMB's multipole space. Our model predicts that the Hawking proposal and modified conformal cyclic cosmology will leave marks on the CMB sky. These signs include geometric patterns in temperature and polarization, which could be discovered by future satellite missions like CMB-S4. Our research also discovers connections between the CMB sky and cosmic web structures, which could provide evidence for modified conformal cyclic cosmology. This model also predicts the existence of primordial black holes in the Solar System, which could be confirmed through gravitational lensing or Gravitational Wave observations. Our findings also link the LHB and EHB populations to contraction phases, resulting in black hole formation and the creation of primordial black holes, which could be confirmed through the detection of small mass black holes in the Solar System. Our research offers multiple lines of evidence and prediction that could be tested and validated, which provide strong support for modified conformal cyclic cosmology. This model also resolves several long-standing cosmological issues, such as the dark matter and energy problems, the Big Bang's singularity issue, and the problem of black hole information paradox. Our research offers a complete and consistent framework that explains the universe's evolution and the creation of black holes and the CMB. This model also predicts that the observable universe is not the only universe, and that there are other universes with the same properties but in the process of contraction, which could be confirmed through the detection of multiverse gravitational lensing. Our research offers a robust and consistent framework for the study of cosmology, black holes, and the CMB, which could be used to validate or rule out modified conformal cyclic cosmology through future observations and experiments. By defining prototypes as representative points, prototype-based methods effectively minimize epistemic uncertainty through matching and prototyping. However, for categories with limited data, the prototypes themselves are uncertain, leading to poor performance even with large latent spaces. To address this issue, we propose a new framework that learns high-quality prototypes for each category even with only a few samples, without relying on extensive unlabeled data. Our framework, Prototype Refined Latent Learning (PRLL), first identifies a prototype for each category through a prototype-point matching process, then refines the prototype by maximizing the prototyping likelihood in the latent space. To overcome the few-sample challenge in each category, we develop a strategy that leverages data from related categories, allowing for the sharing of prototypes, and employ a method to select diverse prototypes across categories. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that PRLL achieves state-of-the-art performance in low-data learning across 20 categories in the mini-ImageNet, 5-shot and 1-shot settings, and also achieves comparable performance to methods without prototype uncertainty reduction in transfer learning and in data with no category labels. The code is available at https://github.com/zhengyangwang/PRLL. The models trained on mini-ImageNet also achieve top-1 rank in few-shot learning in the recent V-Curve Challenge, with a test accuracy of 83.4% on 1-shot 5-way and 84.5% on 5-shot 5-way in the recent V-Curve Challenge, and the details can be found at https://sites.google.com/view/vc-curve-challenge/leadersboard. A crucial step in ensuring MRI data quality is reliable is the validation of the MRI system. This paper takes a comprehensive approach to addressing this challenge by redefining the problem in the context of generalizing across multiple dimensions. We introduce a new framework that accounts for variations in imaging protocols, anatomical regions, and patient conditions to achieve generalized performance. Intel introduced Optane as a revolutionary nonvolatile memory technology which essentially serves as an intermediate layer between memory and storage. Unlike DRAM, Optane doesn't require power to retain data and has a much lower price point. It has the potential to significantly improve system performance as well as reduce power consumption and costs in various applications. This paper outlines the basic performance benchmarks for an Intel Optane DC Persistent Memory Module (ODC), which is an advanced type of nonvolatile memory. It provides results for four fundamental metrics: latency, bandwidth, write acceleration, and data survival. These findings can serve as reference points for evaluating the performance of ODC in more complex scenarios and systems. Across different use cases and protocols, ODC exhibits consistent latency below 60 ns and bandwidth above 96 GB/s. When coupled with DRAM, ODC delivers notable improvements in bandwidth and accelerates sequential write speeds by at least 5x. It also demonstrates exceptional data retention capabilities, surviving for extended periods without access without losing stored information, across power cycled environments and system-based workloads. Overall, the results indicate that ODC delivers on its promise of enhancing system performance, reducing storage-related bottlenecks, and mitigating storage-related power consumption and costs. Finally, we highlight potential areas for future research in evaluating and benchmarking nonvolatile memory systems and suggest a set of application-based performance metrics that could provide a more comprehensive understanding of system performance. These metrics include response time, throughput, energy consumption per transaction, system cost per transaction, and value per dollar of capacity. Ultimately, future generations of nonvolatile memory and storage systems will require a similar set of fundamental performance benchmarks that take into account both traditional performance metrics and application-based costs and requirements. If we establish these metrics early on, we will be able to design and develop more effective and efficient systems that meet the needs of modern computing workloads. If we delay this until later, we risk developing systems that excel in benchmarking tests but fall short in real-world scenarios due to an imbalance in performance, cost, and power consumption. As such, we recommend that researchers and industry leaders collaborate on finalizing these metrics and developing a comprehensive benchmarking framework that can be used across all types of nonvolatile memory and storage systems. If we take this approach, we can ensure that future generations of memory and storage systems provide the performance, efficiency, and value that modern computing workloads demand. Theories beyond the Standard Model, such as QCD at high temperatures and densities, or within composite Higgs models, often require a more fundamental level of description and typically predict the existence of extra baryons and mesons beyond the visible spectrum. A recent lattice QCD calculation has provided a precise threshold for baryon number violation at very high energies, which is directly related to the density of net baryons required for matter - matter equivalence in QCD. This density corresponds to an energy scale, typically in the range of 10-100 GeV, and serves as a key ingredient in predicting extra baryons and mesons in alternative theories that may relate this energy scale to the composite Higgs scale. In this study, lattice QCD's understanding of QCD's fundamental properties is used to make a series of general predictions regarding extra baryons and mesons, which can serve as a guiding framework for experimental searches in both fixed-target and collider experiments. For example, quark models that predict same-quark same-antiquark interactions will likely result in scalar meson loci at 1.2-1.3 GeV, whereas QCD's density for matter - matter equivalence will likely fall within the range of 10-50 GeV, a finding that significantly narrows the search window for experimenters. Additionally, QCD's chiral Lagrangian formulation will likely result in tetraquark meson loci at 3.5-4.0 GeV. It is also anticipated that baryon loci will likely emerge at 2.0-2.5 GeV, and hexaquark bound states, or dimeric baryons, will likely emerge at 2.5-3.0 GeV. These predictions provide a framework for exploring the fundamental properties of QCD and the potential for new physics beyond its reach. Experimental verification of these predictions will not only contribute to a deeper understanding of QCD's characteristics, but also provide insight into the underlying principles of physics that may relate this to the composite Higgs scale, even in the absence of direct evidence for new physics. Furthermore, this study highlights the value of combining lattice QCD with alternative theories through the density of net baryons, which can result in precise, experimentally verifiable predictions for extra baryons and mesons that may emerge in a variety of scenarios. As a result, this study offers a compelling justification for a thorough examination of the specified energy ranges in both fixed-target and collider

Our investigation combines two sources of data to resolve the cosmic distance ladder, by pairing Type Ia supernovae with weak lensing estimates of the Hubble constant. We utilize the Pantheon supernovae sample and the DESv5 weak lensing measurement of H0. Our key finding is that no specific cosmological model is required to reconcile these two values, as they become consistent when considering the scattering of H0 estimates from weak lensing analyses and the scatter of Type Ia supernovae supernovae absolute magnitudes. Approximately 21% of the discrepancy between H0 values is explained by the scatter of Type Ia supernovae, and approximately 79% is accounted for by the scattering of weak lensing estimates. These are lecture notes for a 6-hour mini-course on stochastic partial differential equations presented at the University of Oxford in April-May 2019. The aim of the course was to provide an in-depth exploration of the stochastic Navier-Stokes equations, beginning with the stochastic analysis foundations in Chapter 1. This chapter delves into the analysis of Hilbert-space-valued stochastic integrals and develops the tools necessary for studying SPDEs. Chapter 2 establishes the existence and uniqueness of solutions for the stochastic Navier-Stokes equations using the abstract approach of the monotone operator theory. This is accompanied by concrete results for the abstract formulation of the stochastic transport and reaction-diffusion equations. Chapter 3 focuses on obtaining almost sure existence and uniqueness of solution options for certain SPDEs, primarily facilitated by an innovative approach to establishing the boundedness of the stochastic integral in probability space. Chapter 4 is devoted to analyzing the stochastic Navier-Stokes equations in the whole domain using the abstract approach of the monotone operator theory, in addition to establishing almost sure uniqueness of solutions in this setting. Chapter 5 explores the analysis of the fractional stochastic transport equation and discusses further generalizations of this equation. Chapter 6 is an introduction to stochastic fluid dynamics, with an emphasis on determining observable quantities in the stochastic Navier-Stokes equations. Chapter 7 is an overview of research related to the stochastic transport equation, while Chapter 8 is devoted to the analysis of the stochastic heat equation with Hamiltonian flow, in addition to generalizations of the parabolic equation. Chapter 9 is an introduction to the study of stochastic PDEs with the mean-field interaction, with a focus on the stochastic Navier-Stokes equations in the whole domain using the abstract approach of the monotone operator theory. Appendix A provides an introduction to the basic concepts of the monotone operator theory, while Appendix B addresses frequently asked questions regarding stochastic analysis. These lecture notes are intended for graduate students and researchers in mathematics and related fields with an interest in analysis, PDEs, and stochastic analysis. They are designed to be accessible to those with a basic understanding of real and functional analysis. Due to the extensive nature of the material, it is recommended that readers refer to suitable reference texts, particularly for previously known results. Three-dimensional models of molecular gas in galaxies often rely on line emission data from various spectral lines to make predictions and constrain their parameters. Since the line emission is observed under different conditions in different positions, as the line of sight passes through different phases of the gas both within and outside the galaxy, a significant variation in line flux is observed. This thesis research aims to explore an alternative approach to gathering line emission data, as the current use of multiple lines for a thorough understanding of galaxies may not always be feasible with every observational data set. Specifically, it investigates whether a limited set of lines can be sufficient to account for the fluctuations in line emission as the line of sight passes through different gas phases, potentially reducing the number of lines required for such observations. To achieve this, a line selection method was developed in the course of this research using a randomised approach for least-squares deconvolution, and the results obtained were compared with a method that involves solving a linear system of equations with a sparse matrix. The new method demonstrated comparable or even better performance in terms of reducing the variance of line flux ratios when compared with the established approach, showcasing its effectiveness in reducing the number of lines required for such observations. Furthermore, the results obtained with this method suggest that even a small set of lines, such as 5-10 lines, can sufficiently capture the fluctuations in line emission as the line of sight passes through different gas phases. This research provides a line selection method that can be employed with any observational data set, and the results obtained with this method are presented for two well-studied galaxies, NGC 4555 and UGC 8833. Context plays a significant role in object detection, where objects within a scene are interconnected. While advances in deep learning have improved detector accuracy, there remains a perception that these models often struggle to account for contextual information when identifying prominent objects. To gauge the importance of context in this scenario, we conduct a comprehensive contextual benchmark, evaluating the performance of state-of-the-art object detectors in a diverse dataset that considers both individual objects and those within contextual frames. Our findings indicate that top-ranking detectors excel at identifying isolated objects but require further improvement at capturing contextual information. To further push the boundaries of excellence in object detection, we emphasize the significance of incorporating contextual data into training and challenging top performers with a broader understanding of scene composition. Our dataset and assessment are significant contributions to the field, providing a standardized framework for assessing context-aware object detection and paving the way for contextual learning strategies. Moreover, we introduce Context-Agnostic and Context-Sensitive metrics to gauge a detector's performance in isolation and when considering context, respectively. Our evaluation of context-aware learning methods indicates that incorporating context does indeed enhance the retrieval of context-sensitive information, resulting in improved scores on our benchmark. Ultimately, our work underscores the importance of context in object detection, along with the necessity for a broader understanding of scene composition that goes beyond individual objects. To this end, we emphasize the significance of incorporating contextual data into training and challenge the research community to develop learning strategies that prioritize context-sensitive information. Using effective field theory for quasi-real photons and considering the connection between charged and neutral currents, we have conducted a comprehensive analysis of double longitudinal spin SIDIS processes for leptons. Specifically, we have examined the $\cos\phi_n$ dependence in hadron pair production, even in cases where the final state contains only one hadron. In our research, we have identified the key contributions from excess quark and diquark correlative twist-3 charm structure functions, and have demonstrated that these terms yield significant $\cos\phi_n$ oscillation patterns in various kinematical regions. Our study reveals that the oscillation patterns in dihadron production are more pronounced when compared to single hadron production, and that the associated amplitude ratios exhibit notable $\cos\phi_n$ variations, which could be experimentally verified through a detailed $\cos\phi_n$ analysis of measured SIDIS data with double longitudinal spin, particularly for large $x_B$ and $x_F$ conditions. These findings have important implications for our understanding of the complex spin structure of the nucleon and the role of quark and diquark spin interactions in SIDIS processes at various twist levels. Moreover, our theoretical framework provides a clear path for extracting information on the nucleon's spin-dependent structure functions, specifically the diquark spin contributions in various quark flavors, through a comprehensive analysis of SIDIS data with double longitudinal spin, combined with lattice QCD calculations and quark model constraints, which will be crucial for further investigations into the nucleon's spin-dependent structure. This framework significantly expands upon the limited cases previously considered by Fock. Using our method, we demonstrate that the famous Hawking-Bekenstein formula, relating an object's surface gravity to its thermal energy, remains consistently valid even as the object undergoes rescaling and shifting, encompassing both gravitational and non-gravitational systems. Our method also enables us to derive new solutions for non-minimally coupled scalar fields within both Einstein and Jordan frames, showing that these solutions are equivalent and can be mapped onto each other. Notably, we derive a simple, analytical solution for a complex, nonlinear partial differential equation governing non-minimally coupled quintessence fields in both cosmological and de Sitter universes. Our method employs a novel change of variables, inspired by a combination of Fock's transformation and a coordinate transformation initially proposed by Lema\^itre, followed by a change of variables that can be viewed as a form of Legendre transformation. This new framework for transforming solutions, along with discussions of related mathematical concepts, is presented in an appendix. This framework is comprised of two components: a Wikipedia diagram embedding method and an entity suggestion engine. The embedding approach generates vector representations for Wikipedia sections and layers, allowing us to capture their semantic relationships. The suggestion engine builds upon these embeddings to recommend entities to users based on their specified criteria within the Yahoo! Knowledge Network. It employs an innovative strategy to combine semantically related entities from Wikipedia layers, thereby expanding the set of suggested entities. The effectiveness of this framework is demonstrated through an entity suggestion interface, showcasing the effectiveness of our approach in identifying relevant entities for users. Notably, it outperforms a baseline approach that uses in-network suggestions by an average of one-fold, or 25%, more relevant suggestions. The Ideal Kidney Exchange (ICE) algorithm is a highly respected method for solving multiple kidney exchanges. It has the advantage of being easy to implement and highly effective in matching donors and recipients from different chains. However, one major limitation of ICE is its requirement that incoming kidney donations be perfectly compatible with existing chains, which isn't always the case in real-world scenarios. In this study, we introduce two new algorithms that can handle incompatible kidney exchanges while still achieving optimal results. In some instances, these algorithms can even accept incompatible exchanges even when the ICE algorithm cannot, which we refer to as "ideal acceptance" or "IA" property. We also establish strict guidelines to determine whether a given exchange is acceptable under the new algorithms. We have discovered explicit connections between two neural network functions, 
which guarantees their equal output when the input is the same. In this report, 
we prove that this equality is automatically maintained even if the networks 
are combined implicitly, as long as their internal workings remain unchanged. 
We used this finding to speed up significantly the search for explicit connections 
between two pre-trained neural networks, by first verifying if their implicit 
connections meet the criteria, as stated in Proposition 1, as opposed to 
systematically scanning all possible combinations. We were able to confirm the 
validity of several previously unverified claims regarding Proposition 1, as well 
as derived additional useful implications from it. We also introduced a new 
corollary, which addresses the scenario in which one of the neural networks is an 
identity mapper. We conducted an exhaustive analysis of implicit connections 
between two neural networks that are trained in parallel, as part of our experiments 
on the minimal footprint of two-stream methods. The results of our search for 
implicit connections between two pre-trained neural networks are also presented, 
with some striking discoveries made along the way. In particular, we found an 
implicit connection between two ResNets, which were trained in parallel for 
action-recognition, comprising over 1 million parameters. The associated code 
and model files are available at: https://github.com/shervin-ahmadi/implicit-connections. 
The findings presented in this report have been added as new sections to the appendix 
of our earlier paper, titled "Low-Rank Connections: A General Framework for Two-Stream 
Methods", which can be accessed at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.07843v2. Moreover, we 
have derived additional supporting evidence for our proposed framework, as well 
as identified potential applications for implicit connections in transfer learning. 
In light of these discoveries, we have further solidified our initial hypothesis, 
which can be found in Section 2 of our earlier paper, as follows: all low-rank explicit

Recent studies utilizing neural networks for sentiment analysis have shown impressive results but often rely on pre-trained models that can be task-agnostic. It has been commonly assumed that these models effectively capture the underlying semantics of a dataset by simply learning its patterns. However, our analysis reveals that word representations within these models can be misleading, potentially leading to circular reasoning. We extracted the word embeddings of 125 most frequently used words from the Loughran-McDonald financial dataset and found their polarities to be inconsistent with actual dataset values. Moreover, many words with negative and positive connotations were found to be intermingled, contradicting our everyday language understanding. To demonstrate the limitations of these models, we conducted a simple experiment where we observed that neural networks trained on only word co-occurrences learned more accurate polarities of words than models trained on the Loughran-McDonald dataset itself. Our research raises the question of whether the knowledge captured in word representations is sufficient to tackle the original task it was derived from. In an effort to address this concern, we proposed a novel evaluation metric called the Word Comprehension Score that assesses the extent to which word representations align with the underlying semantics of a dataset. We applied this metric to the Loughran-McDonald dataset and obtained the WCS scores for multiple neural network-based word representation models, revealing that none of them achieved a score greater than 0.5, indicating a clear need for models that can effectively comprehend the underlying polarities within a dataset by capturing its semantics through word co-occurrences rather than relying on pattern-based learning. Our analysis suggests that word representations derived from models trained on multiple tasks may not be reliable and, as such, we propose the introduction of a word comprehension task that learns word representations from a given corpus with the explicit goal of comprehending the underlying semantics within that same corpus. We also outline several challenging tasks derived from the Loughran-McDonald dataset that can serve as a starting point for researchers to explore novel neural network-based word representation models that prioritize comprehension over mere pattern recognition. Our analysis and the proposed evaluation metric framework have been made available as an open-source repository for the benefit of the research community. In addition, we have explored the application of our proposed evaluation framework to other semantic analysis datasets and offer our results within the supplementary materials accompanying this paper. Furthermore, we have investigated the role of pre-training in word representation models and offer our findings within the accompanying supplementary materials. Revisiting experience replay in interactive systems through optimal transference is a promising approach to supporting reinforcement learning methods. By assuming that the cost function remains stationary within a certain interval, a key issue arises from the varying costs being incurred by different episodes. This problem is exacerbated when using a maximum storage constraint in an replay buffer, as it divides the data into non-overlapping segments, further increasing the differences between them. This research proposes an innovative framework that addresses these challenges by reducing data variance in experience replay. Initially, a mathematical model is established to describe the optimal transference and a measure of variance is defined. Then, an optimization problem is formulated to minimize this variance subject to certain constraints. Finally, the efficacy of this framework is validated through two simulated scenarios of urban cargo delivery. The results show that it is possible to reduce variance by at least 50% across both scenarios, as shown in Figure 1. In addition, combining this framework with a variant of the policy gradient method yields a more efficient and 3 times faster solution than baseline in Scenario 2. In contrast to other variance-reducing methods, our approach requires no explicit modeling of system dynamics. The code for this research can be found at https://github.com/argexlab/VarREDER. The theoretical analysis and the results indicate that this framework is capable of decreasing variance by at least a 50% reduction in experience replay, leading to more efficient reinforcement learning. This implies that it is feasible to obtain high-performance solutions in reinforcement learning by scaling this framework to larger, more complex settings. This innovative framework is built on Python and combines its versatility with two advanced algebraic development tools: sympy for symbolic manipulation and automatic generation of efficient numerical codes, and libcommute, a C++-based library that utilizes optimized templates to create highly customized and performance-driven diagonalization routines. MultiTalk is a complex conversation framework with extensive branching, addressing an significant shortcoming of linear dialogue systems. These systems suffer from a critical flaw: they fail to effectively handle crucial elements of real conversations, namely, the frequent reevaluation and revision of previously expressed opinions. In conversations, individuals frequently adjust their stance in response to new information, new questions, or contrasting viewpoints from others. This common phenomenon is known as "grasp-and-revise," a key aspect of our analysis. We've investigated this element through a combined crowd and professional labeling process, defining specific markers for detecting the "grasp-and-revise" feature in dialogues. These markers, along with additional indicators for other crucial aspects of conversations, such as "coherence" and "consistency," are used to guide our dialogue system through careful selection from a vast menu of responses, thus ensuring it not only understands the "grasp-and-revise" feature but also prioritizes coherent and consistent conversations. Our evaluation of an 800k data set for conversational evaluation, along with human assessments, has confirmed the superiority of our models over linear models with similar parameters. One of the notable differences is that one of our model has achieved 34% flat rate for reevaluating previously expressed opinions in conversations, a skill that linear models failed to acquire even with significantly larger models. We introduce a novel computational approach that swiftly completes full N-body simulations for a variety of altered gravity theories. This method involves a simple, general potential function that represents a vast family of non-Newtonian gravitational forces, which can be refined to accommodate specific theories. Our model makes use of a conformal framework that allows for the incorporation of dark matter as a scalar field attached to galaxies, as well as a scenario in which dark matter exists only within these objects. By linking the behavior of dark matter in an N-body simulation, we demonstrate the ability to simulate any collisionless gravity simulation with a corresponding number of dark matter particles, without the need for costly and intricate simulations of galaxy interactions. This technique also facilitates the exploration of how initial conditions influence the outcome of such simulations, including scenarios where dark matter is limited to forming galaxies through collapse, rather than participating in N-body simulations. This approach is particularly useful for large N-body simulations, for which our potential function simulation runs on a standard desktop computer in a matter of hours, as opposed to the usual months or even years required. We present two types of collisionless simulations: one resembling the distribution of galaxy rotations and a scenario in which galaxy luminosity follows the $L$-$v$ relation. We also make use of our new approach to investigate how collisionless gravity simulations behave in the presence of modified gravitational force laws, specifically focusing on the role of dark matter in such simulations. MediaWiki-based websites like Wikipedia have long been regarded as outstanding examples of effective knowledge production, achieved through a collaborative effort of numerous contributors. By leveraging the capabilities of a fully-fledged collaborative content management system, such platforms have successfully addressed fundamental challenges associated with cooperative research, notably ensuring the consistency of research data across pages and resolving inconsistencies in existing findings. These issues have sparked the development of advanced tools and methods tailored to their specific research needs, surpassing the innovative solutions available within the broader Wikipedia community. Inspired by the success of Wikipedia and the expertise of its users, our project WorkingWiki seeks to create a versatile research platform built on top of a MediaWiki framework. By integrating a detailed data structure and incorporating custom features, WorkingWiki aims to provide a robust infrastructure for addressing the intricacies of cooperative research, thereby serving as a model for adapting MediaWiki in a broader academic context. Specifically, our prototype has addressed two critical problems common to cooperative research: the management of inconsistent data (already successfully tackled by Wikipedia's community) and the systematic exploration of knowledge. By offering a comprehensive data structure based on a structured ontology, WorkingWiki allows each contributor to create an up-to-date overview of their personal research landscape. This data structure, built from an extension of the Category and WikiData technologies, has been designed with two key components: an abstract representation of entities and their relationships, along with a hierarchical classification system. By integrating a tour of research feature, WorkingWiki has found a suitable solution for the exploration of knowledge, providing an engaging user experience through an interactive tour generator, crafted from a combination of Category and WikiData features. By showcasing its data structure and tour generator in an immersive way, the WorkingWiki system has demonstrated its potential to revolutionize the way cooperative research is conducted, setting a valuable precedent for the broader Wikipedia community. By highlighting the potential of MediaWiki-based platforms as cooperative research tools, our project has sparked the development of advanced tools and methods that not only excel over general Wikipedia community solutions but also address fundamental issues associated with cooperative research, ensuring the consistency of research data across pages and resolving inconsistencies in existing findings. By successfully tackling these issues, WorkingWiki has proven that MediaWiki-based websites like Wikipedia are not just outstanding examples of effective knowledge production, achieved through a collaborative effort of numerous contributors, but also excellent examples of how to produce high-quality data in a collaborative setting. By combining the expertise of Wikipedia users with the success of Wikipedia, our project WorkingWiki has shown that MediaWiki-based platforms are not just suitable for producing high-quality data in a collaborative setting

We've developed an advanced method for predicting active flames within turbulent jet fires. This method involves active sensing technology and is based on the linearized time-dependent and space-dependent combustion model. By applying a new solution technique for the time-dependent combustion equation, we've successfully demonstrated the method's applicability to modeling reaction dynamics in turbulent jet fires. This achievement is particularly notable because it allows the reaction dynamics to vary freely over time, unlike previous methods which relied on steady-state analysis. This breakthrough has significant implications for our understanding of combustion phenomena, especially in situations where acoustic vibrations significantly impact the flame's behavior, such as in large-scale industrial processes like those in oil refineries and chemical processing facilities. To validate our new method, we conducted a detailed analysis of a specific experimental study in which a turbulent jet fire was stimulated by acoustic vibrations, and the results showed a high degree of accuracy with the observed data, including the production of sound waves at frequencies of 20 Hz and Schlieren pattern changes every 0.13 seconds. Notably, the method accurately predicted key factors influencing combustion, including Kelvin-Helmholtz instability at the fire's surface, the formation of vortex rings, and the production of sound waves due to the collapse of these rings. Building upon this success, we explored the method's potential for modeling other combustion systems that involve interacting flame structures and sound waves, such as in pool fires, and demonstrated its applicability by applying the method to a related problem in this context. This involved analyzing the effects of acoustic vibrations on the combustion process and predicting key phenomena, including the generation of sound waves, Schlieren pattern changes, and the production of vortex rings and breakdowns. This has shown that the new method can provide valuable insights and predictive capabilities for a broader range of active combustion systems.
