A specific lattice computation is outlined for a particular correlator ratio that leads to the photon amplitude of $\eta_c$, and we discuss the expected sensitivity of this decay rate on the lattice cut-off based on lattice data for quark masses ranging from the mass of mass of mass $m_{s}$ to twice $m_{u/d}$. A thorough explanation is provided for our choice of correlation function over the widely used one for this calculation, citing the significant impact of operator mixing on photon amplitudes in $\eta_c$ decay, which necessitates a more intricate set of sum rules that cannot be fulfilled with current lattice ensembles due to limitations on quark mass reach. Nonetheless, we remain optimistic that our approach will pave the way for a lattice determination of the $J/\psi$ to two photons decay width, a crucial benchmark for non-perturbative tests of QCD, despite the significant hurdles associated with the $J/\psi$ decay on the lattice. A notable issue that arises when attempting to directly relate lattice data for the decay width to the continuum value is also addressed in the paper. A numerical estimate for the continuum decay width of $\eta_c$ to two photons, derived from a lattice computation using large momentum transfers for quark and $Nf=2$ configurations at three different quark masses spanning the range from $m_s$ to $2m_u$, yields $\eta_c\rightarrow 2\gamma$ width values of approximately $5.37\pm0.84 keV$. A detailed examination of system effects, lattice cut-off, and quark mass on this outcome is presented in the study. A notable observation made in the study is the significant discrepancy between lattice-determined values for the photon amplitude of $\eta_c$ and those obtained through perturbative calculations in NLO at small quark masses, amounting to a $1.5\sigma$ deviation, which could be an early indication of the non-perturbative nature of mass dependence in this decay. A major obstacle in studying correlated systems using neural network models is the "Hubbard Sign Problem." It prevents the direct exploration of system dynamics by causing the neural network's weight constraints to be violated. We address this challenge through the use of complex-valued neural networks without Hubbard signs, thus separating system dynamics into two less onerous sign problems. By applying a hybrid representation and incorporating imaginary-time and worldline aspects into the neural network, we circumvented the sign problem without the need for artificial barriers in the network, thus achieving a more natural and efficient representation of system dynamics. Our method demonstrates its effectiveness in accurately modeling the half-filled 1D Hubbard model, even in regimes plagued by sign problems, using only moderate sizes of neural networks, and shows potential for broad application to other complex-valued problems. Despite the absence of artificial constraints, the costs associated with training these complex neural networks are comparable to their real-valued counterparts, mainly due to the efficient convergence facilitated by our hybrid representation, which combines imaginary-time and worldline aspects, resulting in a well-balanced loss landscape that facilitates training. By leveraging this method, we were able to obtain results for the half-filled 1D Hubbard model that agree with existing data for cases that did not have sign problems, but also produced novel findings for instances traditionally considered intractable. For example, our method finds that in the mid-range interaction regime for an 18-site chain, the neural network represents a Néel state, characterized by antiferromagnetic long-range order and a unique energy landscape that matches that of the exact theory, although this result may change for larger chains as indicated by our findings on spin correlations in 1D Hubbard models, which show an abrupt yet order-parameter-based continuous transition from a Néel to a spin-density wave state as interaction increases due to competing ferromagnetic long-range order induced by mid-range correlations. Furthermore, our method discovers that in higher-site chains, protracted regions of intermediate interaction still exhibit Néel order, albeit at very low temperatures as shown by our method's data for nematic order parameters in one-dimensional Hubbard models, which reveals that in intermediate-sized chains, there are short ranges of strong interaction where neutral particles develop nematic order, order that nematic is Néel-order-parameter-based, and that this order types switch system size. We investigate topological entropy and factor complexity in non-periodic shifts generated by finite sets of words, exploring their behavior under specific transformations. Given an infinite sequence e_0, e_1,... over alphabet A, we define a mapping φ that produces a new sequence over an expanded alphabet A ∪ {e∞}. We demonstrate that topological entropy and factor complexity may not be comparability preserved under φ, even when φ results in sequences from which periodic subsequences have been removed. Building upon previous work, we also examine similar responses to shifts in free groups, specifically examining the effects of altering basis dimensions. Our results enable construction of topological entropy and factor complexity pairs that solve problems established by Makar-Lindley and Solomay, and we solve an additional problem proposed by Nasu. Our findings also provide solutions to three new problems presented by the authors. Our research primarily focuses on one-dimensional shifts and free groups, although some results for higher-dimensional shifts are also provided. Our results largely answer questions previously raised by other researchers, and in some cases, results for some parameters are compared against related, previously known data. Our results can be summarized as follows: (1) We solve problem P1 by creating a 2-dimensional shift with topological entropy 0.5 and factor complexity 2^32768 at any free group basis dimension n ≥ 1. (2) We solve problem P2 by creating a 2-dimensional shift with topological entropy almost equal to 0.5 and factor complexity almost equal to 2^2 \* 3^3 \* 5^5 at any free group basis dimension n ≥ 1. (3) We solve problem P3 by creating a 2-dimensional shift with topological entropy almost equal to 0.5 and factor complexity 2^2 \* 3^3 \* 5^5 at any free group basis dimension n ≥ 1. (4) We solve problem P4 by creating a 2-dimensional shift with topological entropy almost equal to 0.5 and factor complexity 2^65536 at free group basis dimension n = 2. (5) We solve problem P5 by creating a 2-dimensional shift with topological entropy almost equal to 0.5 and factor complexity 2^(1+1.9^p) at free group basis dimension n = p. (6) We solve problem P6 by creating a 2-dimensional shift with topological entropy almost equal to 0.5

When a model is tasked with multiple related problems, it's logical to assume that learning several tasks simultaneously would be beneficial. However, in many real-world scenarios, models are often forced to generalize across new, unseen tasks with minimal or no supervision. This challenge is particularly pronounced in scenarios where models are expected to generalize across diverse task conditions - something that current methods are not well-equipped to handle in an unsupervised setting. In such situations, models may leverage their existing knowledge to some extent, but their performance still tends to suffer significantly when compared to supervised learning. This paper introduces a groundbreaking, unsupervised framework called Cross-Task Generalization through Retrieval (CTG-R) that enables models to generalize across unrelated task conditions with no supervision. By assuming access to a diverse dataset that contains samples from various tasks, the model can learn to recognize and make the most of relationships between data points that are implicit at a task level. To achieve this, we've developed a novel method that uses a memory bank to represent each task's unique distribution and retrieve relevant examples that are statistically similar to the model's current performance. This allows the model to learn from a mix of high-confidence correct classifications and challenging, hard-negative examples from the broader dataset. Through extensive experiments on the Cross-AutoFill benchmark, our method has demonstrated the ability to generalize across 21 unrelated tasks with only 1,000 unlabeled examples, outperforming the original performance by a significant 25%. Moreover, our method has shown a 10% improvement when compared to supervised learning on each individual task. This is in addition to a 50% reduction in the number of task-specific examples required, along with the ability to generalize across task conditions with only 10% of the required data in settings with unlimited data, underscoring the framework's effectiveness. Our code has been made available at https://github.com/strmlab/ctg-r. Leveraging our method's capabilities, we've also made several new benchmarking challenges and achieved notable breakthroughs in three areas: generalizing across different dataset conditions (-Shapenet-CAD, Cross-Split Learning, and generalizing across natural language processing tasks at different scale levels). Our research offers a pioneering solution to the cross-task generalization challenge and has far-reaching implications for the broader machine learning community. In particular, our method can facilitate the transfer of knowledge between machine learning researchers from diverse backgrounds, along with breaking down barriers that exist when experts encounter novel task conditions with little or no supervision. The gaming industry is gaining momentum and its numerous stakeholders are in need of systematic approaches to develop and operate high-quality, engaging, and revenue-generating games. This research provides an in-depth examination of requirements engineering methodologies in the gaming sector by offering a thorough evaluation of existing research, a categorical framework for reference purposes, and a detailed analysis of strengths and weaknesses of various methods. Our study is divided into three sections to cater to three primary types of stakeholders in the gaming industry: developers can benefit from practical guidance on requirements engineering, research community members will appreciate theoretical contributions, and business leaders will receive valuable insights to support their strategic decisions. Our comprehensive review of requirements engineering in the gaming sector is now freely accessible on a digital platform, enabling continuous updates and expansions of our research. At its core, our study serves as a valuable resource for all gaming industry stakeholders seeking reliable information on requirements engineering and ways to enhance their products and services. This research has been presented at the 2021 Australasian Research in Engineering, Mathematics and Applied Science PhD Conference, where it received the Best Presentation Award in the Software category. The advancement of adversarial machine learning techniques forces us to reconsider the safety of machine learning (ML) with profound concern. While significant research has focused on enhancing the robustness of ML models, the impact of hyperparameters on their security has remained largely unexplored. In our work, we identified a crucial aspect of differential privacy that is influenced by hyperparameters - differential utility. Based on extensive experiments, we established general guidelines for adjusting hyperparameters to balance privacy guarantees with desirable performance. These findings served as validation for our proposed framework, which prioritizes the efficient tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal differential utility under constraints of privacy and performance. As a case study, we selected Residual Neural Networks (RNNs) for image classification and demonstrated that our framework delivers results comparable to those obtained through exhaustive hyperparameter tuning, while requiring significantly less computational resources. The benefits of our approach are illustrated through the RNN example, where we provide a set of optimized hyperparameters for consideration by other researchers. In support of our methodology, we have made our experiments reproducible by openly sharing all hyperparameter tuning configurations through a dedicated repository. Our work provides a foundation for the development of advanced techniques for hyperparameter tuning in differential private machine learning. In particular, we invite future researchers to explore the application of our findings to a broader spectrum of ML models and to consider the potential integration of our framework with optimisation methods that promote high-quality solutions. Through the enhancement of hyperparameter tuning performance, it is our expectation that the field of differential private machine learning will experience a notable boost in interest and growth. Ultimately, our work is an effort to create a more secure AI ecosystem by laying the groundwork for the development of sophisticated machine learning systems that balance performance with robust privacy guarantees. In line with this vision, we have made the RNN experiment dataset freely available for exploration in an interactive environment powered by Apache Spark. This joint effort aims to facilitate collaboration between the machine learning and security communities, with a view to fostering a culture of security awareness within the ML community and to encouraging the design of more secure machine learning models that provide a reliable foundation for the development of a broader range of secure applications. In this context, we have released the RNN experiment dataset under an open-source licence that accommodates both academic and industrial contributors. The Euclid satellite, set to launch in 2022, will significantly impact cosmic void observations with its visible and near-infrared spectrophotometer. To assess void properties, such as the Ly-alpha forest, it relies on its NISP device's near-infrared flux measurements. The rapid dissemination of digital rumors poses a threat to public health, social stability, and national security. Understanding the underlying mechanisms and consequences of the spread of digital rumors, especially during crises like the COVID-19 pandemic, is crucial. This paper provides an in-depth analysis of Chinese-language social media posts from the early outbreak to peak pandemic periods. Our results show to be true the theory that massive, sudden increases in rumors can be attributed to certain key events, and that certain types of users, such as young, highly active individuals with a history of contributing to online communities, tend to produce and disseminate rumors at high rates. Our research also reveals that certain online platforms, such as Weibo with a large number of followers, can facilitate the spread of rumors through their existing users, and that certain topics, such as health-related information, are easily misinterpreted and become susceptible to being turned into rumors. Our study found evidence supporting the idea that online counter-measures can be effective in reducing the spread of rumors, and that consequences of believing in these rumors can be quite severe, leading some individuals to correct their predecessors who had spread rumors, and that certain types of users, such as those with a history of online disputes, are more prone to engaging in online disputes triggered by believing in these rumors. Our study found that online counter-measures can be less efficient than the spread of rumors, and that the impact of these rumors can persist over time, with some individuals continuing to seek offline medical attention even after the pandemic peak. Our study provides actionable recommendations to government agencies, online platforms, and health organizations to combat the spread of digital rumors during public health emergencies. Our research is the first of its kind to examine the dissemination and consequences of the spread of digital rumors in China during the COVID-19 pandemic outbreak. Our study is unique in its use of a large-scale, high-frequency dataset from multiple online platforms, and our research is the first to analyze the effectiveness of online counter-measures, the impact of offline consequences, and the evaluation of the impact of the spread of these rumors over time. Our research is the first to propose a multi-dimensional, multi-stage model that captures the spread of these rumors, and our study is the first to design and execute a large-scale, high-frequency experiment to collect data from multiple online platforms. Furthermore, this study discerns between irremovable and removable factors influencing this vulnerability, with the latter amenable to optimization via meta-optimization, which raises the possibility of devising a general framework for identifying deep learning models that are insensitive to loss function alterations in future work. A key finding is that a non-vanishing Pauli susceptibility exists when the GL free energy is minimized, enabling us to compute this susceptibility in an orbitally limited fashion. When the nematic order is absent, this reduces to a standard expression from BCS theory. This, in turn, creates opportunities for experimental identification of nematic superconductors through magnetic field-dependent specific heat studies. One of the main challenges in robotics research is the limited amount and quality of feedback provided by supervisors, which typically falls into two categories: corrective and evaluative. Evaluative feedback indicates whether a task is successful or not or assigns a score to the achieved performance. In contrast, corrective feedback suggests changes to the actions performed by the agent. Despite the significance of these types of feedback, there is a lack of systematic methods for learning from them in robotics, likely due to their diverse nature and the difficulty of modeling the relationship between actions and outcomes. This study introduces a new framework called DFCF, which learns from both constructive and destructive forms of feedback in a theoretical framework, and demonstrates its practical applications through four diverse experiments, involving a simulated robot, a 3D simulation, a real-life household robot, and a game, all of which use the same set of algorithms to achieve high performance on complex tasks. These experiments, in turn, reveal valuable insights on how the DFCF framework can be optimized, such as the importance of selecting suitable tasks for learning and the effect of different forms of constructive feedback on learning rates. Continuous phase modulation detection techniques were initially designed to eliminate the effects of carrier recovery, pulse clock recovery, and threshold adaptation while maintaining high data rates. This tradition dates back to the 1970s when high-performance coherent detection was not yet developed. This article examines six classic single-sideband CPM constellations and compares their receiver system performance under both coherent and non-coherent detection methods, showcasing the performance gains achievable by non-coherent detection at the expense of increased symbol timing tolerance. A theoretical 8-PSK/2^3 CPM analysis indicates that sideband selection has no impact on delay tolerance and demonstrates the optimal selection for maximum tolerance in higher-order CPM formats. A practical 8-PSK/2^3 CPM prototype was implemented and tested, verifying the predicted increase in symbol timing tolerance from 0.5 to 1.5 T_s, resulting in a 6-dB receiver system performance loss for a 10% bit error rate. This article also explores alternative CPM designs featuring enhanced delay tolerance and presents several examples with increased tolerance in the osmosis zone, defined as the symbol duration to 3T_s. These designs exhibit only a 4-dB system performance loss compared to their coherent detection counterparts, representing a considerable delay-tolerance vs. loss-of-signal-strength trade-off. Leveraging this delay-tolerance osmosis, this article proposes several delay-tolerant differential detection techniques for carrier recovery and pulse clock recovery that are uncomplicated, devoid of threshold adaptation, and compatible with high-data-rate transmission systems. These techniques are applicable not only to CPM but also to other continuous-phase modulation techniques and are primed for integration with advanced multi-carrier transmission systems. This research is a culmination of the investigators' earlier contributions to delay-tolerant differential detection techniques and constitutes a significant expansion of their earlier findings. Rain significantly hampers optical flow computation and subsequent video restoration tasks. Common pre-processing methods for video restoration, such as deraining, typically rely on distinct approaches than optical flow estimation and often ignore the underlying connections between rain formation and elimination. These disconnections can result in deraining methods that either introduce artificial data or fail to consider preservation of physical quantities, namely light flux, which is crucial for both rain formation and elimination tasks. These issues are addressed in this paper by introducing a novel rain formation model based on optical flow, which is part of a comprehensive framework that combines rain elimination with light flux preservation. This framework, through rain elimination using disentangled transformation, facilitates both rain-free image creation and video restoration. Experiments conducted on two challenging rain elimination datasets demonstrate the proposed model's superiority over benchmark methods, and the resulting video is restored through the flow computed from the disentangled image transformation. Notably, the proposed rain formation model is shown to accurately simulate real-world rain by accounting for 95% of flow divergence in synthetic flow datasets, which is substantially higher than the 45% achieved by the state-of-the-art rain model, MRF. Systematic analysis of flow divergence components highlights an unseen rain elimination pathway and highlights potential research directions in both rain and flow communities. Code is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/Closing-the-Circuit.

Reward learning with little to no explicit feedback is a leading issue in unsupervised learning for Sequence Video Games. Human evaluators are overwhelmed by the required comparison ratings of action sequences, limiting the effectiveness of their input due to their extensive nature. To address this challenge, we introduce an innovative method called Visually Supported Cluster Ranking, which boosts the impact of human evaluators in the learning process by at least 5 times. Unlike traditional methods, our approach uses cluster rankings instead of individual action sequence ratings, taking advantage of human expertise in categorizing action sequences into relative order based on performance. We first transform action sequences into a more interpretable visual representation using action embeddings, and then cluster them according to their performance by incorporating self-supervised temporal action embeddings. A Streched Grid Search algorithm efficiently identifies near-optimal action sequences within each performance cluster by taking advantage of the human-provided cluster rankings. As a result, our approach achieves superior performance to state-of-the-art methods in three diverse sequence video games with significant human involvement, often outperforming them by two to five times. Human experts compare action sequences in a learning process that does not rely on feedback. These comparisons are in the form of ranking action sequences in a particular order, rather than comparing individual sequences. This form of comparison provides more information than comparing individual sequences, allowing for a more effective use of the provided information. As a result, the learning process is more efficient, due to the use of a more informative comparison method.

These techniques typically involve calculating the covariance matrix, which can be challenging to estimate for a large number of assets. A renowned method called the Maximum Diversity Portfolio has the advantage of bypassing this estimation, constructing a portfolio that maximizes asset diversity while meeting size and weight constraints. However, its classical implementation is confined to a limited number of assets due to computational constraints. We investigated the gate-dependent conductance of underdoped superconducting NbN nanowires, focusing on their behavior in normal metal constraints. Contrary to the prevalent theory of coherent quantum phase jumps through superconducting constraints, our research revealed significantly varied conductance responses to gate voltage for different starting points, with some exhibiting abrupt changes and others more gradual, exhibiting Coulomb blockade characteristics. Both scenarios can coexist within the same device, depending on the quantum metrology parameters and we propose a framework to differentiate between these situations based on start-to-start conductivity variations. Our study suggests that devices with higher start-to-start conductivity variation ratios exhibit quantum phase jump behavior, while those with lower ratios exhibit Coulomb blockade characteristics, presenting an assessment of the interplay between these phenomena. Moreover, we outline an method to estimate the required length for coherent quantum phase jumps in an unconfined superconducting wire. Our research provides new insights into the interplay between coherent quantum phase jumps and Coulomb blockade in constrained superconducting devices and we propose an experiment involving time-domain reflectometry to further study quantum phase jump coherence in such systems. Futhermore, a discussion on the potential for our findings to be applied to the study of quantum phase jumps in graphene edge states is included. interactions are pronounced due to high-spin conditions, allowing for the

Modeling infectious disease dynamics within complex systems necessitates a balanced approach that combines realistic modeling with practical application feasibility. Using the 2003 SARS outbreak in Hong Kong as a case study, particularly focusing on bus network transmissions, our analysis reveals that a simplified model of mixed connectivity performs better than more intricate urban transmission models, which are based on real transportation pathways. This well-mixed model representation utilized a parameter that reflected the buses' contribution to overall transmission potential, known as the 'urban Foreman parameter'. This parameter, denoted as beta (β), measures the potential for infectious individuals to transmit the disease to others within the urban environment. Our findings indicate that this parameter is significantly influenced by various factors such as population density and individual behavior, rather than being solely dependent on urban bus network connectivity. Specifically, we uncovered an attack on IKEv2 using its cookie feature, although this attack is largely circumvented by a design modification. While we acknowledge a method for mitigating the risks associated with unrepeatable encryption, which we refer to as rE, we also explore its security characteristics as well as potential countermeasures. A cryptographic technique known as functional encryption enables users to efficiently compute outcomes of specific functions while keeping the underlying input data private. One of the most well-known functional encryption methods is keyless functional encryption, where a user can perform computations without needing an encryption key. In this study, we introduce the initial concept of keyless functional encryption for classical messages transmitted in Gaussian noise channels, a fundamental and broadly applicable cryptographic framework. Leveraging an existing scheme designed for binary inputs and additive white Gaussian noise channels, we developed a method to extend its security guarantees to include manipulations of signal power and possibly adaptive attacks, all without the need for an encryption key. This new keyless functional encryption framework can be used to securely enable various applications, such as secure computation for privacy-preserving classification and securely outsourcing encrypted storage, both with power-controllable and uncontrolled attacks. Our findings demonstrate that this new keyless functional encryption framework offers superior performance over its key-based counterpart, featuring significantly lower encrypted message lengths with comparable computation costs. This improvement in efficiency enables secure computation for a wider range of signal power levels and reduces the risk of power-controllable attacks in protocols employing random padding. This paper expresses a nearly conformal gradient Ricci soliton on a Sasakian manifold in terms of a conformal potential of the vector field generating the soliton, under the assumption that the soliton's eigenvalue is positive. We establish a connection between the conformal potential and the vector field, deriving a theorem that classifies the soliton in this setting. We also investigate a specific case where the soliton's eigenvalue is nearly zero and a specific scenario where the soliton's eigenvalue is distinct for each eigenvalue. Lastly, we offer a definition for a conformal gradient Ricci soliton on a Sasakian manifold and demonstrate its relation to a potential of the soliton's vector field. We conclude by outlining several open questions related to these solitons.

Despite the fundamental differences, there are both functional and theoretical similarities between the magnetospheres of planets and celestial bodies. Like terrestrial planets' magnetospheres, which protect their surface from harmful solar winds, gas giants' magnetospheres expand to encompass their surrounding environment, influencing the wind patterns around their moons. The magnetospheres of celestial bodies, however, can also be influenced and redirected by the rotation of their parent planet, as seen in the increased extension of a captured moon's magnetosphere when in the planet's shadow. This dual magnetic field interaction can result in the redistribution of the moon's atmospheric particles, turning the fast wind streams into conic-shaped formations and creating'magnetospheric winds' that can impact the parent planet. The discovery of these'magnetospheric winds' has provided a possible explanation for the observed differences in the erosion rates of the moons Ganymede and Io. Io's greater volcanic activity is believed to be a result of the heating of its interior by the Jovian core, as well as the unique interaction between the moon's magnetic field and the intense plasma surrounding it, which in turn powers its volcanic activity. This new understanding of the interaction between magnetic fields and the high-energy plasma surrounding celestial bodies and planets has highlighted the significance of cross-disciplinary study and knowledge exchange between researchers in these fields. As such, this special issue aims to facilitate this exchange by presenting the latest research on the magnetospheres of planets and celestial bodies from a theoretical as well as observational perspective. Key areas of study will be the characteristics of solar wind and the various plasma sources that contribute to the wind in the magnetospheres of planets and celestial bodies, the detection of their magnetic field interactions and the unique features that these interactions can exhibit, as well as the impact of these interactions on the surrounding environment and the distinctive phenomena they can result in. As such, contributions from researchers working on the Io - Jovian magnetosphere, magnetosheath and the moon's volcanic activity are particularly welcome. This special issue will provide an opportunity for the exchange of ideas between researchers working on planetary and celestial body magnetospheres through the presentation of their latest research findings. This will be a part of the main conference program, as well as a workshop on the Io - Jovian magnetosphere and the moon's magnetic field and volcanic activity that will take place during the meeting week. The properties of adjacent layers can significantly influence the spin-orbit coupling of a specific material. This effect, also known as the proximity spin-orbit coupling, can cause a change in the spin of electrons as they move through the materials, affecting phenomena such as superconductivity and magnetism. Our study focuses on a specific instance of this effect, where a thin layer of bismuth (a non-magnetic material with strong spin-orbit coupling) is placed near a layer of cobalt (a ferromagnetic material with weak spin-orbit coupling). Our research involves a combination of transport and structural measurements on Bi/Co multilayers, as well as theoretical calculations, to understand how the proximity effect influences the spin-orbit coupling and the magnetization of cobalt. Our results show that the magnetization of cobalt can be maintained even when there is an optimal thickness of bismuth, despite the strong spin-orbit coupling in bismuth. This optimal thickness is linked to the extent of grain boundary scattering in the materials, with its specific value dependent on the crystal structure and the size of the grains. Our results have implications for the design of devices that utilize the proximity effect, suggesting that the choice of materials and the control of grain boundaries can significantly impact their performance. Furthermore, our study provides new insights into the unique phenomenon of spin-orbit coupling in materials, specifically the effect of boundary scattering on its magnitude. This knowledge can be applied to modify the properties of materials through the control of boundary scattering, potentially unlocking new capabilities in devices that rely on these materials. Our research also raises the possibility of using materials with strong spin-orbit coupling, like bismuth, as a layer to modify the properties of other materials, even when those materials have a thicker layer of the same type. This finding is significant because it contradicts a common assumption in the study of proximity effects, which holds that the effect diminishes rapidly with increasing thickness of the adjacent layer. Our study has identified a new threshold for this reduction, linked to the size of the grains in the materials, with potential applications in the study of materials with strong spin-orbit coupling, like bismuth, when they have a similar structure to that studied in this research. Sequential models are highly effective in translating phrases, yet they rely heavily on statistical precedents from large corpora. We argue that this limitation results in inconsistent translations when the source and target languages are the same, as seen in the Basque-English-Basque task. For instance, translating "nire amak" to English as "my mother" instead of "my father" due to the original English translation causing an expectation of a gender-based consensus in the reverse translation. We propose a sequence-to-sequence model that seeks to circumvent this issue by producing a direct translation from "nire amak" to Basque without relying on the English intermediate, which we demonstrate achieves a 1.5% improvement in reverse translation accuracy without using additional training data and achieves parity with fully supervised models with just 85% of the training data. Our method also yields a 5.5% gain in error reduction for low-frequency words and demonstrates the ability to transfer knowledge from reading to writing in 45% of cases. Ultimately, our model achieves 11.6% fewer errors on the test set compared to a fully supervised sequence-to-sequence model. Our code is available at https://github.com/aliyajeh/basque-consensus. One potential to build upon our work could be exploring alternative methods for enforcing the consensus, such as utilizing a consensus-preserving generator or discriminator in a GAN framework, or integrating a system that enforces the consensus during translation, such as WordNet, that could be applied to other under-resourced languages. Due to the unique nature of our dataset, our results cannot be directly compared to existing literature, but our method's ability to achieve parity with fully supervised models at a lower training budget suggests that it is highly efficient. This efficiency, combined with the method's ability to yield a 5.5% gain in error reduction for low-frequency words, makes it an attractive solution for low-resource machine translation tasks. However, our model's largest shortcoming is its limited ability to transfer knowledge from writing to reading in just 45% of cases, which leaves room for further improvement. We hypothesize that this difficulty stems from the model's tendency to produce more complex Basque sentences when translating from English to Basque, which hinders its capacity to learn the required consensus during the reverse translation. We develop a level-set method for approximating sensitive functionals with discontinuities, leveraging a piecewise-stiff map formulation. This involves defining a highly variable energy functional based on a given target energy $J$, and establishing a relationship between the original and approximated functionals. A significant advantage of this method is its robustness to map singularities, enabling the use of a piecewise-stiff map formulation even in cases where the original map exhibits severe variations. A key component of this method is a new type of level-set formulation, characterized by a piecewise-stiff map $H$-surface evolution equation. We also investigate a simplified version of this equation, including a related existence and uniqueness result for a time-discontinuous map $H$-surface equation. Ultimately, we employ this framework to develop an algorithm for approximating sensitive functionals with discontinuities, and provide an example application to a problem involving a Stefan problem. This study is part of a broader examination of third-generation leptoquark that encompasses both scalar and vector forms, and involves Drell-Yan and semi-leptonic leptoquark pair production. Conferencing platforms offering high-quality video conferencing tools also collect user data for personalized services and advertising purposes. To maintain confidentiality and comfort during such meetings, users must decide between customizing their settings and participating. This dilemma raises ethical concerns that have been addressed by researchers through the lens of game theory, looking at remote workers as primary stakeholders. This study expands on existing research in this area by incorporating a crucial aspect - the cost users incur when choosing between customizing their settings and participating in conferences. This cost, represented by a monetary fine, is imposed on users who prioritize confidentiality over customization. To investigate this aspect, the study designates one important player - the remote worker with the power to customize and influence confidentiality settings. To address this issue, the study proposes two solutions: a first-refugee problem and a Stochastic Game Model. The former is an iterative solution, while the latter is a dynamic solution, and both aim to find an equilibrium that can guide platform designers in making data-driven decisions. To validate these solutions, the study conducts an experiment involving 60 participants. The results show that both solutions can function effectively in real-world settings, and the Stochastic Game Model outperforms the first-refugee problem in terms of efficiency. However, due to the long $\lambda$ used in such contexts, this approach may introduce a beam instability driven by the regeneration process itself, limiting charge bunching potential. Every year in our solar system, multiple close approaches between asteroids and the Sun or other asteroids occur, leading to potential breakup of asteroids that are in binary or larger orbits. A byproduct of such events can be found in the form of asteroid pairs, composed of two linked asteroids, where one is significantly smaller than the other. This study aims to identify binary asteroids through analyzing pairs of asteroids in our solar system that are separated by a short distance. Researchers have been comparing the orbits of these pairs around their common mass center, some showing characteristics of stable orbits while others exhibit signs of an unstable, elliptical path. To validate their approach, the team assessed pairs of asteroids that are not linked, using their knowledge of asteroid shapes and sizes to rule out any false positives. From a large dataset provided by the Pan-STARRS1 survey, consisting of over 1600 near-Earth asteroids and 24000 main belt asteroids, only a small number of potential binary asteroids were found, along with their supporting evidence regarding the stability of their orbits. This research laid the groundwork for a more in-depth analysis of all pairs of asteroids in our solar system, using higher resolution data that incorporates information on asteroid shapes and sizes, in order to determine how many of these pairs can withstand the gravitational forces exerted by the Sun and each other. This determination will be crucial in predicting future close approaches and breakups of asteroids that are in binary or larger orbits, helping scientists to better understand the origin and distribution of small objects within our solar system. This field of research also has the potential to contribute to a greater understanding of how binary asteroids are formed and how they function. This study used its findings to support a proposal for a new survey aimed at identifying potential binary asteroids and their approaches, breakups, and other related phenomena, which if executed, will provide valuable insights to researchers in the field of small body astronomy. The Rio Grande Rift system in Southern Brazil and Northern Argentina represents an outstanding example of an intra-plate continental rift that formed during the break-up of Gondwana. It is characterized by extensive and deep- seated E-W to NE-SW oriented fault valleys. These valleys are a result of tens of millions of years of stretching, separation and drifting of Gondwana. Although the Rio Grande Rift system appears to be inactive today, studies indicate that it underwent neotectonic activity during the Quaternary period. This system has been of interest for several decades but there is a notable absence of detailed kinematical analyses on its rift system. This study aims to fill this knowledge gap by conducting a kinematical analysis to classify the Rio Grande Rift system in Southern Brazil and Northern Argentina based on its natural break points. The results of this study reveal that the rift system is composed of several first-order units with distinct spatial orientations and that they have exhibited different patterns of development and evolution. It has also been found that some of these units have displayed linear development and others have developed in a more curved manner. This study further found that some of these units have shown evidence of both extensional and lateral movements while others have only exhibited linear kinematics which is likely a result of various factors such as changes in crustal thickness, temperature and the presence of magmatic intrusions that may have influenced the system's development and evolution in a non-uniform and anisotropic manner. This study provides a detailed kinematical classification of each unit within the Rio Grande Rift system in Southern Brazil and Northern Argentina based on their spatial orientation, development patterns and types of movements. This classification has resulted in a comprehensive and in-depth map that displays each unit's unique features. This study is a significant contribution to the understanding of the Rio Grande Rift system and its development and evolution in a non-uniform and anisotropic manner. It is also a demonstration of the application of a kinematical analysis to a complex and large-scale intra-plate continental rift system. In medical imaging, optimizing information retrieval from images is crucial, especially with limited annotated data, for both image segmentation and classification. This problem is compounded by the presence of noisy and irrelevant regions in medical images that don't contain vital information. To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework for medical image partitioning that leverages a balanced information measure, known as Tsallis diversity, to selectively focus on relevant regions while minimizing noise. To ensure that our method is efficient and scalable, we integrated information maximization and learning into a self-supervised framework, allowing it to learn from boundary information and produce robust segmentations. Experimental results on two diverse medical image datasets demonstrate that our proposed framework achieves superior segmentation accuracy compared to existing methods, even without the use of external annotations. Furthermore, we showcase the applicability of our framework to classification by dividing medical images into regions prior to classification, achieving notable gains in classification performance. This study explores the role of an AI dungeon supervisor in Dungeons and Dragons, focusing on its communication and direction capabilities. We introduce a new approach called the "Dungeon Supervision Framework," which leverages machine learning to enable the AI to deliver high-quality storytelling by delivering relevant hints to the players. We collected and analyzed data from human dungeon supervisors, their counterparts in the D4D system, and user assessments of the D4D stories. We discovered several key differences between human supervisors and the D4D system, including variations in hint quality, narrative alignment, and overall player experience. Building upon these findings, we created a dataset centered around the D4D system's "intents" and "mindset," which we used to train new models for the D4D system. These models achieved better data efficiency and lower disconnection risks compared to the original D4D system. We also explored the influence of the dungeon supervisors' "mindset" on player experience and found that an optimal mindset can lead to a more engaging experience with higher narrative understanding and satisfaction. We developed multiple variants of the D4D system's architecture, incorporating both the new dataset and previous data. Our results show that the new models can deliver comparable player experience to the original D4D system while reducing disconnection risks. We discovered that the optimal mindset varies depending on the system architecture, but we did not observe a clear connection between the models' performance and the data they were trained on. We explored various communication approaches, including simple and complex hints, and found that the D4D system's performance is relatively robust across these variations. We also investigated the influence of human supervision, combining human directions with the D4D system's automatic deliveries. We found that the D4D system can deliver high-quality stories even with minimal human supervision, but additional supervision can lead to better narrative alignment and overall player experience. Building upon these findings, we created a user interface for the D4D system that can effectively deliver complex hints to the players, but we did not evaluate the user interface due to time constraints. We anticipate that the D4D system's user interface will require further refinement to match the standards of human dungeon supervisors. We believe that our research lays the foundation for the development of more sophisticated AI dungeon supervisors that can deliver high-quality storytelling in Dungeons and Dragons by leveraging machine learning and advanced communication approaches. Our proposed system, LexSemDet, builds upon existing knowledge by not only identifying multi-word transfers but also lexical ones in both source and target languages.  Through the analysis of large parallel corpora, LexSemDet uncovers a significant portion of these transfers that existing machine translation systems have not captured, as evidenced by the evaluation of our method against data enhanced by human translators.  A particular emphasis is placed on transparent code and the availability of LexSemDet on both Model-Adaptive Translation and Universal Machine Translation frameworks, with the latter outperforming the former in detection accuracy.  Interestingly, it was observed that the latter framework discovers a much larger number of shifts than the former, with results suggesting that existing models may still have difficulty handling a substantial number of these transfers with just 32 Gigabytes of training data, implying a significant path for future work in this domain.  All of LexSemDet's code and data has been made publicly available at https://github.com/nyu-dl-guild/LexSemDet. Certain beyond-standard-model leptoquark composites, specifically those of flavor singlets, could potentially explain several observed anomalies. We examine a scenario where two specific types of leptoquarks exist: one that interacts with electrons and u-quarks, and another with muons and u-quarks. We investigate the creation of these leptoquarks in pairs, considering all possible combinations of leptoquark masses and assuming they are identical in mass. We focus on an scenario often referred to as the "uneven case", where the mass difference between the lighter and heavier leptoquarks is substantial, exceeding half of their average. As a result, at most one of the two created particles survives beyond a distance where it can interact with detectors, leaving little to no detectable evidence of the other particle's existence. We also explore the possibility of these particles being detected in other high-energy colliders. Experiments in life sciences, such as gene expression studies and protein activity assessments, frequently yield temporal series data that is rich in detail but sparse in duration and high in dimensionality. This type of data poses a significant learning challenge due to its inherent sparsity in both time and feature dimensions, necessitating a more robust form of learning that involves periodic observations with varying labels. We introduce an active learning algorithm, called Monitored Learning, that prioritizes data collection based on labels and, when combined with efficient kernels, delivers exceptional performance in predicting temporal series data in high-dimensional spaces. Our approach ensures that, with each observation, the model is learned in an optimal way to accommodate the data most effectively. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in multiple scenarios, including the analysis of yeast cell-cycle expression using gene-expression data with 619 dimensions and 18 time points, or, equivalently, 46 data points. Our results show that Monitored Learning surpasses traditional learning methods by a significant margin, improving prediction accuracy by up to 50% in certain cases. Furthermore, we investigate the model's performance under various assumptions regarding data collection and provide a comprehensive comparison with other active and passive learning methods. Our findings indicate that Monitored Learning consistently delivers the best results, achieving a 10-50% improvement in prediction accuracy in certain scenarios. We also examine the model's behavior when data are collected under different conditions and discover that it is highly robust and adaptable, yielding a 10-50% improvement in prediction accuracy in certain scenarios. Our approach is particularly well-suited for temporal series data with distinct phases, delivering a 10-50% improvement in prediction accuracy in certain scenarios. We also introduce a novel application for our learning method, known as Multiway Learning, that focuses on discovering latent temporal series within high-dimensional data sets and, using yeast cell-cycle expression data with 619 dimensions and 18 time points, show that it is 10-50% more accurate in predicting temporal series data in high-dimensional spaces compared to traditional learning methods. This report outlines our approach to addressing the MUD Challenge, a task that involves identifying musical devices across multiple genres using only a limited number of examples. We achieved notable success in the 4-shot category and made notable gains in the 1-shot and 2-shot categories, while also improving upon the existing leaderboard in the 5-shot category. Our method builds upon a hierarchical framework introduced in our initial assessment, resulting in MIRNAs being recognized in one-shot cases and musical devices in just a few shots. Our key innovations include the optimal selection of prototypes, reduction of prototype variance, and the implementation of a score weighting system. We have ensured the method's usability for both human and automated experts by providing an interactive tool for selecting prototypes and refining the model's predictions. Our code and data are publicly accessible for both the MUD Challenge and the MIR Challenge, to which we are contributing 128 MIR-NAs in both domains. Furthermore, we have introduced an evaluation protocol that is also accessible to other researchers. It is essential to note that, at the time of submission, our method was the top-performing entry in every category, with an overall average success rate of 73.33%. It is worth noting that, due to the simplicity of prototypes, our method may be considered as an alternative to fine-tuning, rather than a true few-shot learning approach. Systematic evaluations and case studies are presented in Section 5, along with an examination of how expert knowledge can be incorporated into the model through additional score weighting. It is essential to note that, due to the strict adherence to the challenge's protocol, our method is limited to using the provided data and cannot leverage additional information about musical devices, such as their technical specifications. Building upon our results, we have explored this limitation in more detail and have identified several potential improvements, along with several open research questions, that are also discussed in this report along with our conclusions and future work. Research papers serve as the primary source of information for numerous subsequent studies but often lack their own own summaries. Despite advancements in paper summaries like arXiv papers and sciumes, they usually focus on condensing content rather than providing a roadmap for further exploration. Our novel approach, called Knowledge Frontiers, seeks to fill this knowledge gap by crafting queries that guide in-depth examinations of research topics. We have assembled a diverse set of 13 distinct categories spanning 9 different domains and within each category, we pose 5 distinct questions that initiate a deeper exploration. These questions not only encourage in-depth examination but also those that invite responses that could be validated against existing information, making them suitable for assessment via future versions of Semeval-style tasks. We invite other researchers to collaborate with us by contributing their own sets of queries and potential responses that could be evaluated against existing research, paving the way for a community-driven effort to prioritize areas of research that merit further exploration based on natural language criteria. We propose a methodology for prioritization that considers both performance metrics and diverse selection strategies to ensure fairness in choosing topics. Through our work, we aim to create an ecosystem where the research community as a whole can guide each other's attention towards the most pressing issues, fostering a spirit of cooperation and mutual support. We have already initiated this cooperation by hosting a Knowledge Frontiers SemEval-2023 Task that attracted over 40 registered teams from across the globe and have since released our initial findings that highlight both the promise and limitations of our approach as well as our plans for further enhancing our evaluation methodology and evaluation criteria in response to valuable feedback from our community, particularly with regards to our proposed method for validating the generated responses against the underlying research articles using both explicit and implicit techniques. We have also incorporated semantic validation for both individual queries and their corresponding generated responses as well as both individual articles and overall category collections. We have initiated discussions with major academic publishers to explore possibilities for integrating our evaluation methodology directly into the publication process of research articles, thereby providing a more holistic understanding of published research that goes beyond its abstracts, references, and content. We have released our evaluation toolkit along with all related data and results at https://knowledgefrontiers.org/. This includes both the data used in our experiments and results from the Knowledge Frontiers Semeval-2023 Task along with all related information on both task and evaluation methodology at https://knowledgefrontiers.org/about/. The rapid spread of infectious diseases like SARS-CoV-2 underscores the importance and urgency of epidemiological modeling. Our paper offers a comprehensive review of modeling frameworks used to study the current epidemic, focusing on SEIR and SIR models, as well as their extensions, including multi-compartment, network-based, and general SEIR models. We examine modeling aspects, such as establishing equations, applying statistical techniques for parameter estimation, and interpreting results in the context of the epidemic. Our discussion highlights the role of modeling in predicting future outcomes, evaluating control measures, and guiding policy decisions, emphasizing the necessity for transparency and clear communication between scientists and the broader community. We also provide considerations and recommendations for researchers working on epidemiological modeling. Our framework is adaptable to a wide range of epidemics, and we conclude by outlining the scientific questions that modeling can address during outbreaks. Our paper is a collaborative effort among members of the Epidemics Network, a community of researchers who contributed their expertise in mathematics, statistics, computer science, biology, medicine, and social sciences to produce this review. Our paper is available under a permissive Creative Commons license, aiming to facilitate the exploration of new research directions and the advancement of methodology in epidemiological modeling. Our paper is now freely accessible at https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.01878, and it has been published in the journal EPJ Data Science at https://link.springer.com/article/10.1140/epjds/s13680-021-00301-5. Our paper has received media coverage from notable outlets, including an interview with the BBC World Service, and it has been downloaded over 100,000 times. Our paper has also been translated into Spanish by the journal Revista Cubana de Ciencias y Tecnologías de la Información, and it has been published in Volume 15, Issue 2, 2021, at https://link.jsc.journals.academicdoam.com/index.php/revcubicti/article/view/1036/1036. We analyze the properties of Majorana fermions in a quantum system that has been prepared in an appropriate state, as described by an anti-symmetric correlator matrix. This study focuses on a specific linear combination of Majorana operators and examines the general properties of its distribution. We establish that the mean values of these operators are independent in each direction and follow a normal distribution. Additionally, their variance follows a linear model. Furthermore, this study investigates the unique properties of this linear combination and demonstrates that it is inherently linked to its zero-mode state. We also investigate the conditions under which this combination is independent of mode-specific properties and discuss the implications of these conditions in experimental preparations that rely on real-time measurements of linear combinations of Majorana operators. These findings are relevant to experiments aimed at detecting Majorana fermions in nuclear environments, as described in the context of lattice gauge models, such as the two-flavor lattice QCD. We based our analysis on the work of Cao and Liu (Phys. Rev. X 9, 041017, 2019), which explored the same topic but assumed that the distribution is independent and ascertained that this assumption is valid only when the variance meets a specific criterion. In contrast, this study delves into the aspects of this combination that are not accounted for by this assumption and provides a more comprehensive understanding of its properties. We also propose a new, more general variance model that encompasses various forms, including the one examined in the mentioned study. This new model is based on the established relationships between the anti-symmetric correlator matrix and the distribution of linear combinations of Majorana operators and may serve as an adaptable framework for examining the properties of these operators in any given quantum system. This study is an expansion on our earlier research presented in the one-column paper "Characterizing Linear Majorana Particles" presented at the 2021 JACOW web site, where we first introduced the proposed variance model, but did not have access to the underlying details of this model's derivation. Topological insulators represent a groundbreaking concept where specific properties are safeguarded by geometric arrangements, ensuring robustness against environmental disruptions. Topological phases have been successfully incorporated into quantum simulations with cold atoms and molecules, as well as in systems of interacting fermions, often involving sophisticated setups. In contrast, three-dimensional nodal surfaces in momentum space, such as those found in momentum-space versions of Dirac and Weyl points, can provide analogous topological protection without the need for sophisticated setups. Recently, research has focused on realizing three-dimensional nodal surfaces in momentum space using photonic and other systems. These advances have revealed that surface modes associated with these nodal surfaces can exhibit unique characteristics, including robustness, circular symmetry, and connection to dark modes. Furthermore, recent implementations have demonstrated the practical value of these surfaces in momentum space, enabling the efficient confinement of modes, as well as the creation of mode pairs connected by winding numbers, and have shown potential applications in optical data processing and other fields. In this review, we discuss recent theoretical developments, as well as experimental implementations in photonic crystals, metamaterials, and other systems, and outline potential directions for future research. We also explore the unique characteristics of nodal surfaces in momentum space and their implications for future research in topological physics. In the context of photonic systems, we discuss the life beyond mode pairs connected by winding numbers and discuss potential applications in optical data processing and communication. We expect that the positive experiences gained from researching three-dimensional nodal surfaces in momentum space will accelerate the exploration of other topological phenomena in momentum space in photonic and other systems. Ray tracing in high-dimensional spaces has various real-world applications, such as image synthesis and light field rendering. However, when dealing with unknown variables, calculating rays can be challenging due to obstacles such as surface irregularities and water, which significantly hinder the progress of ray tracing and subsequent analysis. To address this issue, a novel shadow casting method is proposed, which is unique in its use of differential evaluation. By modeling shadow effects mathematically and incorporating them into the equation for light transport, this method becomes an integral part of light field reconstruction. This method is an improvement over traditional techniques in several ways: it is more precise, free of artifacts, and compatible with optimization methods. When incorporated into light field reconstruction, it eliminates the need for separate rendering steps and can handle a larger number of light sources. Experimental results demonstrate that this method yields better reconstruction quality than existing solutions. Furthermore, this method is distinct in its use of differential evaluation, which enables it to be integrated into inverse light transport optimization methods. This is particularly useful for the reconstruction of water and surface irregularities, which are fundamental components of scene geometry. This method sets a new standard for shadow casting in light transport and light field reconstruction, and is expected to have a significant impact on various applications that rely on light transport analysis and modification. Traditional video deinterlacing approaches have primarily focused on processing pre-recorded material. This project differs by targeting real-time processing of live video. Existing methods are hindered by their reliance on analysis from previous frames and are often compromised by slow motion, over-scanning, and scene changes. To address these limitations, a novel framework has been developed that leverages macroblock analysis from a companion H.264 encoder to refine processing. This framework enables efficient handling of motion patterns, over-scanning, and scene changes, ensuring fast and effective processing even in the presence of these common video issues. Experimental results show that this framework yields superior outcomes compared to conventional methods, as verified across diverse evaluation metrics and H.264 encoder configurations. Specifically, it demonstrates notable improvements in PSNR, SSIM, and subjective assessment, achieving a 2-3 dB PSNR gain and outperforming the SSIM threshold of 0.93 in over 95% of test cases. This project offers a groundbreaking solution for real-time H.264 live video deinterlacing, presenting a challenging problem solution that can be adapted to other compression formats. Experimental evaluations utilizing a range of evaluation metrics have been conducted across 18 diverse H.264 test sequences, highlighting potential applications in broadcasting, surveillance, and other settings with H.264 codec support. Compared to existing approaches, this project has notable PSNR and SSIM gains, demonstrating its potential as a premier solution for real-time H.264 live video deinterlacing. Precise flood infrastructure management relies on accurate and swift flood depth predictions. Tradational methods based on inertia models possess high computational costs, hindering their use as operational forecasts continue to increase in complexity. In contrast, the use of finite volume methods has been shown to be computationally efficient for predicting flood depths. This paper presents a novel approach that leverages the same flood height predictions from finite volume methods but employs a deep learning framework to bypass time-to-time predictions, instead utilizing the methods' capabilities to solve the shallow water equations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in predicting flood depths on two scenarios and show that the predictions made by the deep learning framework and traditional methods are comparable, with the former achieving significant computational speed-ups. This method has been implemented as an operational tool by the Dutch national flood early warning system system operator, Deltares. 

This research is now ongoing at the University of Oxford, and Deltares is collaborating on it. The code for this project can be found at https://github.com/oxford-cvrg/flood-forecasting and has been adapted for use with the Oxford University's supercomputer, Nomad. This note presents an updated version of the b-principle, incorporating the Mumford conjecture for smooth surfaces. We believe our research provides valuable insights for the scientific computing community on the pros and cons of balanced and unbalanced approaches for solving nonlinear partial differential equations with strongly discontinuous coefficients. We anticipate that our research will contribute to the development of more effective and scalable solvers for solving cardiac muscle models in the near future. Open-world learning assumes that there is no a priori limitation on the variety of objects that can be recognized within a given environment. This research focuses on developing a learning framework that addresses two significant challenges in open-world settings: the presence of incorrect or misleading information and the need for continuous calibration to ensure assurance levels. To address these issues, the proposed framework builds on top of a previously introduced context-aware representation model by incorporating two key components: a topological-aware ambiguity model and a contrastive assurance calibration framework. The ambiguity model addresses the issue of incorrect information by redefining the normative and non-normative classes in a way that considers the complex relationships within each class, such as symmetry, asymmetry, and bi-directionality. This results in a more robust representation of objects and their relationships. A contrastive assurance calibration framework is then used to fine-tune the representation of objects based on their normative or non-normative classification. This framework involves a contrastive loss function that compares the representation of each object with that of its context, as well as a temperature scaling mechanism that adjusts the difficulty level of the classification task. Experimental evaluations conducted on multiple open-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, particularly in scenarios with limited labeled data. Furthermore, in-depth analysis of the proposed framework is conducted through an examination of its energy-based representation and a visual demonstration of its ability to learn in an open-world setting. Declarative processes monitor system events for compliance and take corrective actions, but their effectiveness depends on real-time event data. Unfortunately, events can go unrecorded due to technical issues, causing false negatives, and leading to incorrect compliance assessments. Taking this into account, we develop a new approach that treats events as persistent, allowing our framework to accurately determine compliance even in the presence of data disruptions. Our solution utilizes event persistence to filter out temporary disruptions, ensuring that declarative processes based on averages remain unaffected, while those relying on maximum/minimum values are protected against false negatives. To illustrate this, we create two examples: one showing our approach prevents false summaries in a healthcare scenario, while the other demonstrates our method's effectiveness in handling declining sales trends. Our technique also enhances robustness by preventing false alarms caused by temporary fluctuations, eliminating the need for explicit handling of transient disruptions. And, interestingly, our approach is compatible with existing techniques for handling technical difficulties, ensuring that events resulting from system failures are treated as temporary and do not impact compliance assessments. Our new method is called SEPM, and we prove its correctness through soundness and completeness properties. Additionally, SEPM is applicable to both finite and infinite event sets, and we provide a formal definition for its implementation, while demonstrating its practicality through a prototype application for financial risk monitoring. Our experiments show that SEPM's performance is comparable to traditional approaches, while our case studies and a user survey indicate that SEPM is both efficient and effective in real-world scenarios. Our new approach is part of a broader event-based monitoring framework, and we outline several directions for further research and improvement. This research is an extension of our previous work on event-based monitoring, and all our solutions and examples are formally defined using the Declare language for declarative process specification. A possible explanation for this phenomenon is provided by considering the role of bulges, which mark a turning point in the structure of galaxies. At $10.5\le\log(M_{{\rm bulge}}/M_\odot)\le11.0$, there's an observable shift from an exponential disk to a bulge dominated by by dark matter. Above this mass range, the dark matter influence in bulges starts to dominate galaxy evolution, leading to a divergence from the typical one-to-one SFR-mass relationship due to an increased matter reservoir available for future star generation. This discovery offers a more detailed explanation for the turning over of the SFR-mass relation, and suggests that bulges play a crucial role in determining a galaxy's star formation history. We introduce an innovative multi-task model that leverages related datasets to improve sentiment analysis when there is a language barrier. The key challenge in this task is the lack of English sentiment scores for paraphrased sentences, which hinders the learning process. We propose a solution to address this issue by incorporating two complementary datasets: a target dataset for primary training and a secondary dataset for ongoing refinement. The secondary dataset, although not directly tied to the target dataset, shares the same sentiment scores but differs in language. The model's ability to learn from these related datasets is key to success. By doing so, it becomes skilled in translating the learning signal from one language to another, ultimately enabling it to generate relevant information for the target dataset even when primary training data is scarce. To test our approach, we created an ensemble dataset that combines English sentiment data with paraphrased content in another language. The results show our method outperforms single-task and other multi-task models, demonstrating that our approach is the most effective way to learn this task. The code is available at https://github.com/pardeep-kumar/xlsa. The ensemble dataset and models are available at https://github.com/pardeep-kumar/paraphrased-sentiment. The model's ability to generalize is evaluated through a systematic study of different ensemble configurations, which forms the basis of our contributions. The study reveals that our model is robust and capable of learning from a wide array of related datasets, spanning multiple language pairs and sentiment domains. To further generalize, we explored the idea that the model's performance is optimal when the secondary dataset contains a similar proportion of positive and negative sentences as the target dataset. This insight enables us to introduce Data Balance for Cross-Language Sentiment Assessment (DBXSA), which is a novel approach that uses secondary datasets with balanced sentiment proportions. The results show DBXSA achieves even higher accuracy, demonstrating the model's ability to generalize across datasets with differing positive and negative ratio through self-supervised learning. The improvement is particularly noticeable in datasets with a small proportion of positive or negative sentences, where the model's performance is within 2% of the best configuration in all tested settings. The paper also presents an evaluation of the model's ability to generalize to datasets with a completely different sentiment taxonomy, such as adapting the model to predict IEMOTIVE sentiment scores from paraphrased sentences, which are trained to predict Plutchik sentiment scores. X-ray images contain subtle information that can predict the severity of COVID-19 patients requiring intensive care unit (ICU) admission, as evidenced by the successful implementation of data-driven models as described in published studies. To further explore this concept, a dataset consisting of COVID-19 X-ray images with corresponding ICU admission labels was analyzed using both qualitative and quantitative assessment methods. Initial evaluations using a pre-trained classification model and 8 distinct feature extraction methods revealed the following key observations: (1) there is no uniform pattern in X-ray images indicating ICU admission, as described in published studies; (2) however, a pattern does emerge in the dataset, characterized by a distinction between COVID-19 patients requiring ICU admission and those who do not; (3) four out of eight feature extraction methods yielded classification performance exceeding that of a baseline model, indicating that these methods capture relevant information from the X-ray images; (4) two-dimensional projection techniques failed to achieve optimal results, likely due to overfitting; (3) the dataset's diversity, calculated using both label and image-based metrics, is a critical factor in model generalizability; and (4) future research should prioritize both diversity in COVID-19 X-ray datasets and the underlying clinical characteristics, as well as address the issue of limited data size. To address the challenge of limited data size, a new dataset named COVID-ICU-256 was created, comprising 256 pairs of COVID-19 X-ray images and corresponding ICU admission labels, as well as 512 additional images without ICU admission labels, for further exploration and validation of data-driven models predicting the severity of COVID-19 patients requiring ICU admission. To ensure the dataset's high-quality diversity, both image-based and label-based diversity metrics were employed, resulting in models that achieved significantly improved classification performance, with an average accuracy of 94.07%, in comparison to a recent baseline model, in support of further development and refinement of COVID-19 diagnosis systems utilizing X-ray images. To facilitate access to the created dataset, both image data and model codes have been made publicly available for research communities, in the hope that they will contribute to building more reliable and robust data-driven models for predicting the severity of COVID-19 patients requiring ICU admission, as well as to provide valuable insights for constructing high-quality datasets, featuring diverse data, essential for accurately training and validating such models. In addition, the study highlights the significance of both qualitative and quantitative assessment methods in evaluating data-driven models, in comparison to exclusive reliance on either method.
