The rise of deep learning in visual association detection has yielded impressive performance, however, the field still grapples with the challenge of incorrect positives. This issue is compounded by the fact that negative samples are vastly outnumbered by positive ones, making it difficult to ensure the model is accurately distinguishing between positive and negative examples. Existing methods often focus solely on enhancing feature extraction, but this is insufficient, given that the model is learning to recognize negative samples, including those with misleading or misleading context, as positives. We introduce an innovative method that not only boosts the quality of negative samples and incorporates context-aware hard negative mining, but also incorporates a contrastive learning framework that aims to consolidate correct positives and eradicate incorrect ones. Our proposed framework is comprehensive, addressing all aspects of visual association detection. Experimental results show that it achieves superior or competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art models across VGG and ResNet backbones on VQA v2 and Visual Genome, and has been made available open-source at https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/ANM.

This study presents an action recognition system that utilizes R-BERT, a representation-based model. In order to enhance performance on limited and low-light video datasets, the proposal incorporates data reduction and preprocessing techniques. Specifically, delta sampling is introduced as an effective method for compressing constrained and noisy datasets by rationally selecting a minimal amount of data for training. Experimental results demonstrate that delta sampling R-BERT achieves superior action recognition accuracy compared to baseline models in low-light and full-light settings, in accordance with expectations. However, the notable improvement in constrained datasets is attributed to data-specific findings. Moreover, the proposed method's efficacy is validated across multiple dataset evaluations. In contrast to other compression methods, delta sampling outperforms them by a significant margin of 10-20% in action recognition accuracy in all evaluated datasets. In practical application, the proposed method achieves tangible benefits, such as reduced training time, compressed model size, and increased generalizability. In particular, the model's ability to generalize well to full-light videos, after training on low-light datasets, has implications for developing more robust action recognition models. In addition, the proposal's results support the idea that action recognition in videos is distinct from image recognition in terms of data requirements. In conclusion, delta sampling R-BERT has the potential to address the persistent issue of action recognition in low-light and constrained datasets, underscoring the need for more advanced and robust models that can generalize well to full-light and high-quality datasets, without the need for explicit data augmentation methods. In order to foster further research in this area, the proposal provides comprehensive experimental results, in-depth analysis, and actionable insights. In addition, the proposal introduces an open-source implementation of delta sampling R-BERT, along with an accompanying dataset compression tool, both available on GitHub under the permissive MIT License. In particular, the proposal's evaluation framework, which leverages the well-established Hyperopt-Distribution-Free (HDF) library for efficient and reliable hyperparameter optimization, enables reproducible experimentation and effortless hyperparameter tuning. We introduce a novel Concept called Content Addressable Concurrent Processors (CACP), which combines the speed of content-addressable memory with the versatility of programmable processors, leveraging this to tackle complex, data-driven problems. By serving as a programing framework as well as a hardware design, CACP enables both researcher and engineer to benefit from its capabilities. We have designed and constructed an operating system for a reconfigurable CACP using a Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA), which can support up to 64 concurrent searches within its 36 look-up tables, or we can change this to accommodate other types of search operations on the CACP array. We have also successfully applied CACP to solve two difficult problems: solving a Rubik's Cube in all possible permutations and identifying all possible permutations of a given sequence. Our results with CACP show an impressive speedup over software-based solutions, with CACP outperforming them by as much as 450 times for certain data sets, especially those with higher levels of duplication, primarily as a result of its ability to search multiple locations at the same time. In a system with a CACP and a host computer connected via a bus, we have observed a slight performance impact due to the overhead of communicating with the hardware, but we believe this can be mitigated by optimizing the communication protocol and using a faster bus. We have made FPGAs-based CACP available for public use and we believe it has the potential to be useful for a wide range of applications, such as searching large databases, searching for patterns in large datasets, and system management, among others. We have also discussed possible ways to improve CACP further, such as using a more complex search operation, using a different type of memory, and using a different type of interconnect, and we have designed a possible way to integrate CACP with a software system using a host computer, but we have not built or tested these variations. We have presented the design and performance of CACP in detail, including its hardware and software components, but we have not discussed its relationship to other concepts, such as neural networks, and we have not mentioned its potential to be used as a tool for teaching computer architecture and systems. We have written this paper in a formal and objective style, but we have not followed all the guidelines, such as providing a clear statement of the problem and a detailed description of the scope. We have cited some related work, such as memory systems, but we have not discussed the differences between CACP and these systems

We've conducted an in-depth analysis of nine galaxies at $z=2.7$ within a distant cluster that accretes stars, using Hubble Space Telescope observations and modeling of their structural development. These galaxies have mass ranges from $10^{9.2}$ to $10^{11.2}$ $M_{\odot}$ and exhibit diverse morphologies, with some featuring disordered star formation and others possessing orderly stellar patterns. A comparison of 24 individual galaxies at $z=2.7$ and $z=3$ has revealed that 12 of them possess orderly stellar arrangements at $z=2.7$, with 7 of these displaying disordered star formation at a higher redshift. These findings indicate that 50% of galaxies with orderly stellar arrangements at $z=2.7$ transition from disordered to orderly star formation, while 37% exhibit disordered star formation at $z=2.7$ that transitions to orderly at a higher redshift. A comparison of 12 individual galaxies at $z=2.7$ and $z=3$ has shown that 7 of them possess disordered star formation at both redshifts, with 5 displaying orderly stellar arrangements at a higher redshift. Bulge development is prevalent among galaxies with orderly stellar arrangements, whereas those with disordered star formation primarily form irregular stellar mass accumulations. This research focuses on connecting a specific class of set-theoretic solutions to the Yang-Baxter equation, as described in [1], with quasi-bialgebras. It is demonstrated that every set-theoretic solution lying within a particular variety, along with its associated matrix units, can be used to construct a quasi-bialgebras. Conversely, it is shown that any quasi-bialgebras of this form is an element of that set-theoretic variety. Furthermore, this connection between set-theoretic solutions and quasi-bialgebras is utilized to establish and prove certain criteria for a given variety to contain solutions equivalent to a specific quasi-bialgebras. An example is also provided to illustrate the concept of graded or diagonal solutions within this context. Finally, the paper investigates its main theorem when restricted to single generators, providing an alternative proof for several known results in the field.

This paper introduces quaternary and binary Golay complementary structures in multi-carrier formats, specifically applying them to OFDM and FBMC. Initially, we create a FBMC-GC structure and demonstrate its energy efficiency in quadrature amplitude modulation. Then, we design a 16-QAM FBMC-GC structure by combining two 4-QAM FBMC-GC structures in a manner analogous to octagonal frequency hopping multiple access. Both theoretical and measured results indicate our 16-QAM FBMC-GC structure achieves a 32% power saving compared to conventional FBMC and a 12% power saving compared to FBMC-OQAM with 16-QAM, under certain channel conditions. Our proposed designs also exhibit similar performance to their single-carrier counterparts in terms of BER. Additionally, we propose a method for constructing FBMC-GC structures with larger sizes and discuss potential applications and future research directions for these structures. Experimental demonstrations of our proposed designs, including a 16-QAM FBMC-GC structure with an OFDM-FBMC composite structure, show both reduced out-of-band power and improved spectral efficiency. Introduction Multiple-carrier formats such as OFDM and FBMC have become widely adopted in various wireless communication systems due to their ability to counteract frequency-selective fading. In recent years, research has focused on reducing the out-of-band power of these systems through the application of Golay complementary sequences in multi-carrier structures. Such configurations have been explored for their potential to decrease the side lobes of a system's spectrum, thereby enhancing system performance. Quaternary and binary Golay complementary structures have been explored for FBMC-OQAM and OFDM, respectively. Quantum computing's future relies heavily on vacuum-controlled interactions between precise, adjustable variables - in this case, spin and valley states. This study leverages sophisticated scanning tunneling microscopy to manipulate and study silicon surface atoms with precision. By placing a xenon adatom nearby, researchers efficiently coupled and separated the valley and spin states without interference from hyperfine interactions. This achieved transfer of spin or valley information through direct exchange or orbital alignment, or a combination of both, using the adatom as a mediator. Finally, this work demonstrates robust valley-dependent exchange and the potential for chemical manipulation of surface sites to enhance desired interactions over intervalley gaps, laying the groundwork for complex operations between coupled qubits located near molecules. In response to irradiation, the system exhibits resilience, indicating the adatom's efficacy as a bridge between silicon's surface and its core, setting the stage for integrating group of qubits via a mediator. This work is also relevant to research involving silicon-vacancy centers in diamond, demonstrating the feasibility of precise, chemical manipulation of vacuum-based interactions in silicon. This is further highlighted in the accompanying editorial by Jelezko. Complex systems across multiple disciplines, including finance, biology, and social networks, exhibit intricate behaviors resulting from interactions between their components. Due to the difficulty of predicting their overall dynamics from scratch, researchers often leverage existing data to train graph neural network models, which can in turn provide valuable insights into the system's underlying structure and function. While such models excel at predicting future states and behavior, our work takes a different approach, focusing instead on using trained graph neural network models as a means to infer the system's underlying dynamics and architecture. By applying this method to multiple datasets, including financial time series and network processes, we demonstrate its effectiveness in accurately identifying latent factors governing the system's evolution and revealing information about its structural properties. Our approach is susceptible to diverse enhancements, including optimization technique variations and structural knowledge integration, which further amplify its capability to analyze complex systems, as validated through our experiments. Our research on graph neural network-based system analysis paves the way for exploring other aspects of complex systems and potential applications in various domains. Due to the difficulty of validating theoretical models for complex systems, which often require extensive periods for full realization, our work introduces an innovative, efficient method to assess their equilibrium, critical properties, and dynamics by utilizing trained graph neural network models, which are in turn utilized in follow-up studies to create realistic simulations and scenarios, as shown in our supplementary materials. Our work is further represented through an accompanying leaderboard featuring metrics derived from our analysis framework, which is designed to evaluate the effectiveness of various graph neural network models in capturing a system's dynamics and architecture for further use in realistic simulations and scenarios. In conclusion, our research on graph neural network-based system analysis has shown great promise and there is even greater potential for its many applications in multiple disciplines waiting to be explored and analyzed with this approach. Due to the difficulty of predicting the future behavior of complex systems through graph neural network models, our work is highly recommended for practitioners and researchers who need to analyze and understand its vast ecosystem. We introduce a counting principle called 'partitioning', enabling the counting of distinct arrangements of objects in various contexts. This is subsequently applied to homotopy theory to count specific configurations of diagrams, potentially with flaws, across diverse dimensions from 1 to 10. These counts are made available through an online database at the website homotopycount.com. Our calculations involve advanced mathematical concepts like modular forms, elliptic curves, and Galois representations. To facilitate understanding, we present detailed explanations and proofs of most counting results in an accompanying textbook style reference at refer.homotopycount.com. Notably, we prove the homotopy count conjecture first proposed by Jaffe and Katz, which asserts that certain homotopy counts correspond to the distribution of isomorphism classes of elliptic curves among all genus-one curves. Our results also cover various partitioning scenarios, including those with identical components in different configurations and those with the symmetric group W_A, the latter extending the earlier work by Armstrong. Additionally, we explore connections between homotopy theory and other areas such as algebraic geometry, geometry, and combinatorics, as well as potential applications in the study of elliptic curves and modular forms. Our research involves both computational and theoretical aspects, with a focus on the interplay between these elements. We believe that our work will not only contribute to the development of homotopy theory but also shed light on fundamental concepts in other areas. Ultimately, our goal is to create an open-source framework for the study of homotopy types, encompassing not only partitioning but also other computational aspects, with a comprehensive database of reference cases available at refer.homotopycount.com. We anticipate that this project will attract the attention of both experts and students in mathematics, potentially leading to new research directions, such as the analysis of our general partitioning conjectures, or the exploration of homotopy types in other categories, as well as the visualization of our results through the development of our accompanying visualization library, viz.homotopycount.com, or the application of our results to his field of study. We hope that our work will inspire a broader exploration of the connections between mathematics and computer science within the academic community. Clinical experts at tertiary hospitals across Asia leverage their judgments in ASCOT (Adams & Stratton's Cerebral Atrophy Test Scheme) to assess cerebral disorders. A pioneering Asian dataset, ASCOT, is established based on these judgments and in conjunction with diverse MRI data, thereby facilitating the development of cutting-edge brain lesion prediction models. A cutting-edge framework, named Progressive PAC-VAE, is introduced to address this difficulty. PAC-VAE, a cutting-edge framework, endeavors to craft realistic cerebral lesion masks through an adversarial approach while generating plausible cerebral region maps. Cerebral region map generation is achieved via an encoder-decoder model, whereas a trained discriminator facilitates the creation of realistic lesion masks in a progressive manner, guided by progressive training and expert feedback. The effectiveness of the progressive PAC-VAE framework is demonstrated through the unparalleled performance it achieves on the newly introduced ASCOT dataset, outperforming a range of baseline models. Notably, this model has potential applications in the creation of synthetic, annotated datasets, an invaluable resource for medical researchers. The code for the introduced model is available for reproducibility purposes. This enhanced model has shown remarkable improvement on the ASCOT dataset, especially when processing MRI scans with different resolution levels. Our findings demonstrate that the unextendable product bases (UPBs) within these contexts remain resilient to both classical and environmental attacks, exhibiting robust quantum nonlocality in a wide range of situations. GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, also suitable for specifying and generating programs. GP 2 has inherent symmetry which simplification techniques take advantage of to produce more effective and readable code. The GP 2 compiler has undergone enhancements to leverage symmetric properties in its algorithms, leading to better code performance, readability, and reliability. Despite its potential, GP 2 has seen limited use, likely due to the compiler's limited capabilities and the absence of the GP 2 toolkit. We present an updated GP 2 compiler, embedded within a enhanced GP 2 toolkit with a user interface and all development open-source and freely available. We demonstrate the compiler's effectiveness by applying it to various program verification scenarios and comparing its outcomes to those from existing program verification tools. The GP 2 compiler and the GP 2 toolkit are both available at https://github.com/andreabacchini/GP2. We invite researchers to experiment with the compiler and the toolkit, expressing their opinions through the GP 2 forum at https://github.com/andreabacchini/GP2/issues. We discuss potential applications and case studies for the GP 2 compiler and the GP 2 toolkit, highlighting their versatility and adaptability, as well as our vision for the future of the GP 2 compiler and the GP 2 toolkit. Attribute extraction, a subject of current interest, is not fully mechanized despite significant academic efforts. Our proposed model, a unified structure that incorporates Self-Supervised Contrastive Learning for Attribute Extraction (SSCLAE), makes notable breakthroughs in this area. SSCLAE is a data-independent framework that leverages pre-trained visual representation tools and simplifies the attribute extraction task to a single contrastive learning step. This simplification eliminates the need for explicit attribute classification modules and instead utilizes K-means clustering to directly assign labels to visual features. Our experiments demonstrate SSCLAE's effectiveness and efficiency on the ADE20K dataset, achieving exceptional performance without relying on complex architectures, vast datasets, or sophisticated optimization methods. Our results show that SSCLAE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on evaluation sets without relying on evaluation set data during training and surpasses industry-leading methods that require independent attribute extraction models. Our implementation of SSCLAE on the STC dataset produces underwhelming results, attributing this to the dataset's limitations. Conversely, our findings on ADE20K indicate that attributes are easily extractable when based on object classes, as confirmed by our reevaluation of both datasets with a focus on object-class-based attribute extraction. Our research on ADE20K sets a new high mark for the attribute extraction task with a 57.57% map score. Our work on SSCLAE proposes innovative solutions to attribute extraction-related challenges and offers a versatile framework that facilitates research on this subject. Furthermore, our research on the relationship between objects and attributes opens up new research avenues and provides a perspective on combining object detection and attribute extraction. Our work on the SSCLAE model and its extensions, made available at our GitHub repository, is an example of the potential of self-supervised contrastive learning to unify structure in attribute extraction. As attribute extraction is a one-time task for each attribute on a given dataset, our research suggests that a more practical approach is to treat attribute extraction as a one-time task rather than a learning process. Our work on the unified structure for attribute extraction raises questions regarding scene parsing, an area with connections to attribute extraction, and proposes a simple yet effective method for extracting semantic attributes from visual data. Lastly, our research on the SSCLAE model and its underlying principles can facilitate exploration of other data-independent learning problems through the application of self-supervised contrastive learning. Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires custom implementations for each new variable, even for an established algorithm like Group Lasso. This research proposes an Enhanced Group Lasso method to automate the process of handling categorical data by adapting the Lasso objective function using a technique called "grouping by hashing," which enables the discovery of relevant categories without prior knowledge and reduces overfitting by regulating the hash collision rate. Our theoretical analysis and empirical studies demonstrate that ENHANCE, as the method is called, offers equivalent performance to traditional Group Lasso when working with numerical data and successfully extracts valuable categorical information in multiple scenarios, including real-world datasets. Compared to other high-dimensional learning algorithms, ENHANCE shows comparable performance with state-of-the-art methods but has the unique advantage of handling categorical variables without needing custom code, making it an attractive option for big data with numerous categorical variables. This new algorithm is particularly well-suited for fields like genetics, medicine, and social sciences, where variables often have a binary or nominal nature and can have up to 50 dimensions in some cases. By applying ENHANCE to the DREAM Challenge dataset and several other genetic datasets, we have observed encouraging results, including instances where the algorithm selected only a few key genes in microarray data with thousands of variables. This discovery is significant because it demonstrates the ability of ENHANCE to effectively handle a broad category of variables, including both numerical and categorical data, and highlights its potential as a universal sparse modeling algorithm capable of dealing with various types of variables without the need for custom feature engineering. This research provides a detailed explanation of the Enhance Group Lasso method, including a comprehensive theoretical analysis of its properties and extensive empirical evaluations of its performance in multiple scenarios. This work also introduces a new hashing framework for sparse modeling, called HFS, which offers a more flexible way of discovering relevant features by grouping data points using a technique called "feature hashing." This framework can be applied to both numerical and categorical data, and its properties are extensively evaluated in this research. By combining the grouping by hashing technique with the Group Lasso objective function, this research derives a new sparse modeling algorithm called Enhance Group Lasso, which can automatically discover relevant features without prior knowledge and reduce overfitting by regulating the hash collision rate. Large language models like T5 have demonstrated impressive capabilities in tasks like question answering and summarization. However, their performance can be further enhanced by leveraging structured knowledge, particularly when confronted with complex, loosely related information. To address this, we present a knowledge infrastructure that combines 800 Wikipedia entities and their 13,000 describing sentences into a set of structured knowledge graphs. These entities are then mapped to a vocabulary of 50, allowing for the creation of knowledge graphs with over 300 million possible entity combinations. Our method, SKILL, infuses these structured knowledge graphs into T5 through the generation of a precursor module that sets the context for relevant entity combinations. As a result, SKILL exhibits notable improvements in RACE and SQuAD when compared to a baseline model relying on unstructured knowledge. Moreover, human evaluators have confirmed the safety of this knowledge-infused model. Despite its substantial knowledge base, SKILL shows no signs of significant factual errors when evaluated using the Fact-Checked Dataset. With considerable potential for broad applicability, we believe our approach offers a viable path for integrating structured knowledge into extensive language models. We have made SKILL available for the community at https://github.com/google-research/skill. We have also explored various infrastructure modifications and have included these explorations in our study. However, some experiments were conducted over longer training periods than our primary evaluation, which is defined by a 100-million-parameter T5 as our standard model. We have used this model to demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in other evaluation benchmarks, including additional T5 parameter counts, models like BART and ALBERT, as well as in two real-world applications involving the generation of program summaries and legal documents. Our results indicate that our method yields consistent gains over a baseline model relying on unstructured knowledge for all models and scenarios examined. We have included our methodology for generating program summaries and legal documents along with our code and knowledge infrastructure in our full implementation, which is accessible at https://google.github.io/skill-demo/. We have addressed several safety concerns that arose over the course of our experiments and have outlined strategies for safely integrating structured knowledge into extensive language models. These strategies involve the implementation of entity-based masking, the enforcement of knowledge graph constraints during the generation of context, and the inclusion of fact-checking within the training loop. When combining panoramic images, devices like 360 cameras and smartphones automatically activate their stitching mode to merge images. However, this feature often fails when the user tilts the device, limiting its usage in various situations. To overcome this restriction, this paper explores basic methods for stitching images, considering how users naturally move their heads in response to external forces. By applying mathematical formulas to describe these movements, we transform the stitching problem into a 2D geometric challenge. To validate our approach, we developed two minimalistic prototypes, one for circular and another for angular movements, and tested them against a broader range of head movements. Our findings show that both methods can handle various tilting, scanning, and rotational head movements with equal ease, and therefore, provide a significant improvement over the existing features of 360 cameras and smartphones. This research explores the relationship between certain Gelfand-MacPherson intersections and the elimination of poles of Eisenstein series on $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$. Specifically, for given degree $k$ and weights $\mu$, we establish the equivalence between a specific combinatorial problem and the description of the elimination of poles of Eisenstein series in the form $E(\gamma, k, \mu)$. Our analysis extends to polynomial Eisenstein series and their generalizations in $GL(n+m,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$. Our findings build upon prior work by Gelfand and MacPherson, Hanzer and Muić, and Jiang, among others. Our main contribution is a bijective mapping between irreducible partitions of $\{1,\ldots,k\}$ and the elimination of poles of Eisenstein series, expressed as a combination of Gelfand-MacPherson intersections. This connection enables us to determine all irreducible combinations of these intersections for $k \leq 5$. Our analysis reveals that some of these combinations correspond to polynomials with positive coefficients, aligning with conjectures of Jiang and Muić. Our research also establishes connections between the combinatorial aspects and sieve-related questions. Our analysis involves the examination of polynomial combinations over number fields and local fields, including non-Archimedean settings. Our results provide a foundation for further exploration and potential applications to areas such as automorphic forms and algebraic geometry. Our work is complemented by illustrations of these objects, along with their representations in various mathematical structures, including monoids, lattices, and finite groups. We've created a biophysical computational model of a primate basal ganglia to understand the neural mechanisms behind Parkinson's disease. To develop this model, we leveraged recent advances in Parkinson's research, specifically those identified in a previous study involving marmoset monkeys. This model incorporates specific changes in brain activity patterns and neural characteristics that are associated with the disease, as identified through in vivo recordings and brain tissue analysis. Specifically, it incorporates the abnormal synchronization of beta oscillations, enhanced gamma amplitude, and altered spike phase responsiveness in the globus pallidus. We've tested this model's ability to replicate the abnormal beta oscillations and spike phase resetting curves observed in the globus pallidus of marmoset monkeys with Parkinson's disease-like symptoms. Our results show that the model is capable of producing beta-thalamus synchronization and simulated in vivo spike phase resetting curves similar to those found in marmoset monkeys with Parkinson's disease-like symptoms, and that optimizing key model parameters is crucial for replicating their brain activity patterns. We also explored the model's predictions for the effects of deep brain stimulation on beta oscillations and found that it accurately replicates the observed effects of this treatment. Overall, our data-informed biophysical computational model of Parkinson's disease provides a valuable framework for predicting the underlying neural mechanisms and potential treatment outcomes and can be a useful tool for guiding experimental designs and future studies. Furthermore, this model can be a useful starting point for modeling Parkinson's disease in other primate species. We have made this model publicly available to facilitate its further development and to provide a resource for researchers working in this area. We believe that this model will contribute to a better understanding of the underlying neural mechanisms behind Parkinson's disease and can be a valuable asset for the research community. We have already used this model to guide our experimental design for an upcoming study, and we are confident that it will be a valuable resource for other researchers working in this area. We have attached a copy of this model to this report, and it can also be downloaded from the following website: https://zenodo.org/record/7214950. To regulate and limit greenhouse gas emissions, remote-sensing technology is used to monitor land use through various spectral images. This monitoring is achieved via Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models that classify images into predefined climate categories for further analysis in the preparation of emission regulations. However, the limited availability and diversity of existing datasets in this field hinder accurate emissions assessments. To address this challenge, a new multi-class dataset called Climate-500 is introduced, comprising 5000 high-resolution images from 12 distinct climate regions across China, characterized by diverse terrain, vegetation, and urban areas. Due to limited and expensive spectral data, enhancing datasets via super-resolution techniques is also explored. The Climate-500 dataset is utilized to assess the spectral and spatial generalization of CNN models in both targeted and novel settings. The results of experiments using UNET and DeepSat highlight the significance of model transfer in accurately monitoring emissions, emphasizing the need for further research on generalizable models in this field. The Climate-500 dataset is available for download at https://github.com/zwang-ewu/Climate-500-dataset, providing a valuable resource for researchers in the field of emission forecasting and environmental monitoring. In addition, methods developed in this study are also applicable to enhanced datasets in the field of land cover classification. In contrast to monolithic approaches, the proposed framework offers a new methodology for enhancing and evaluating spectral-spatial models through the Climate-500 Enhancement and Assessment (CEA) framework. The CEA framework is comprised of two primary modules: a data enhancement branch and a performance assessment branch. The data enhancement branch is characterized by the incorporation of novel spectral and spatial attention mechanisms in UNET, enabling the enhancement of datasets in both the spectral and spatial dimensions. On the other hand, the performance assessment branch is centered on the evaluation of models using diverse evaluation metrics for both monolithic and hypertask scenarios. Moreover, an innovative hyperspectral classification task is introduced to assess the capability of models to handle complex, unseen scenarios at evaluation time. Furthermore, the CEA framework is used to investigate the effectiveness of model-based enhancement in both monolithic and hypertask scenarios. The results of experiments using the CEA framework highlight the significance of model-based enhancement in both monolithic and hypertask scenarios, providing the framework's implementation at https://github.com/zwang-ewu/Climate-500-dataset. Finally, the CEA framework is introduced as an open-source platform that is highly adaptable and is expected to serve as a benchmark for the evaluation of generalizable models in the field

Unlike previous studies, our approach avoids artificial boundary layers by maintaining the same viscosity for both fluids and eliminates the need for turbulent closure models through constant viscosity and heat conductivity values. Our project involves a single column where water vapor and dry air coexist, and we apply a similar approach to resolve thermal and flux boundary layers. Our method simulates convection using basic physical equations with minimal external influences, resulting in the development of chaotic and persistent patterns similar to those found in laboratory RB convection experiments. Our study reveals how both updrafts and downdrafts maintain their respective speeds through buoyancy forces, and how water vapor viscosity impacts the flow by an amount equivalent to the viscosity impact when considering only dry air. Our research also shows how water vapor viscosity affects both flux and temperature profiles within both the bottom and top boundary layers. Our study provides a foundation for expanding this two-fluid model to a three-dimensional model, representing the atmosphere as multiple fluids, in an effort to better understand atmospheric circulation through the simulation of RB convection. We investigate a scenario in which two distant, uncorrelated atoms undergo Jaynes-Cummings interactions with respect to separate beams of quantum light. This scenario allows for the creation of genuine entanglement in both atoms, even when they start out in a correlated state with respect to an arbitrary variable. A specific approach to achieving this is outlined when the atoms are initially correlated according to a Werner state - this method demonstrates the ability to control the final outcome through adjustments in various key parameters. A particular focus is on identifying conditions under which the resulting state is most highly entangled, as determined by the entanglement measure known as the von Neumann entropy, as well as the stability of this outcome when minor changes occur in the initial state or the parameters involved in the Jaynes-Cummings process. A novel application arises from the fact that the described Jaynes-Cummings interactions can mimic the actions of a cavity, even when the two distant, uncorrelated atoms are connected by an lossy channel - this raises the possibility of genuinely entangling uncorrelated photons in separate locations. The Compact Muon Solenoid at CERN's Large Hadron Collider undergoes an upgrade, featuring a new forward pixel detector with enhanced capabilities. As part of the new system's development, a prototype detector was tested with lead-proton collisions from 2016 LHC data, featuring a new readout system and chip design. The study focuses on a prototype component known as the B-layer prototype, specifically a section called the "outer" slice with increased gain values. A detailed analysis of this prototype's performance was conducted using a lead-proton collision dataset of 12 TeV center-of-mass energy and 144 nanobarn of integrated luminosity. The examination of the prototype's performance showed improved hit efficiency results for the increased gain values, with efficiencies reaching 99.5% in the highest gain setting. Additionally, hit position and momentum dispersion were found to be comparable to design specifications. A 1.3 millimeter square feature was found to be reconstructed in some instances, demonstrating the detector's ability to handle complex geometries. The evaluation of track finding systems revealed no significant differences in efficiency or momentum dispersion. However, a slight increase in efficiency was observed in smaller gain values due to higher hit detection rates. The study demonstrated the B-layer prototype's ability to operate effectively during lead-proton collisions at the LHC, providing valuable insights for the further development of the detector. These findings are also relevant to other LHC experiments that utilize silicon detectors. As such, the study's results are being presented at the MIP2016 and 12th Conference on Discrete Optimization in Large-scale Electromagnetic Computing Fields workshops. Furthermore, the study's results have been submitted for publication in the Journal of Physics: Conference Series and the Journal of Instrumentation. A crucial aspect of quantum field theory is the study of hadron structure through form factors and the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectrum. This work presents the analytical Kall\'en-Lehmann representation of the scalar glueball's form factor and spectral density within the SU(2) gauge theory, enabling semi-quantitative interpretations with theoretical models. A notable feature of the SU(2) theory is that lattice artifacts vanish at the point of measurement, allowing for a more direct comparison between theoretical predictions and experimental data. This comparison is carried out for the SU(2) glueball's mass in its ground state, with the result being $m \approx 1.16\pm0.02$ GeV, a value that aligns with the mass ranges estimated through lattice QCD at a comparable lattice spacing. This work also explores systematics in lattice QCD, identifying a possible explanation for discrepancies in lattice QCD mass predictions, which could be addressed by considering quark mass dependence within each lattice regime rather than treating it as a constant parameter. Ultimately, this study upholds the view that the SU(2) glueball provides a suitable testing ground for the fundamental principles of quantum field theory. This research also includes an evaluation of model systematics against lattice data, with an emphasis on quark mass dependence in lattice QCD, with implications that extend to the study of hadron properties in lattice QCD. The success of advanced methods in computing, such as deep learning and evolutionary algorithms, has been consistently demonstrated across multiple fields. However, there is still a significant challenge to be addressed - the problem of combining computational models with physical laws to predict the behavior of dynamic biological systems, particularly those affected by external influences and subject to seasonal changes. As part of the G'dai Project, our research focuses on applying this type of prediction capability to address critical issues in agriculture, such as plant disease management. To illustrate its value, we present a disease management system for strawberries utilizing a predictive model that incorporates a method to determine the effectiveness of control measures. By leveraging a structured assessment framework, we evaluate the performance of different control strategies in a systematic way, providing specific recommendations for a strawberry crop scenario based on data collected in the state of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The results show that the assessment framework can identify the most reliable control methods, even in the presence of uncertain predictions, resulting in a 25% reduction in disease severity when compared to standard sensing-based approaches, such as visual inspection and temperature measurements, and a 50% reduction in unnecessary control actions. Furthermore, this disease management system, using a predictive model, demonstrates its potential to improve crop yields by more than 20% in controlled experiments, highlighting the potential benefits of this approach in agriculture. The implementation of this technique in strawberry disease management also sets the stage for its broader application across multiple crop types and regions, such as corn, soybean, and coffee in Brazil, as well as wheat and barley in the United States, among others. Additionally, this research is an invitation to the broader machine learning community to explore and address this significant challenge in computational biology through the G'dai Competition, a new benchmarking initiative launched in conjunction with this work. The competition challenges participants to develop more accurate predictive models capable of handling dynamic biological systems by submitting their entries to the competition platform, which is accessible via the website at https://www.aicrowd.com/datasets/3429. The leaderboards for different problem scenarios can be found at https://www.aicrowd.com/teams/3423/submissions/16 and https://www.aicrowd.com/teams/3423/submissions/17. The underlying data and analysis code are available at https://github.com/ricardo-cpw/gdai-strawberry. The disease management system, along with its assessment framework and predictive model, are available at https://github.com/ricardo-cpw/gdai-strawberry/tree/master

360-degree travel videos allow viewers to navigate a scene in any direction, but creating an engaging viewer experience also demands attention from the viewer. Current studies have focused on detection systems for specific actions, but these systems require real-world references and often struggle with natural language instructions. In contrast, our research centers on predicting viewer behavior based on subtitles, which are now a standard component of 360-degree videos. We leverage advanced artificial intelligence techniques, including attention mechanisms and bidirectional transformers, to forecast which parts of the scene viewers will focus on and in what direction they will navigate when prompted by subtitles. Experiments revealed that our viewport forecasting system excels at detecting viewer attention and navigation following natural language instructions, outperforming systems that rely solely on natural language or scene data. Moreover, our evaluation showed that incorporating subtitles into our framework enhances the system's overall performance. We believe that predicting viewer behavior based on subtitles and scene data will contribute to designing more effective, data-driven 360-degree travel videos. We also found that certain phrases in travel videos trigger similar viewer actions and encourage travel producers to employ these phrases in their subtitles, which in turn can be used as a basis for a travel vocabulary that anticipates viewer behavior. We have made our dataset and forecasting system available for further development of travel video content and related systems. Nonetheless, our research indicates that producing high-quality 360-degree travel videos with a strong viewer experience requires not only visually appealing scenery but also engaging subtitles that anticipate viewer behavior. Consequently, we propose the challenge of forecast-based travel video editing, which involves reordering video segments based on a given instruction to enhance the viewer experience, as an area worthy of exploration by the research community. We have demonstrated an initial approach to solving this problem, but it is essential to address the significant differences that distinguish it from other video editing problems. Specifically, our problem involves a larger vocabulary of instruction phrases, a more extensive range of navigation actions within unstructured 360-degree scenes, and limited real-world examples of high-quality 360-degree travel videos that demonstrate excellent viewer experience. Therefore, validating the results of travel video editing systems is more intricate than with other types of video, as it necessitates the use of objective metrics that evaluate the system's forecast accuracy in addition to subjectively assessing the viewer experience. We have introduced an innovative method for assessing the viewer experience by combining forecast accuracy with subjective ratings from real-world travel data, but this method needs to be refined further. Nonetheless, our research has underscored the significance of forecast-based travel video editing as a promising direction for further exploration

The Microscope space mission, launched in 2016, aims to set limits on the cosmological violation of the weak equivalence principle by testing the ratio of the accelerations of two test masses under relevant frequencies and temperatures. To achieve this, Microscope measures the position of a gold mass relative to a platinum mass in the same environment, monitoring any possible differences in their inertial and gravitational masses which would manifest as a relative displacement. The mission's success relies on controlling temperature fluctuations and mechanical anomalies known as glitches in the two masses' behavior. The statistics and analysis of these glitches are crucial in establishing the mission's sensitivity limits and potential biases, and it is essential to assess their impact and combine the constraints on the mission's parameters accordingly. This paper presents the method for statistical analysis of glitches and their influence on the evaluation of the weak equivalence principle, and it sets the framework for the derivation of bias correction terms for the M√ller-Maier-Saupe parameter, $ \Lambda_{MMS} $, employed in the analysis of the Microscope data. This assessment reveals that Borel-Bessen and variational approaches for this distribution are remarkably close to each other. As a result, we obtained a well-defined and well-behaved Borel integral for the color dipole gluon distribution at very low values of x, which is consistent with the expectations from saturation models. Conversely, the impact of infrared renormalons leads to the introduction of an extra factor of around x^-1 when comparing Borel-Bessen and variational approaches to the color dipole gluon distribution to saturation model approaches, ultimately indicating that the latter are dominated by the leading logarithmic contribution. Furthermore, we found that the variational approach for the color dipole gluon distribution at very low values of x is dominated by the leading logarithmic contribution, which is in line with the findings from impact parameter space evolution equations that demonstrate the UV stability of TMD PDF. As a consequence, the observed discrepancy between Borel-Bessen and variational approaches for the color dipole gluon distribution at very low values of x remains unresolved. In addition, we extracted a preliminary estimate for the variance of the logarithmic integral for the color dipole gluon distribution at very low values of x, which is consistent with the predictions from BFKL evolution, while also identifying the influence of initial conditions on this quantity, which is governed by the ratio of initial conditions for the dipole and jet functions, denoted as R, which is equal to around 10 for N=4 SYM but only around 3 for two-colour QCD. Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. Despite some successful constructions for specific modules (notably those associated with cyclic groups and their direct products), the task becomes significantly harder when dealing with more complex modules. For instance, even basic information about the lattice of submodules is not known for certain modules like the permutation module over the symmetric group S4. This paper addresses this gap by S4 by systematically determining the lattice of submodules of its permutation module in a comprehensive and explicit manner. Building on this achievement, the paper also explores and establishes connections between different constructions of the lattice of submodules, using them to verify local completeness and other properties of the lattice. These constructions rely heavily on an in-depth analysis of the module's composition series, and utilize a novel approach to combine disparate submodules, demonstrating the applicability of these methods to specific composition series. The paper is a follow-up to an earlier conference paper presented at MSJ-RCM 2017, and has far more comprehensive and detailed results. We examine a critical problem in system identification, where an unknown node's values are determined by a majority of its neighbors' observations, assuming a quadratic cost function and maximal reliability. Specifically, we focus on a robust version of this problem, where the determination of the unknown node's values is affected by an external malicious force. We investigate this problem for two types of connections: any subset of nodes can form a strong connection, implying that an identification algorithm exists; however, we have found instances of 4-node clusters and 5-node clusters that require nearly the total number of nodes for a strong connection in the general graph scenario, as well as an examination of geodetic identification in tree-like structures, although there are non-triangular structures that cannot be fully identified through geodetic connectivity. We developed an efficient identification algorithm for specific strong connection patterns, including linear connection, and demonstrated its performance in practice, although we were unable to establish any general positive results for strong connection. We established a NP-hard classification for the robust geodetic identification problem, focusing on positive solutions from our results rather than complexity. We proposed a dynamic programming approach that leads to near-optimal performance in practice and derived specific near-optimal bounds for certain strong connection patterns, including linear connection and a connection similar to a triangle, and demonstrated the effectiveness of this strategy on various instances, although we were unable to generalise this approach for any strong connection due to limitations in our knowledge at the time of publication. Imitating complex behaviors typically demands substantial labeled data, which is often a significant obstacle. Another issue arises from common supervision methods that force an agent to replicate exact actions, rather than capturing the underlying principles of the task. This limitation is highlighted by requiring the agent to navigate from a random start to a goal position in a diverse set of maze environments, using only sparse rewards, and then recreating the optimal path using only a limited and randomly sampled subset of trajectories. Our solution, known as TRAIL, employs an unsupervised transformation to enrich the imitation data by transforming the diverse starting positions into a single standard start, successfully reducing the necessary labeled data by sevenfold for certain maze configurations. When evaluated on a broader range of maze shapes and sizes, TRAIL proves particularly effective at imitation when compared to alternative methods, such as data augmentation and robust optimization, as evident from our findings presented at the Thirty-Ninth International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2021). Our research provides the first systematic analysis of the close-to-ideal imitation learning paradigm and offers TRAIL as a viable solution to be tested on other behavior replication tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/main/trailencode. Our paper is available at arXiv:2107.00806v2. Our paper has been cited 23 times and our code has been downloaded 104 times. Since its publication, our research has been presented at two workshops: the Imitation Learning Workshop co-located with ICML 2021 and the Learning from Low-Data Shots Workshop co-located with ICLR 2022. Our research is ongoing, and we continue to explore new starting position transformation methods. One such method, known as TRAIL2, combines the unsupervised transformation used in TRAIL with a supervised transformation, using a learned map, and has shown promising results, requiring only a 2x reduction in labeled data compared to baseline imitation learning on a specific maze configuration. TRAIL2 is an active area of research in our group, and we anticipate presenting our findings at a conference in the near future. TRAIL2 is available at https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/main/trailencode. This paper proposes a framework for evaluating code performance in the PAC metric, a flexible and asymmetric measure of error that diverges from traditional Hamming distance. Due to its computational advantages, several coding optimization techniques compute an equivalent but more tractable distance, such as the generalized Hamming distance for irregular graphs. In contrast, the Hamming distance is computationally expensive for large-scale applications, such as training and inference in deep learning-based compression methods. Our framework addresses this challenge by introducing a binary representation of code word comparisons that enables PAC values to be calculated efficiently. Specifically, we demonstrate the computation of PAC for regular low-density parity-check codes and propose an extension to turbo and polar codes, leveraging their underlying structural connections, which further enhances computational efficiency. Our results show that, in many cases, the simplified distance measures closely approximate the true PAC values with high accuracy, indicating our framework's practical usefulness for a broad code ensemble. Our code is publicly available on an open-source platform. Furthermore, we explore the trade-off between computational complexity and accuracy in our framework, finding that slight density irregularities can yield high accuracy at a lower computational cost, which we exemplify through the construction of irregular low-density parity-check codes. In these examples, the proposed framework achieves a computational complexity of $O(n)$ in comparison to the naive method's $O(n^2)$, where $n$ represents the number of code bits. Leveraging our framework, we investigate the fundamental properties of PAC codes, uncovering insights that could guide code design, such as the fact that large-scale low-density parity-check codes cannot achieve a zero PAC error under certain conditions and that the distribution of PAC values in code ensembles exhibits distinct patterns, distinguishable from random permutations. Our findings suggest that our framework is applicable to a wide range of codes, indicating its utility in evaluating and designing various codes. One significant challenge in neural machine translation (NMT) is improving the diversity of generated sentences. Despite significant research in this area, current methods still struggle to prevent the test set from being dominated by a small number of high-frequency sentences. One key obstacle to achieving diversity is the restriction of only considering the previous source sentence as input, which hindering the ability to select diverse outputs in comparison to other data-driven tasks. To overcome this limitation, our proposed method leverages reinforcement learning to unlock the potential of the source sentence corpus to guide the translation of each individual sentence. However, a significant hurdle in implementing this idea is the enormous size of the action space, which is equivalent to the total number of source sentences. To address this, we developed a novel technique that reduces the action space while preserving its representativeness, resulting in substantial gains of up to 1.31 in test set diversity and no significant reduction in translation quality. Our model also achieves state-of-the-art performance on eight different data sets, outperforming the baseline by 0.17 in BLEU metric while increasing the diversity by a substantial 1.19. One notable observation is that the model's ability to choose diverse outputs does not come at the cost of quality. Our quantitative analysis reveals a substantial 12.4% rise in the number of good-quality translations alongside diverse outputs. One key factor contributing to this gain is the model's ability to select outputs with higher frequency and higher quality in the eight data sets. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/Reinforced-Source-Sentence-Selection-for-NMT. Within this framework, various applications such as stability in atomic and molecular structures, chemical bond formation, and material stability depend on the interplay between relativistic and quantum effects. It has been established that in certain situations, relativistic and Fermi pressures not only coexist but also complement each other to maintain equilibrium. This equilibrium is characterized by a specific, self-contained environment called the QFS-zone, where both pressures exert influence. A key feature of this zone is that it harbors stable atomic and molecular states within it, and its boundaries are defined by the overlap of an atom's or molecule's potential energy and the influence of its boundary, known as the 'wall potential'. A notable aspect of the QFS-zone is that it enables the existence of bound states for positive energy levels, and it is possible to adjust this environment by modifying the wall potential's shape or its curvature, thereby creating novel opportunities for discovering novel atomic and molecular states. A discussion of the parametric dependence of quadrupole and magnetic moments within this zone is also presented, and it is demonstrated that both moment values are generally large compared to their free space counterparts, and they exhibit significant variations as a function of curvature or potential shape. Our investigation discloses a diverse array of problems related to the term issue for members of the R. Thompson group V, extending previous related findings by the authors in [1]. A key area of study involves determining whether some non-trivial elements of V that are inherently periodic have a finite-related term issue. Along with this objective, we establish a broader category of elements with related term issues and correlate this with specific properties of restricted words in V. Additionally, our research identifies an unbounded, cyclic subset of problems related to the term issue for elements of V and demonstrates the implications of this for the complexity of resolving whether two given elements of V share the same underlying structure, a problem that is known to be decidible but not computable in a computable theory context. Finally, we establish an equivalence between two different formulas for calculating the order of elements within V and show this order determines the related term issue for elements that are inherently periodic. As an order-based formula can be calculated using a Turing machine that operates within V, this, in turn, confirms the related term issue is computable for such elements. Nonetheless, since V contains undecidable problems, this computable aspect is inherently embedded within an undecidable component, making this the simplest instance of an undecidable problem that is computable within a computable theory. Ultimately, due to the presence of non-trivial, inherently periodic problems within V, neither its order nor its structure can be fully captured by either a linear order nor a tree-like order. Consequently, both the order and the structure of V demonstrate similarities with that of the group denoted as F, as both are distinct from that of the group denoted as R, thus resolving a conjecture put forward by the authors in [1]. Systematic methods for generating either order-based or structure-based formulas for determining whether two elements of V share the same underlying structure or have the same order, respectively, also form a key component of our research findings presented here. Ultimately, our research extends previously established facts presented in [2] and [3]. This architecture leverages a recursive framework that allows for flexible scaling and allows for the capture of intricate patterns through the Edge-Gating unit. However, verifying the correctness of transactions in MongoDB is complicated due to its underlying technology, known as multi-document ACID. In addition, MongoDB's snapshot isolation has distinct characteristics that differ from standard implementations. To address this challenge, a validation system is required. Existing validation systems are confined to relational databases and do not cater to NoSQL databases like MongoDB. Our research introduces a novel validation framework tailored to MongoDB's transactional architecture and shotnap Isolation, employing a custom abstract syntax tree to validate transactions. Furthermore, our approach is highly efficient, with a validation time of 0.15 milliseconds on average. We investigate the properties of chromatic symmetric polynomials, specifically their contained monomials, in relation to the parameter $e$. Our findings show that any contained monomial of a chromatic symmetric polynomial, after being divided by a power of $x_1x_2$, has non-negative coefficients for an expansion related to the Schur polynomial. However, this property does not hold universally, as demonstrated by examples from graph theory. Our results do extend to certain sums of chromatic symmetric polynomials, but not universally either. The contained monomials of these extended cases can be expressed as sums of products of inverse Kostka matrices, but only in situations where these matrices maintain their original, non-degenerate form. The contained monomials of chromatic symmetric polynomials, after being divided by a power of $x_1x_2$, can be represented as a mixture of the expansion coefficients of Schur polynomials and the degenerate or non-degenerate inverse Kostka matrices, reflecting the nature of their coefficients. The coefficients of these monomials being non-negative when $e$ is positive is attributed to the characteristics of the degenerate inverse Kostka matrices, which are essentially bimodal and have a specific symmetry that contributes to this property. The contained monomials of chromatic symmetric polynomials, after being divided by a power of $x_1x_2$, share some similarities with the monomials of power sum polynomials, which are known to have non-negative coefficients for any $e$, but the former does not generally have non-negative coefficients for any $e$. The degenerate or non-degenerate inverse Kostka matrices provide a new area of study for future research, particularly in understanding the relationship between these matrices and the property of $e$-positivity. The contained monomials of some specialized chromatic symmetric polynomials, such as those related to alternating permutations, show different characteristics and may have generalizations to other areas of combinatorics. We contend that the perception of a task's difficulty can be understood through the lens of a comparison, specifically by examining how a proposed solution contrasts with alternative approaches. Within this framework, we explore the concept of executive function in relation to problem-solving, focusing on three aspects: metacognition, goal management, and habituation. In the realm of finance, we apply this framework to investment decisions and coin the term "value executive function." We create a simple model illustrating its components and habituation's effects on decision-making. Through a backtesting process, we find that value executive function tends to perform better than other strategies and is resilient in the face of market fluctuations. However, its performance can be inconsistent over extended periods. We also discovered a third aspect of value executive function, which we referred to as comparative habituation, and found it to be a crucial element in achieving success. Additionally, we observed similarities between value executive function and other areas that rely heavily on executive function, such as cognitive tasks and learning new skills. We recognized three stages in the development of value executive function: an initial phase characterized by a trial-and-error approach, a middle phase marked by a more methodical and disciplined strategy, and a later phase distinguished by an even more refined and effective investment plan. We identified several key characteristics that value executives possess at each stage of their development and proposed the term "hindsight summarizers" to describe individuals with a high level of value executive function. We proposed a set of criteria for evaluating a stock as a hindsight summarizer would, which we referred to as a "hindsight summarizer's comparative framework." We acknowledged the subjective nature of such a framework but found it to be a crucial component of a value executive function investment approach. The evaluation of medical image analysis models for prejudice requires custom-made datasets with diverse, artificially generated data labeled as biased or not. However, creating such datasets is extremely time-consuming due to the necessity for expert annotation across the entire dataset. This problem is addressed in this work by introducing a novel approach to detect intrinsic prejudice in medical image analysis models directly from their output on any given dataset, without relying on additional annotation. This method leverages contrastive learning to identify samples that trigger a model's biased behavior and uses those samples to weight the model's performance on each individual image according to its level of bias. A model that can learn to detect intrinsic prejudice on just five annotated samples per class is presented, and it demonstrates its effectiveness on two large, publicly available datasets (+2.5% and +5.6% in fair accuracy for ChestX-ray14 and DermAtlas, respectively). Notably, this approach also facilitates the identification of image regions that contribute to a model's biased performance, enabling qualitative analysis of intrinsic prejudice. Speech emotion recognition is a complex task that has gained significant attention in various applications including customer service evaluation and emotional human-computer interaction. Although deep learning methods have improved speech emotion recognition, there are significant challenges in adapting these models to new domains. A major obstacle in adapting to a new domain involves determining the optimal data sampling strategy. A domain-adapted deep reinforcement learning framework is proposed to efficiently utilize data from source and target domains. This proposed framework leverages reinforcement learning to select the most informative data for training in each domain, thereby minimizing the performance drop during adaptation. A data-sampling policy is designed to balance the utilization of data from both domains, and a value function is employed to evaluate the performance of this policy. Results indicate that this proposed framework achieves a 25.8% improvement in mean absolute error when adapting to a new domain when compared to the baseline cross-domain evaluation method. Furthermore, this framework is capable of reducing the performance degradation by 34.5% when compared to the baseline method for target speech emotion recognition. Additionally, the proposed framework is data-efficient, achieving a 1.5 times improvement in validation accuracy when compared to the baseline method for the target domain. This research tackles the challenge of sequencing operations at an airport, where flights are mixed with takeoffs and landings, and nearby airports are also considered, allowing for discrete shortest paths. Some errors inherent in these processes are caused by inaccuracies in estimating flight times and calculating distances between locations. We aim to provide upper limits for these errors in discrete shortest paths, including those with bypassing, and apply this to optimizing free flight routes. Only cases with sequential takeoffs and landings are analyzed for discrete shortest paths, and we derive error limits for these cases. We found that in certain situations, error limits for discrete shortest paths are similar to those of the continuous shortest path, but with different orderings of takeoffs and landings, the impact of errors can be significantly greater. For discrete shortest paths without bypassing, we found an even stricter condition for an error limit, but were unable to derive a general solution for cases with bypassing. Despite this, we were able to use an alternative approach to set a general error limit for discrete shortest paths, and discovered that in some instances, this limit can be tighter than the continuous error limit. We also found that in our application to free flight path optimization, the 8-ball rule used by air traffic controllers is generally consistent with our error limits, although there are some exceptions. We conclude that our research provides a more rigorous analysis of discrete shortest paths and their applications, and could be a useful tool for setting and evaluating sequencing policies used in airport surface management systems. We also consider the potential benefits of using more advanced algorithms that take into account the monotonically increasing error property, and highlight the importance of further research into sequencing problems with takeoffs and landings at nearby airports, and with discrete shortest paths, and especially with bypassing. We discuss the potential sources of errors in flight time and distance calculations, and consider the impact of calculating discrete shortest paths in both forward and backward directions, and the resulting potential for different solutions. We also consider the implications of our research for other applications that involve sequencing operations, and the importance of further research into these types of problems. This research introduces a method where options are valued in a way that reflects the costs of repeatedly hedging them. This approach involves a specific formula for hedging, and we've developed an equation to calculate the price of an option seller, taking into account the costs of hedging. Taking into account the cost of hedging leads to a condition for an option to be free from default risk, which is that its value must be non-negative. This research also identifies the maximum amount an option seller can lose in a single day of trading and estimates it as an average of the squared differences between an option's actual and predicted deltas, multiplied by the variance of the differences between the prices of underlying assets. This research is primarily focused on options written on stocks, but it also considers assets with stochastic volatility and interest rates, providing a formula to value option sellers in these cases. However, it's observed that the cost of hedging can lead to option prices higher than those calculated by standard formulas, potentially up to twice as much, and that this increase varies proportionally with the square of the change in the underlying asset's value. Parallel optimization of each subdomain is achieved through the exchange of compressed gradients, scored weights, and reference points. Fairness and security constraints are enforced by exchanging compressed vectors, scored weights, and reference points in parallel.

A critical vulnerability exists in the widely used decoy-state quantum key distribution (QKD) system, specifically with its phase encoding version, where an eavesdropper can successfully bypass detection by randomly disrupting the beam's phase on a partial basis. Research indicates that if the phase disruptions are limited to 2πn/N, where N represents the number of pulses, the attacker's intervention may go undetected even with the current method of sifting. A new analysis reveals that if the ratio of classical bits generated per pulse (r) is set to 1, the number of vulnerable applications is significantly expanded, potentially including various practical applications such as authentication and encrypted communication. A novel approach has been discovered to neutralize this threat by adjusting the ratio of classical bits generated per pulse (r) to a value greater than 1, thereby eliminating the security risk without diminishing the system's efficiency. Consequently, if the phase disruptions are limited to 2πn/N, the eavesdropper's intervention will induce an observable discrepancy in the system's operation, thereby detecting the attack. Moreover, this countermeasure does not impede the system's performance, as its impact on the system's overall efficiency is negligible and solely dependent on the system's initial configuration. Notably, this solution is applicable to all phase encoding QKD systems that rely on the encoding method discussed, regardless of the source's type. A theoretical analysis along with experimental findings have validated this approach, revealing that it is capable of safeguarding the system's security even when the number of vulnerable applications is substantial. Ultimately, this research provides a concrete solution to a critical security flaw in the field of quantum cryptography, ensuring the safety of various applications that utilize QKD system with phase encoding. Furthermore, this finding highlights the significance of thoroughly examining a system's underlying principles to identify potential security risks and all necessary measures to prevent them. In the context of quantum cryptography, this discovery underscores the importance of continuous advancement in system design to address emerging security concerns and various system configurations that bases on different applications, ultimately emphasizing the value of close collaboration between scientists and the industry in developing robust and secure quantum system for real-world use cases. A new approach to preventing this attack, involving partial phase randomization of the source laser, has been proposed and implemented but was found to be detectable by the eavesdropper.
