Quantifying connectivity in complex systems across domains utilizing partial information from variable temporal series is a challenging task. Despite the utility of connectivity information for controlling and steering multiple systems, the limitations of previous methods, particularly their lack of automation and accuracy for connecting systems naturally, have hindered progress. A novel algorithm called DCeCE is introduced that uses a neural network to automatically predict connectivity in complex systems across multiple domains by leveraging temporal series data. This algorithm can be an essential tool for researchers and practitioners by providing an open-source framework for predicting connectivity in systems across disciplines, facilitating the exploration of new applications and contributing to the development of advanced control methods such as steering multiple systems. In order to validate the deep dynamic connectivity estimator, DCeCE was tested on three temporal series data sets, including an artificial dataset, a cardiovascular dataset, and a brain dataset containing 16 different regions, that used all available variables at once and partially. The results showed that the DCeCE model produced similar connectivity estimates when compared to traditional methods but achieved this with significantly better generalization when tested against new conditions. Additionally, the DCeCE model performed significantly better than traditional methods when tested against their respective ground truth matrices, indicating a high level of precision in all three data sets. The code for the DCeCE algorithm is available at https://github.com/CompNeuroGroup/DCeCE and can be accessed through https://www.nature.com/articles/s42367-023-00849-5#tab1. Moreover, pre-trained models for all three data sets used in this study can be found at https://www.nature.com/articles/s42367-023-00849-5#tab2. Furthermore, the DCeCE model has been made available for the community to further explore its potential in various applications and it is expected to facilitate the development of new control methods such as steering multiple systems. In addition, the DCeCE model has been used to investigate the functional connectivity of the brain across different ages by analyzing temporal series data from the ABIDE dataset, that contains functional magnetic resonance imaging scans from over 900 subjects spanning a wide age range. The results from this study showed that the DCeCE model can be an effective tool for uncovering the brain's functional connectivity across different ages by analyzing temporal series data from large-scale studies. Cellular activities within a living being are influenced by various external factors such as the being's nervous system, the flow of nutrients, and sound waves. These factors stir movement within the being, causing its cells to shift and resulting in the formation of patterns on its surface. A novel computational approach is proposed to extract this biological activity from video recordings by first removing the being's overall movement. This method leverages video data combined with mathematical descriptions of the being's cell mass and its form to produce a quantitative measure of the activity's impact. This measure is then utilized to compare the effectiveness of two main approaches: one that relies on the Mosaic Template Model and another that employs M-templates. Despite initial limitations in order sensitivity, we have successfully upgraded it to handle orders of of $10^3$-to-$10^5$, contingent on specific $AB$ matrix characteristics. We have observed that this upgraded version exhibits comparable convergence speeds with other iterative methods, even showcasing superlinear convergence in some instances, and we have obtained a general formula for determining optimal starting values. We have implemented this method on a GPU for a real-world applications consisting of a large system of $10^4$ equations, resulting in an average reduction in computation time to approximately 1-2 days compared to 4-5 weeks using a direct inversion method. We have also explored the use of this method for a method known as the Quasi-Neutron Method. We have made our code publicly available for download. Due to its efficiency and low memory requirements, we believe this method should be considered for any application involving large matrix inversions. We have designated this upgraded method as RNRM. We have tested it against other iterative methods, including RRGM, ANRM, NRM, and a method known as the Neutron Source Method, and have obtained a general order variation technique known as RNRMVOT. In quantum systems under steady-state excitation, a well-known phenomenon arises where specific channels rapidly accumulate scattered intensity, while others quickly diminish it. Certain properties of these scattering channels have been extensively explored, but little is known about the remaining unaccounted ones. A fundamental aspect of our research is the introduction of a general metric that quantifies the intensity gain in each channel across multiple scattering iterations. Based on this measure, we defined eigenstates of cumulative intensity after multiple scattering events, referred to as eigenstates of dynamic origin (EDOs). Our research reveals that only a limited number of EDOs are sufficient to describe the overall scattering behavior when considering an average over all incoming quantum states. Specifically, we show that the average scattering response can be predicted by just a few EDOs in each scenario, regardless of system size or type. Furthermore, we observed that in cases where certain static eigenstates exhibit non-zero scattering, the corresponding intensity gains are directly related to their initial scattering matrix elements. In contrast, in scenarios where static eigenstates exhibit no scattering, we found that the intensity gains are instead correlated with each other, in a manner that is unique to each individual static eigenstate. Building upon these insights, we were able to design new materials with optimized energy dissipation properties, demonstrating that the scattering matrix can be understood through the lens of a few critical EDOs, and that manipulating these EDOs can effectively shape the overall scattering behavior. Our research provides a foundation for the exploration of complex scattering phenomena in quantum systems through energy absorption eigenstates. Ultimately, this work holds the potential for addressing broader challenges related to scattering, in areas such as optical communication, magnetic resonance imaging, and rare event detection, by providing a new framework for the analysis of scattering processes. This framework can be applied to any open quantum system capable of scattering, and may be combined with a variety of driving mechanisms, including laser driving and acoustic driving, as demonstrated through our numerical simulations. In conclusion, our research on energy absorption eigenstates has revealed new insights into the underlying structures that govern open quantum systems, and has shown that these systems often exhibit a simpler and more intuitive nature than previously suspected. By understanding and manipulating the energy absorption eigenstates within these systems, we have shown that it is possible to effectively design and control their behavior, and to shape the overall scattering response in a desired manner. This work has the potential to contribute to a broader range of applications, and our results provide a foundation for further exploration into the complex phenomena that govern open quantum systems. Due to the model's symmetry, we can incorporate a key perturbation in either of two forms: either the long-range hopping term on the A-subunits has an opposite sign from its counterpart on the B-subunits, or the on-site potential on A-subunits is opposite to that on B-subunits.

When this perturbation is evenly distributed, it creates a topological Anderson conductor bordering on two phases: the trivial phase and the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger phase.

The model exhibits strong robustness against various types of local and serial disorders, particularly it remains topologically non-trivial when subjected to a long-range interaction in an arbitrary direction, as well as various types of off-site and on-site disorders that are not symmetric between A and B-subunits.

The model can be realized with ultracold atoms in an optical lattice, using either bosons or fermions, and it offers the possibility of controlling the model's topology through binary disorders, providing a foundation for the study of topological Anderson insulators.

As a result, numerous extensions of the Standard Model have emerged, with the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM) being one of the most popular choices. This particular ratio is largely insensitive to new physics beyond the on-shell Higgs boson and is primarily governed by the stop squark sector. We evaluate and extend the concept of linearity in network autoregressive models by considering additional interactions beyond a linear model. Specifically, we examine the efficacy of Gaussian non-degenerate kernels in facilitating linearity and thereby enabling the capture of conditional mean relationships similar to linear models. Through a comprehensive simulation study and a real-world application, we investigate the modeling benefits and limitations of non-degenerate kernels in autoregressive models. Our findings suggest that these kernels can effectively capture conditional mean relationships even in the presence of non-linear effects and provide a promising solution for modeling complex systems with latent variables and endogenous effects. Ultimately, our research offers a linearity framework that is adaptable to various kernel specifications and enables the exploration of linearity in extensive network data sets. Our code is openly accessible at the link provided. Furthermore, the paper is currently under review for publication in the Journal of Computational Graphics and Techniques. Initially, this research was presented at ICML 2020 in Vancouver, Canada. Introduction: Linearity in Network Autoregressive Models: Modern statistical models often aim to capture complex relationships within large datasets. In the case of network autoregressive models, linearity refers to the simplest form of these relationships. However, the validity of linearity can easily be compromised by non-linear interactions between variables. Historically, models have addressed this issue by incorporating non-linear functions, such as splines and neural networks, but at the cost of significant model complexity and difficulty in interpretation. Recently, machine learning-based autoregressive models with flexible graphical structure have been developed, enabling the exploration of linearity in network data. Gaussian Network AR Model: We build upon existing network AR models by introducing a Gaussian kernel-based model that facilitates linearity. This model, known as the Gaussian Network AR Model (GNAR), leverages a non-degenerate kernel to capture complex relationships within a network. GNAR's kernel allows us to examine linearity in network data, but its non-degenerate nature also raises the possibility of over-estimating linearity. To address this concern, we developed a simulation study to evaluate GNAR's performance under various linearity conditions. Our results revealed that GNAR effectively captures linear relationships but fails in non-linear settings. Notably, our findings indicate that GNAR can capture conditional mean relationships even in the presence of non-linear effects when the underlying variables are latent. In contrast, models that included visible endogenous variables resulted in significant over-estimation of linearity. In this research, we introduce an advanced AI framework called Deep Declarative Networks (DDN), which significantly surpasses previous approaches in both performance and scope. To gain a deeper understanding of DDN's potential, we present two significant contributions in this paper. Firstly, we provide a comprehensive overview of DDN's components and its declarative nature. Secondly, we present two intricate problem-solving scenarios, where we demonstrate the efficacy and versatility of DDN in addressing complex challenges by simply redefining the declarative framework. These scenarios offer valuable insights into the versatility of DDN, where they outperform existing approaches with a notable margin of 10% improvement. Furthermore, these results indicate that DDN's performance gains are consistent across multiple trials, providing a solid foundation for future research on DDN in complex domains. However, it is essential to note that the reference implementation of DDN is limited to small-scale problems due to memory constraints, resulting in slower processing times compared to traditional deep learning methods. Nevertheless, this constraint does not impact the validity of the performance assessments, and it is anticipated that future optimizations will address these memory limitations, enabling DDN to handle larger datasets and further solidifying its position as a premier problem-solving framework. Additionally, the two case analyses presented in this paper are made available through the provided code repository, where they can be replicated under the terms of the associated license. Furthermore, the results achieved in this research exceed those reported in the corresponding paper that inspired this inquiry, where an additional 5% improvement was realized. This discrepancy necessitates an extension to the findings presented in the referenced paper, where the revised outcomes are now included as part of this research. In this paper, we extend the findings presented in Section 3 by incorporating an additional 5000 training examples for the second case analysis, resulting in an enhanced model that achieves an accuracy of 92% on the test dataset, representing an increase of 9% over the previous outcome. This result raises the possibility that further significant performance gains can be realized through the continuation of data collection, albeit at a diminishing rate of improvement with each additional example. This understanding is derived from the observation that the rate of improvement in this case analysis follows a less steep decline with each additional 1000 training examples, warranting further exploration into the intricacies of this particular problem-solving scenario through complementary analysis such as model size expansion, neural network visualization, and rigorous theoretical analysis. This paper also provides an initial foray into the application of DDN to real-world problems through the second case

A cell's behavior during dispersal is influenced by various factors including the movement of individual cells, cell-to-cell interactions and chemical signals in their surroundings. Additionally, changes in the environment can affect the distribution of proteins on lipid membranes within cells by triggering cell migration or altering adhesive interactions with neighboring cells and the surrounding medium. To effectively simulate these events, a method was developed to combine the principles of advection-diffusion and reaction-dynamics. This method can model the movement of cells within a given space, simulate the changes in protein distributions on lipid membranes by factoring in the cells' migration and the underlying environment, and also account for the stimulation of cells by surrounding proteins. By incorporating these elements, this method can facilitate a more in-depth exploration of how environmental changes influence protein distributions within cells by migrating, adhering to neighboring cells or the surrounding medium, in addition to dispersing in their immediate vicinity. Building on existing theories and with consideration given to cells' multi-scale features, this approach has been implemented in a framework that can be integrated with the OpenFOAM software for the simulation of biological cells within complex, variable environments. An application of this framework is provided where it is used to investigate how the distribution of external guidance proteins affects stick splittings in Dictyostelia by simulating cells that change their shape in response to their surroundings. An evaluation of the developed method was conducted in conjunction with observations from real Dictyostelia colonies. Based on these simulations and actual colony data, a model was proposed that shows how the distribution of external guidance proteins influences stick divisions in Dictyostelia by producing specific patterns. This study demonstrates the capability of weakly nonlinear cross-talk models to effectively analyze how the distribution of proteins on lipid membranes within cells is impacted by their migration, cell-to-cell interactions, and the movement of individual cells within varying environments. Building on existing knowledge, a new model was introduced along with its applications in the analysis of real Dictyostelia colonies. These simulations validated previous theories and provided a deeper understanding of how environmental changes influence protein distributions within cells by migrating, adhering to neighboring cells or the underlying medium, in addition to dispersing in their immediate vicinity. This research paves the way for further exploration of how the distribution of proteins on lipid membranes within cells is impacted by their migration, cell-to-cell interactions, and the movement of individual cells within varying environments. With consideration given to cells' multi-scale features, a method was developed to combine the principles of advection-diffusion and reaction-dynamics to effectively simulate these events.

The underlying technology behind a blockchain relies on transactions that are linked together through digital signatures, but the current literature lacks a clear understanding of a fundamental aspect - user currency paths. The complex nature of anonymous wallets complicates the effort to track the origin of currency, leading to potential false deductions when paths are incorrectly inferred. To address this, we developed an effective method to verify currency paths in the Ethereum network by utilizing a set of rigorous rules and a language-based framework. Our proposed method can also detect and flag potentially deceitful paths in just two linearly scaling iterations of the Verifier, User Comprehension Protocol (VUCP). When tested on a full Ethereum archive, VUCP demonstrated exceptional performance, requiring only 83ms and 4.7GB of memory. Our research in user currency comprehension within the Ethereum network raises critical security concerns and highlights the need for more advanced pseudorandom functions that can resist cyber attacks in the full archive setting. However, when the archive is partially loaded, our proposed method offers comprehensively secure and publicly verifiable results, significantly outperforming the current state-of-the-art in both efficiency and security, with an improvement of at least two orders of magnitude in performance. Moreover, VUCP has shown the ability to achieve comprehensively secure and publicly verifiable results in a wide range of currency paths, far exceeding previous benchmarks. Our research has also uncovered the creation of complex cyber attacks, such as the "double spend attack," which manipulates the Verifier by falsifying the origin of the currency, using a combination of multiple mixing centers, and our proposed solution has successfully resisted all types of cyber attacks, including the "double spend attack," in both full and partial archive settings. Large-scale universal quantum computing holds significant promise but is prone to downtime due to malfunctions in its vast array of quantum processors. This vulnerability restricts the potential for real-world applications and compromises the system's functionality, suggesting that error prevention is essential for the advancement of quantum computing. This concept is analogous to an ideal in classical computing known as "fail-safe" design, where the system automatically returns to a default, safe state in response to an issue. Building upon prior work incorporating reinforcement learning in quantum error correction, this study introduces a novel approach centered around coding, the primary method for correcting quantum errors through encoding and stabilizer measurements from a decoder's instructions. This approach was successfully applied to two popular quantum error correction codes, the surface code and the topological code, with positive results. Furthermore, this study demonstrates the possibility of coding for both fault tolerance and minimal latency, achieving a mean end-to-end latency as low as 1.43 the natural logarithm of the number of physical qubits in the surface code, and 2.08 for the topological code, outperforming several established decoding approaches. These findings suggest that coding through reinforcement learning can enhance the resilience and efficiency of quantum computations, paving the way for coders that can adapt to a wide range of system configurations and scenarios, and offering a promising solution for making quantum computing safe from errors, without the need for perfect understanding of system latency, a crucial requirement for its real-world implementation. This research was conducted using near-term quantum hardware, specifically the IBM Q quantum processors, allowing the integration of practical latency profiles, and the development of a novel framework for flexible latency modeling, in addition to an open-source implementation of the underlying reinforcement learning framework, coded in PyQML and PyTorch, and coders in Qiskit. This research is also an outcome of the University of Maryland's Quantum Computing Center's (QCC) research initiatives. Both authors are affiliated with the University of Maryland, College Park. We've developed an unconventional optical metrology setup featuring two interconnected cavities, which allows us to achieve an unusual all-optical version of Leigh's quantum leap phenomenon. This unique system combines two interacting atomic layers, embedded in separate cavities that are linked by an optical connection. As a result of this interaction, one atomic layer can switch from a ground state to a excited state and back to ground in a single step, while simultaneously causing a correlated change in the state of the other layer. This process creates a highly robust entanglement between the two layers, and we've demonstrated that it's essential for maximizing the precision of our metrological measurement. We've created an example of an all-optical leap phenomenon with strontium atoms and showed that it offers a significant improvement over conventional approaches. Furthermore, we believe that our double-cavity network has vast potential for implementing novel quantum processes that go beyond metrology. Overall, our research indicates that combining cavity quantum electrodynamics and atomic quantum leaps can provide a powerful and versatile means of achieving a wide range of scientific and technological advancements. Our research examined direct photon-hadron correlations in Au$+$Au and $d$$+$Au collisions at 200 GeV from RHIC, with a focus on jet interactions with medium in Au$+$Au. Initial observations show similar results for $d$$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$, indicating minimal nuclear modification from cold nuclear matter. In contrast, Au$+$Au collisions exhibit significant modifications, characterized by reduced hadron yields at large $p_T$ on the hadron side, suggestive of jet-medium interactions. This effect is found to depend on charge collection within the medium, exhibiting two distinct patterns: hadrons with positive charge show a more pronounced shift towards large $p_T$, while those with negative charge exhibit a more modest shift, potentially linked to quark and antiquark jet interactions within the medium. These findings are further influenced by the hadron's initial propagation, with an observed dependence on the hadron's initial emission time from the jet. Notably, hadrons with larger $p_T$ but similar $p_T$-correlation to direct photons exhibit enhanced shifts towards large $p_T$, while hadrons with lower $p_T$ but similar $p_T$-correlation to direct photons exhibit reduced shifts, indicating hadrons' $p_T$-correlation with direct photons serves as an effective probe of jet-medium interactions. These results provide new insights into jet interactions within a medium, especially quark and jet properties, which are fundamental to our understanding of medium properties in heavy-ion collisions. Moreover, these findings suggest direct photon-hadron correlations can serve as a powerful tool for assessing jet-medium interactions across various energies and systems. Finally, our analysis indicates hadron's $p_T$-correlation with direct photons is a crucial factor influencing hadron's $p_T$ in Au$+$Au collisions, underscoring the significance of further exploring hadron's emission properties within a jet at various centers of mass energies from SPS to LHC. Additionally, our research emphasizes the importance of investigating hadron's emission properties within a jet via $N$-$N$ and $A$$+$$A$ collisions at different energies, which is now feasible with established jet and medium properties and with newly developed tools for data analysis across various experiments and collaborations. This paper explores the properties of the proposed universal Smarandache's sigma multiplication of digits, a concept that aims to unify the rules governing the digit growth of integer rotations and Fibonacci hits under various modular operations. We provide an innovative algorithm for calculating the universal Smarandache's sigma multiplication of digits and demonstrate its applicability in identifying periodic patterns within sequences of integer rotations and Fibonacci hits under different modular operations. Additionally, we offer solutions to previously unresolved problems related to the digit growth of integer rotations and Fibonacci hits under modular addition and multiplication, respectively. Furthermore, we establish upper and lower bounds for the digit growth of integer rotations and Fibonacci hits under modular multiplication for specific moduli, thereby extending the limitations for other moduli up to $p^3$ for prime numbers $p$. We also establish new lower bounds for the digit growth of integer rotations and Fibonacci hits under modular addition for certain powers of prime numbers. We also provide solutions to three open problems posed by the Smarandache family, including an expansion of the known upper bound for the digit growth of integer rotations under modular multiplication for a composite number 54, a determination of the sequence behavior for the hit sequence of 5 under modular multiplication with respect to the universal Smarandache's sigma multiplication of digits, and a generalization of the known upper bound for the digit growth of integer rotations under modular addition for a prime number 7 up to its cube. We also establish new upper and lower bounds for the digit growth of Fibonacci hits under modular multiplication for a prime number 5 and its powers, including a demonstration of the applicability of the proposed universal Smarandache's sigma multiplication of digits for sequences with a fixed period greater than two. We observe that some sequences of integer rotations and Fibonacci hits under modular operations exhibit distinct periodic patterns at different digit positions, with some sequences displaying fixed periods only in specific digit projections, leading to new conjectures and problems to be resolved. Network-based virtual cluster management tools rely on node network connections to exchange information about available resources, execute tasks, and scale applications. The efficiency of these tools is assumed to provide optimal, balanced, and high-performing execution of applications across the cluster. However, the actual performance of these tools depends on various factors, including the capabilities of the underlying virtualization technology and network protocols used. This research focuses on the performance of OpenStack with KVM and XEN virtualization technologies, and on network protocols such as OpenFlow and SDN. The results show that the performance of OpenStack is highly dependent on the underlying virtualization technology and network protocols, and is significantly affected by the virtualization technology used. This research also reveals that there are significant differences in performance variability among network protocols, with some protocols inducing performance fluctuations of up to 50 times those of others. This research can be used to identify areas for improvement in network-based virtual cluster management tools, with a focus on open-source solutions like OpenStack. It highlights the importance of considering performance variability when evaluating and comparing such solutions, and of conducting thorough, systematic experiments when assessing their performance. This research can serve as a model for evaluating the performance of cluster management tools in the cloud, and can be used as a starting point for further, more in-depth investigations into the performance of cloud applications. We explore a decentralized framework where independent agents take part in a series of bandit experiments with shared goals. Each agent has no knowledge of the others' experiences and environments, and they don't need to share their context with each other. We establish an effective learning method that allows the agents to achieve $O(\sqrt{LT}\cdot\log(T))$ regret in each individual L-armed bandit experiment, where $L$ represents the number of situational variations and $T$ denotes the total number of trials. Notably, this achieves the same scalability as single-agent linear bandit learning for the first time. Moreover, we demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a series of peer-to-peer linear contextual multi-armed bandit experiments conducted on real machines, yielding significant performance gains over baseline methods. This research provides a novel context-independent decentralized bandit framework, offering a range of potential applications, including contextual multi-armed bandits, adaptive reinforcement learning, and online experimentation. Our research seeks to address the uncertainty many organizations face when transitioning to remote working for Scrum teams by exploring the effect of remote working on Scrum project success. With no universal definition of Scrum project success, we employed a multi-criteria approach, combining both quantitative and qualitative perspectives from project managers, developers, and business owners who have experience with Scrum and working from home. The results of our survey and expert assessments were used to evaluate the impact of remote working on Scrum project success from various angles, including team performance, quality, productivity, customer satisfaction, and adaptability. The data revealed a noticeable decline in perceived project success when working remotely, prompting an analysis of potential limitations of remote working, including difficulties in maintaining open communication and collaboration with all team members, promoting a positive and accountable team culture, and facilitating smooth stakeholder interactions. Our study also identified several strategies that teams can employ to mitigate these limitations and increase the likelihood of successful Scrum project outcomes even when working remotely. Finally, we highlight the implications of our findings for both practitioners and researchers, offering potential avenues for further exploration within the field of software engineering. With the increasing prevalence of remote working arrangements, our research provides valuable insights that can be used to adapt and refine Scrum to better suit this working style. Our results are most closely related to Farqi, Kallus, and Kitelli (2020), which demonstrated that specific individualized treatment rules are optimal under distributional shifts. Our work builds upon Farqi, Kallus, and Kitelli (2020) by removing restrictions on treatment alternatives and showing the same rules' effectiveness in cross-validation without knowledge of the target distribution. We also provide a feasible estimator for the ideal distributionally resilient treatment policy and conduct simulations in both homogeneous and heterogeneous settings. Notably, in the homogeneous case, we found that estimates converge at a rate of $O_p(n^{-4/5})$, which is the same rate as models without residual dependence. In contrast, in the heterogeneous case, we observed rate $O_p(n^{-1/2})$ under specific assumptions, which is the rate for standard cross-validation estimators. For the optimal power constraint, the existing literature suggests that this network achieves an extreme dof of up to $K$ user dof. This article solves the Leopoldt's conjecture for the number 7. It does this by showing if an integer $n$ is greater than 2, and if there are two relatively prime integers $a$ and $b$ whose absolute values are less than the square root of 7 to the power of $n/2$, then the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ cannot be satisfied. Additionally, solutions for pairs of the form $(a,b)$ where one is a whole number multiple of the other and is less than the square root of 7 to the power of $n/2$ are also provided, including solutions in this broader category for the number 7 when $n$ is 4 or has a remainder of 1 when divided by 2. Furthermore, solutions for certain values of $n$ that are greater than 2 and fall within the range from 4 to 21, or are greater than 21 and have a remainder of 1 or 2 when divided by 3, are also given. If $n$ is 3, unique solutions for pairs of the form $(a,b)$ that are less than 7 exist, resulting in four solutions, and if $n$ is in the range from 4 to 21, twenty solutions exist. If $n$ is greater than 21 and falls within an integer range from 22 to 39, solutions for all possible values of $a$ and $b$ that satisfy the given condition exist and are determined by applying the method of proof for small cases of $n$. If $n$ is greater than 39, twenty solutions for pairs of the form $(a,b)$ that are less than 7 to the power of $n/2$ exist. This research focuses on enhancing the performance of a monopod hopping on deformable ground using simulation and experimental techniques. Although bipedal robots have historically achieved impressive success in various tasks, they require a substantial amount of space to operate and can be prone to toppling over. In contrast, monopods offer several advantages including reduced size, lower material costs, and enhanced stability in tight environments. However, designing a monopod that can jump and walk in an efficient and secure manner on soft surfaces poses significant technical challenges due to the complex interactions between the robot and the ground, which can lead to unpredictable fluctuations in the robot's movement. To address this issue, researchers developed a novel method for simulating and testing robot-ground interactions by utilizing a non-Newtonian fluid simulation to refine their design, with promising results indicating that a monopod built according to their principles can achieve controlled takeoff and landing on soft surfaces and even execute successful walking cycles when the ground is slightly tilted. The lessons learned from this research can be applied to the development of more advanced hopping robots with multiple legs by providing valuable insights into the critical factors that govern their dynamics and stability. The study demonstrated that a relatively small modification to the robot's foot or body can have a substantial impact on its overall behavior and that both linear and nonlinear forces play crucial roles in determining the best design for optimal performance. We've examined the properties of meson mass splittings using a method that emphasizes the internal cohesion of mesons. Unlike traditional quark models, our approach doesn't rely on assumptions about meson shape factors and instead determines them dynamically as components of the meson's surface energy. With a simple, yet effective formula for the surface energy, we derived an expression for the width parameter, $a$, which is typically used in quark models but has no direct physical meaning. Our analysis indicates that $a$ is primarily driven by the relative magnitude of the meson's size and its potential strength, which is governed by the confining potential and the charge of the quarks within. By applying our method to meson states consisting of three quarks and one antiquark, we gathered evidence that these mesons possess shape-dependent structure, with estimates of their root mean square (RMS) charge radii aligning with prior predictions that they have sizes greater than those of their quarkonium counterparts. Notably, our findings for $J/\\psi$ and $\\Upsilon$ are consistent with experimental determinations of their RMS charge radii. By comparing our results for the $D$ and $B$ meson ground states with data obtained through lattice QCD, we discovered some discrepancies, with our predictions falling in between the two LQCD outcomes for the light quark's contribution to the RMS charge radius. Furthermore, our method allows for the derivation of width parameters for higher excitations and rotationally bound mesons without the need for complex potential models. With the development of more sophisticated understanding of meson structure, our approach provides a framework for investigating other aspects of hadron physics, specifically those involving the study of hadron structure and form factors within scattering processes. With the advent of new experimental initiatives at facilities like the future Electron-Ion Collider (EIC), our method positions us to explore fundamental questions about the internal composition and structure of quark-gluon matter in a more comprehensive manner. Ultimately, our approach offers a unifying framework that can facilitate the interpretation of experimental data obtained through different processes and at different scales. Quantifying the impact of negation on statement meaning is a key task in natural language processing, yet one that has gone largely unaddressed. In an effort to rectify this, we introduce CONDAQA, a novel dataset featuring Chinese pairs of text that differ in their treatment of negation. Each question-answer pair in this dataset is carefully crafted to assess the comprehension of a particular negated statement in a particular context, with that context being the statement's surrounding text. With a focus on clauses and phrases, CONDAQA includes a diverse range of text formats. Our evaluation tools, designed to test a range of negation understanding tasks, indicate that models performance on this dataset is heavily influenced by the model's ability to process both positive and negative information effectively, with the best model achieving a 62.5% score. This score is in turn significantly better than the models performance when the negation is removed from the statement, with that score being 47.5%. With each question-answer pair evaluated independently, there is no requirement for the answer to be unique, allowing for a wide range of responses to each question. This consideration of multiple possible answers for each question is in fact the norm in this dataset. This research paper takes a comprehensive approach at addressing a critical challenge in building information system (IS) hierarchies. Although many organizations have made significant progress in creating taxonomies and ontologies within their enterprises, extending these knowledge bases upwards to form a hierarchy has proven elusive. This issue is particularly pronounced in areas where relationships are fluid and difficult to pinpoint, such as those involving continuous variables and ordinal values. Our proposed model, called HierarchiCS, seeks to address this gap by introducing a new method for calculating hierarchies in a manner that is both expandable and flexible, leveraging a unique combination of linear algebra and mathematical programming. HierarchiCS is then applied to a notable information system scenario, supply chain management, with remarkable results obtained from both theoretical calculations and empirical data analysis. Our findings indicate that the resulting hierarchiCS models possess key properties, such as invariance and discriminant ability, which are critical for accurate prediction and classification. We also uncover some valuable insights into variable importance and their order, providing a useful framework for further research and exploration. HierarchiCS is an open-source R package available for download at https://cran.r-project.org/package=hierarchiCS. The implementation of our model is also presented in a companion R documentation available at https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/hierarchiCS. The R code used in this study has been deposited in GitHub at https://github.com/ivanblasi/hierarchiCS with the following license: we adopt the MIT License. The name of each supply chain is listed in the Table 2 of this manuscript. The data employed in this study is composed of 57 distinct SCs, encompassing 346 variables across all of them. These variables comprise both continuous and ordinal metrics. Quantum annealing and quenching are employed in different variations of quantum computing's simulation and sampling techniques. We investigate the properties of a variational algorithm based on quenching dynamics, specifically examining the 'exact cover problem'. Our research reveals the characteristics of this variational algorithm to be highly sensitive to the length of its quantum annealing interval, which essentially determines the number of swaps between two configurations that must be fulfilled in order for the system to converge. When this interval is optimal, the quenching-based algorithm exhibits precision comparable to quantum annealing. However, even a single swap between states is sufficient to achieve high accuracy in solving the exact cover problem in some scenarios. We explore the algorithm's potential for error, establishing a link between this variation and another known cover problem. Finally, we observe that the quench interval's unique feature allows it to serve as a metric for evaluating the validity of simulated experimental data. In contrast to quantum annealing's interval, which designates specific start and end points, the quench interval is defined by the number of swaps it encompasses, making it a more versatile measure. Notably, this feature holds implications for experimental evidence suggesting that only two out of nine variables were swap-able in the precise cover problem, a finding that warrants further theoretical investigation. As a result of studying this variation of the cover problem, we propose calling it 'precise cover problem' in order to differentiate it from 'exact cover problem'. Furthermore, we propose two new problems derived from 'precise cover problem', namely 'double cover problem' and 'triple cover problem'. Additionally, we explore the possibility of solving linear systems of equations using both quantum annealing and quenching in an unbiased manner, demonstrating that both methods yield comparable results when the interval is optimal. However, when the interval is suboptimal, the precision of both methods drops at the same rate, indicating a similar trend but different absolute values. We also examine the overlap between initial and final states in both scenarios, discovering a correlation between this measure and the precision of the variational algorithm. Finally, we propose two new metrics for evaluating the performance of both quantum annealing and quenching dynamics, namely the 'error floor' and the 'quenching overlap'. We've developed a two-dimensional model that represents an infinite-layer nickelate in its normal and superconducting states, considering that electron correlation and strong interactions are crucial. Located at the (001) surface of GdNiO$_2$, this material exhibits $d$-electron physics similar to cuprates, except with more complex effects due to $3d$ orbital mixing. In a dual-band setup, we've isolated two critical bands consisting of $x^2-y^2$ and $d_{x(y),y(x)}$ orbital combinations and mapped them in an asymmetric potential wells, taking into account the significant influence of electron transfer and crystal fields on the Hamiltonian's spectral characteristics. This research focuses on addressing the security concerns of machine learning models used in client-server applications, specifically those involving a malicious client interacting with a server that has an encrypted machine learning model available to them. We investigated various attacks on the server, including those launching malicious input requests and input manipulation, utilizing auxiliary hardware, and activating malfunctions in hardware components, such as side-channel leakage. Our primary contribution involves developing an framework that can evaluate and benchmark the security of machine learning models against these types of attacks. This framework, known as SIMC 2.0, builds upon a previously established evaluation method and expands on it by incorporating enhanced input manipulation techniques, as well as both hardware-based and software-based methods for managing memory layout and triggering hardware malfunctions. Additionally, SIMC 2.0 includes an updated protocol for secure inference, designed to counter certain types of attacks, such as those from malicious clients. The spiral galaxy M101, located at a distance of approximately 6.4 Mpc, serves as the largest member of a nearby galaxy group. Due to its advanced status as a spiral galaxy and its proximity to Earth, it has been extensively studied in various spectral ranges including optical, infrared, ultraviolet, radio waves, and $\gamma$-rays. A recent 31-channel HI Parkes All Sky Survey (HIPASS) study identified M101 as a high-velocity HI source. Our team employed the Five-hundred-meter Basilicata Radio Telescope (FAST) to conduct a 21-cm line observation of the M101 galaxy group, yielding a total HI mass of $1.55\times 10^{9}$ $M_{\odot}$ for M101 and several smaller HI clouds. By comparing their velocities and positions, we discovered five smaller HI clouds surrounding M101 and ranging in mass from $3.2\times 10^{7}$ to $8.5\times 10^{8}$ $M_{\odot}$. Four of these clouds exhibit kinematic connections to M101 while the remaining cloud, MG1, exhibits a distinct velocity and positional discrepancy. MG1, situated about 260 kpc from the center of M101 on the southeast axis, possesses a mass of $3.2\times 10^{8}$ $M_{\odot}$. In addition to the five HI clouds, our team also discovered a faint, extended HI tail extending from the center of M101 towards its companion galaxy NGG 020-021. This HI tail, measuring approximately 82 kpc in length and with an estimated mass of $1.1\times 10^{8}$ $M_{\odot}$, exhibits a kinematic connection to M101 while displaying a distinct velocity discrepancy. This discovery provides further evidence for the interaction between M101 and its companion galaxy NGG 020-021 and offers valuable insights into the structure and evolution of the M101 galaxy group. Due to its proximity to Earth and the completeness of its optical star count, M101 allows for the calculation of its total baryon mass, amounting to $1.3\times 10^{11}$ $M_{\odot}$. This, in turn, facilitates an estimation of its dark matter mass at approximately $5.3\times 10^{11}$ $M_{\odot}$, thereby providing a unique opportunity to study the composition of this galaxy group. To address this issue, this paper introduces a novel framework that generates high-quality insights for both question and answer through a semantic connection. To begin with, a new evaluation metric is created to assess the semantic connection between retrieved passages and both question and answer. This evaluation metric reveals that both 50% of CQA datasets and human-generated examples lack semantic connection. To address this issue, a new coarse-to-careful framework is created that utilizes both a strong backbone model and a strategic sampling method to generate high-quality insights that are semantically connected to both the question and answer. The proposed framework achieves significant improvements over both current leading models and the strong backbone model without the strategic sampling method. Moreover, the results show that both 90% of CQA datasets and human-generated examples possess semantically connected passages. The proposed framework is found to be data-efficient and outperforms both strong baselines in both automatic and human evaluations. We investigate the ring of square-free polynomials, R_2, within a global domain, D, that is not necessarily integrally closed. Our main finding extends a prior result by Vasconcelos, demonstrating that if D contains exactly two prime ideals with height two, then every element of its fraction field can be expressed as a sum of squared polynomials. This conclusion also holds for Cohen-Macaulay domains that are not necessarily domains with unique factorization, provided a specific height exists. Some examples are provided to show that many of these results are no longer valid in lower dimensional situations. Additionally, we determine the set of squares in the polynomial ring over a global domain, extending a prior result by Gubkenic. Finally, we consider an ideal in R_2, denoted as I_{2d}, whose elements are squared polynomials of degree d, and provide results on its height and prime ideals for specific values of d, particularly d being even or odd. If D has only finitely many prime ideals with a given height, then I_{2d} has that height if and only if 2d is equal to that height and has the same cardinality as D's prime ideals with that height. If D has infinitely many prime ideals with a given height, then I_{2d} has that height if and only if 2d is equal to that height, and all such ideals in I_{2d} are prime if and only if 2d is equal to that height and D's height is greater than one.

We employ photonics to enhance the processing of astronomical data, specifically cross-correlation tasks. A measure of their performance is the Fisher information matrix, and we extract its limit by considering a basic spectral comparison task. This threshold represents the optimal processing capability of any system, whether it is photonic, electronic, or a hybrid. We investigate how this fundamental performance can be achieved with photonic systems that integrate a neural network in their operations. A key aspect of this exploration is modeling the photonic system as a series of operations that amount to a neural network similar to a convolved neural network. Using this framework, we determine the ultimate performance of these photonic systems when they are optimized for the task at hand. Optimization criteria considered include energy efficiency, given the limited power available in laboratory settings. We examine the outcomes of our research in the context of current and planned astronomical missions that involve the cross-correlation of spectra. We also discuss the potential benefits of applying astrophotonic processing units that integrate a neural network in these missions, even if they require the use of larger off-chip analog signal processing components due to the high complexity of the observation programs involved. These systems could provide a significant boost in data processing speed and efficiency, an advancement that could be particularly valuable in the era of Phase II Great Telescope Era missions that will likely be characterized by high spectral resolution across a broad wavelength range and the collection of multiple spectra in each exposure. As a result of our research, we propose a new approach to designing the next-generation of astrophotonic processing units that integrate a neural network, an idea that could also be applied to the development of conventional cross-correlation techniques utilizing electronics or software. This new design philosophy emphasizes the integration of a neural network in photonic system operations to achieve optimal performance, resulting in a processing architecture that is robust, versatile, and easy to model physically. We anticipate that this framework will be particularly useful in guiding the development of processing units for the analysis of data with high spectral resolution across a broad wavelength range and will provide a remedy for the spectral cross-matching techniques used in such data sets. For supervised machine learning projects, using diverse data is crucial, but due to data privacy constraints, accessing a large, unified dataset can be difficult. Typically, researchers gather datasets from various sources, but these datasets are often dispersed and independent. In this paper, a novel Random Stroll Method is introduced to tackle these challenges by allowing independent datasets to participate in a learning process. Each participant creates smaller subsets of data and generates models through stochastic training, after which they enter a "stroll" phase where models are updated locally using a unique two-step optimization process. This process involves first updating the model using a subset of data from the current dataset, then refining it using a subset of data from other participating datasets. This process is repeated for each participating dataset until a predetermined number of steps is reached. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach yields models on par with those trained on unified, larger datasets, even when those datasets are not jointly sampled. This method shows particular promise when dealing with datasets that are independent and scattered, requiring minimal communication and coordination among participants. Our results also highlight the method's potential for producing interpretable models through integration of knowledge-based constraints. Our implementation and data sets are publicly available to facilitate replication and exploration of this method in various machine learning contexts. Our findings suggest that, even with small models, the RSM is efficient, with an average communication cost per participant more than 10 times lower than that of a single unified training iteration. Our code is written in Python using the PyTorch framework and is accessible at https://github.com/andersonbott/Stroll-for-Education, and our datasets are available at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1xQ5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5

Research suggests a positive correlation between psychological well-being and successful rehabilitation for offenders both during and after their release from prison. This study extends existing work by examining the outcomes associated with a mandatory psychological therapy program for prisoners, focusing on the relationship between therapy and psychological well-being at multiple time points. Offenders participating in the program showed improved psychological well-being both during their incarceration and within six months of their release, with this improvement sustained at one year post-release. Notably, the benefits of the program were evident across various demographic groups and were linked to reduced reoffending within the first six months and one year after release. However, reoffending rates in the comparison group without access to the program were actually higher than in the treatment group at one year, although this difference was not statistically significant in the longer-term analysis. The findings suggest that the program has a positive impact on both psychological well-being and reoffending, with implications for the design of interventions within the criminal justice system aimed at promoting successful desistance from crime. Due to methodological limitations, specifically the use of a comparison group without a control for which prisoners were assigned to the program, the findings should be interpreted with some caution. The data analyzed in this study were collected as part of an ongoing randomized controlled trial evaluating the effectiveness of the high-intensity therapy program in reducing reoffending within two years of release. The data used in this report were drawn from wave one to three of the trial, covering 244 participants who completed the program and 246 in the comparison group. The analysis controlled for key demographic variables and accounted for missing data with multiple imputation. The sample characteristics and outcome measures were examined across demographic subgroups to explore potential variations in the effects of the program. Despite significant advancements in healthcare image segmentation through transfer learning, the issue of data loss due to label variability hasn't been adequately resolved. In our investigation, we discovered that existing methods fail to account for the inherent inconsistencies in labeling, which significantly impede their performance in labeling quality, model reliability, and ultimately, overall segmentation accuracy. To address this problem, we developed an unconventional consistency regularization framework that tolerates labeling discrepancies to regulate the variability of unsupervised segments and guide the model using self-supervised data. Our technique, known as Basic Consistency Regularization (BCR), leverages two parallel models to produce consistent outputs on unlabeled data and similar labels on labeled data. By incorporating unlabeled data and refining the model using self-supervised segmenting, BCR enables the discovery of implicit patterns, reduces label noise, and boosts segmentation accuracy in comparison to benchmark methods across various healthcare image segmentation datasets. Our research offers a groundbreaking perspective on the limitations of data loss due to labeling variability and provides actionable recommendations for practitioners on the critical selection of model architecture, pre-trained weights, optimization techniques, and segmenting hyperparameters. Systematic evaluations of different model configurations, conducted in an uncontrolled setting to mimic real-world scenarios, are also presented in our study. Furthermore, comprehensive qualitative and quantitative analyses of the model's performance in relation to labeling quality, reliability, and segmentation accuracy are provided. Additionally, a straightforward guide on reproducing the results as well as the model's implementation is made available for the benefit of the research community. In conclusion, our exploration highlights the potential of uncomplicated yet effective regularization techniques to tackle the challenges of labeling variability and data loss due to label variability, and paves the way for the development of more sophisticated methods that can learn from inconsistent labels. Furthermore, our research underscores the significance of pre-processing raw data in order to extract implicit patterns, and the necessity of conducting thorough experiments to validate the performance of segmentation models. In light of these findings, we recommend the inclusion of consistency regularization as an essential component in the evaluation of segmentation models, and the consideration of qualitative and quantitative evaluation along with quantitative assessment in the evaluation of segmentation models. In addition, our exploration emphasizes the significance of uncomplicated yet effective regularization techniques in comparison to complex methods, and highlights the value of transparent and detailed experimentation in computer vision research. We introduce Articulated Neural Depiction (ANDR) and extend this to animated characters in real-time, using a novel approach to shape and position avatars with dynamic poses. This is achieved through a combination of a pose-governed surface representation and a conditional variational rendering model, which ensures that our prediction is linked to the given pose and targets a specific avatar design. By connecting pose features to a pose graph, we successfully apply our method to complex animated scenes, producing high-fidelity avatar renderings in real-time for any given animation. Our model uses a pose code to forecast a target avatar shape and then uses this code to control a 3D canvas, painting the surface of the avatar in real-time. This code is linked to a 2D sketch of the avatar's shape and articulations, which is used as a training guide for our conditional variational rendering model. This approach enables us to extend our method to a more advanced form, static avatar rendering with user-specified features, as well as animated avatar rendering from video clips and complex animated scenes. This includes the creation of realistic avatar renderings and semi-realistic renderings with enhanced skin detail, producing more lifelike results than standard model-based approaches and style-transfer methods. This is demonstrated in our results, which show our models' ability to accurately depict dynamic poses and produce high-fidelity animated scenes from limited training data. This is further supported by our user studies, which indicate a clear preference for our realistic renderings over standard approaches and style-transfer methods. A method is presented for obtaining an unbiased estimate of a mixture's property, based on an established maximum likelihood estimation technique. This method expands upon previous work by allowing for an assessment of the mixture's property when its components' properties are described by a linear combination of two values, as long as the weights are known. This is particularly useful in the analysis of blends that have been sampled randomly, as it can provide a confidence interval for their property and guide future sampling strategies to ensure a more accurate assessment. The method is demonstrated through simulations and real-world sampling scenarios of polymer blends, where the objective was to estimate their fracture toughness. This technique is now available through an R package called MELQ, which is also used to present the method's application to polymer blends. The package is available on CRAN and on GitHub under an open-source license. Knowledge tracing has gained significant traction in recent years as a practical application of learning analytics that streamlines the skill assessment process for students by leveraging historical performance data. This knowledge tracing technique analyzes user behavior to identify skills previously unknown and accurately predicts future abilities, ultimately enhancing personalized educational content recommendation. We've observed that researchers often reuse existing datasets and methods from previous knowledge tracing studies in their own research, without contributing anything new, likely as a necessary step in the research process. We believe that reimplementing methods from existing studies as part of new research is valuable, but also poses data management challenges due to the complex nature of learning management systems, multiple data collection sources and inconsistent formatting. To address these limitations and facilitate the development of new knowledge tracing methods, we present PyKT, a Python-based framework that provides a standardized data management system and a range of evaluation tools for data collected from Learning Management Systems, Moodle, Blackboard and Canvas, among others. This open-source framework supports multiple representation methods for modeling user skills and knowledge graphs, enabling the seamless integration of various deep learning-based knowledge tracing systems. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we've incorporated PyKT in a new study that focuses on assessing the performance of various knowledge tracing methods using a comprehensive evaluation framework and a diverse dataset of over 20,000 user interactions from multiple subjects, with results that highlight the advantages of KyTrac, a novel knowledge tracing algorithm developed using PyKT, over existing approaches. This research was conducted under the guidance of Prof. Dr. Hook, with the primary contributor being M. Turkan, with M. Turkan and J. M. Turkan serving as equal secondary contributors, and has been successfully implemented as an open-source project on GitHub under the terms of the MIT License. With PyKT, the knowledge tracing research community now has a robust framework that facilitates the development of new evaluation methods and data-driven learning analytics techniques in higher education, in line with the principles of reproducibility and generalizability, and we believe it positions Turkey at the forefront of global knowledge tracing research. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly impede performance. To mitigate this, federated averaging was developed, allowing unconstrained updates from participating devices. However, this method is limited by its robustness in the presence of device drift, a common issue. To address this problem, we developed a novel technique for processing updates in a central server role. In our approach, instead of accepting or rejecting updates as is the case with traditional methods, we create a buffer to aggregate updates from participating devices. This aggregated update, representing the sum of all updates from devices, including those with drift, is then processed by minimizing a regularized empirical risk. Our method boasts several key advantages: it processes updates in a parallel manner, tackles device drift through a regularized optimization framework, and is compatible with a broad spectrum of loss functions and optimization methods, including adaptive methods like FedADAM. We validated our approach through comprehensive experiments, showcasing its capacity to handle complex datasets and challenging scenarios, such as learning natural language processing tasks with a large, distributed dataset. Our results indicate that our method achieves comparable performance to methods that process unconstrained updates, with FedADAM delivering the best results, while also outperforming existing methods in scenarios with substantial device drift. Furthermore, we observed a direct correlation between the degree of drift and performance decline. Our technique's code is available for public access through this link https://github.com/IBM/Buffered-Fed-Avg. Moreover, we pre-trained multiple models, available at this address https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~fmb33/BufferedFedAvg.html, for cross-device learning in various settings, including NLP and with the CIFAR-10 dataset, facilitating the exploration of this research area by the broader community. These pre-trained models provide a foundation for exploring essential research questions, such as the optimal communication frequency, the minimum required level of participation from devices, and how our method compares to recent advancements in federated learning, including FedBoost and FedOptiq. We explore the possibility of transferring acoustic models across languages with similar phonology and phonetic characteristics. We focus on the Germanic languages, developing a shared phoneme set and corresponding acoustic models for English and Dutch. To achieve this, we use a multi-stream system with language-independent features for Dutch, extending the approach to English. Our results show that a Dutch acoustic model can be approximated with an English model, yielding a 11% reduction in data requirements. Conversely, an English model also performs well on Dutch with only a 23% increase in data needed, compared to a fully Dutch-trained model. A cross-lingual evaluation reveals that these models excel in spoken English recognition with a 12% gain, amounting to 1.6 seconds less latency. To further reduce data requirements, we introduce a rough-to-detailed training method, where a coarse-grained model is trained first, followed by a refined model on the remaining data. This approach leads to a 19% decrease in latency for Dutch with an English acoustic model, resulting in 0.7 seconds less latency. Moreover, it enables spoken English recognition with a 9% gain, amounting to 1.3 seconds less latency. Our findings suggest that Dutch and English share sufficient acoustic similarities, enabling the application of our methods to other language pairs, such as low-resource languages with English, or Dutch with other Germanic languages like Norwegian or Frisian. We introduce Twitch, a suite of datasets centered on graph node embeddings, in an effort to address the challenge of proximity and structural role preservation that many existing methods fail to meet. Our data complements the traditional Mujos dataset and extends it to a more comprehensive evaluation framework that encompasses 13 diverse graphs. Each of these graphs is carefully selected to showcase unique role distributions, forcing the evaluation of node embedding methods in contexts where certain entities hold distinct positions within the graph structure. Our experiments reveal that a substantial gap exists between the performance of current node embedding methods in maintaining structural roles and their ability to adhere to the graph structure. Our findings are available through a publicly accessible repository that includes both the Twitch dataset and our comprehensive evaluation results. Furthermore, we have established an open call for additional datasets that feature unique role distributions to be incorporated within the Twitch dataset framework. This initiative aims to provide a thorough examination of the structural role-oriented node embedding methods in a multi-domain setting. Such evaluation frameworks are crucial for the development of robust node embedding methods that are capable of withstanding changes to the graph structure and can be applied in a variety of contexts where the performance of specific entities within a graph is critical. Some examples of applications that rely on the performance of specific entities within a graph include, but are not limited to, bipartite graph matching, community detection, and the evaluation of node embedding methods themselves. Our data and the associated evaluation results are also useful for developing and benchmarking the performance of node embedding methods that prioritize the maintenance of structural roles and unique entities within a graph structure. Our research in the domain of node embeddings is supported by a new research line that focuses on the evaluation of these models, and we are committed to contributing to this community through the provision of publicly accessible datasets and results. When marine robots navigate, they need to balance exploring their surroundings with minimizing risk. Our research focuses on this challenge under the name Marine Navigation, a newly defined problem. Unlike existing problems that involve balancing exploration and safety in changing environments, Marine Navigation takes into account the fact that environmental variations usually occur over extended periods. Taking a stochastic process view of the changing environment, we propose a novel approach, SPAN, which utilizes a Gaussian process to model both the underlying state and temporal changes within the state. Taking into account that many environmental states are known to be stationary and stable over time, SPAN incorporates an adaptive threshold to filter out unnecessary models, thus preventing unnecessary exploration. Taking high-dimensional observations into account, SPAN also uses a neighbor-based approach to efficiently learn across smaller, more manageable subsets of features. Through simulated experiments in diverse underwater scenarios, SPAN consistently demonstrates its ability to learn from limited observations, efficiently navigate its surroundings with minimal risk, and effectively compare against models that either rely on strong assumptions about the environment or are computationally infeasible for real-world applications. A newly developed high-resolution simulation of the galaxy's formation and evolution allows us to analyze the dust content and temperature across its 50,000 cubic kiloparsecs. Observations of the galaxy at multiple wavelengths, with data from SPITZER, Herschel, ATLASGAL, and Planck, reveal temperature ranges from approximately 5 to 50 Kelvin, with a median value of about 14 Kelvin. We investigated the effects of magnetic fields on galaxy collisions in a cosmological context, considering two scenarios with weak and strong magnetic fields, respectively. Our simulations, conducted with the RAMSES code, featured a $1024^3$ particle resolution and a $100\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{kpsec}$ comoving softening length. Two spiral galaxy pairs, with masses similar to those of Milky Way and Lenticular galaxies, were subjected to collisions at various velocities, once in a high-velocity impact and once in a lower-velocity one. In the strong magnetic field scenario, we introduced an artificially increased resistivity to study the field's influence, while in the weak magnetic field scenario, we solved Ohm's induction equation directly. In the high-velocity case, both magnetic field scenarios exhibited analogous results, displaying a similar shape for the magnetic field and its induced electric field, and demonstrating that the induced effects can extend beyond the resolution limit of the simulation. However, in the lower-velocity case, the weak magnetic field scenario led to active electromagnetic non-reversal rates twenty times greater than the strong magnetic field scenario. This discrepancy highlights the critical distinction between collision velocities that do and do not result in magnetic field reversal. In the strong magnetic field scenario, the collision led to the destruction of both gas and stellar disks. In the lower-velocity case, particularly in the weak magnetic field scenario, new spiral arms formed through the warping of both gas and stellar disks due to the angular momentum transfer associated with magnetic field reversal. In the strong magnetic field scenario, colliding gas was shown to be re-directed and accumulated at the collision's center, along with evidence of magnetic field advection there. In the weak magnetic field scenario, however, a different observation was made, where a significant portion of the gas shows a different behavior, where it is broken into smaller fragments that are dispersed across the point of impact. These findings suggest that a weak magnetic field can prevent the destruction of galaxy disks during collisions, and that a strong magnetic field hinders the re-building of galaxy disks even at lower collision velocities. Further research is necessary to confirm these outcomes on a larger scale. Collective motion in galaxy collisions may be influenced by magnetic fields to an extent where it could provide an additional explanation for the diverse shapes of spiral galaxies. Researchers and survey takers often encounter a common issue when reporting quantities, where responses are rounded to the nearest integer. For example, in surveys about income, respondents tend to round their earnings to the nearest hundred or thousand. A notable characteristic of this practice is that it is isometric, meaning that the true value of a quantity is equidistant from two possible responses. As a result of this characteristic, responses are not uniformly distributed around the true value, but rather are more concentrated at the higher end, especially in positive ranges. This phenomenon has significant implications for the estimation of means and totals, which are commonly calculated using the average of individual responses. Since responses are not independent, using their mean would actually overestimate the true mean by a certain amount, which varies with the specific range but is at least 0.5 for positive integers. Consequently, this overestimation has a ripple effect, distorting the calculation of totals, which are often the primary focus of research. To illustrate this issue, we examined survey data on household incomes, finding that the estimated total income based on rounded responses exceeded the true total by at least 25 percent, a discrepancy that could be as high as 1000 in this particular dataset. To rectify this problem, we developed an alternative method for estimating totals, taking into account the ambiguity inherent in rounded responses. This new approach involves analyzing the distribution of individual responses and their relationships to the true values, which allows for a more accurate calculation of totals. We demonstrated the effectiveness of this method using simulated data and real-world survey data on income, income ranges, and election outcomes, which showed that our method yields more precise results than the conventional average, reducing the estimation error by half or more in some cases. This research offers a solution to a widespread issue affecting many fields, from economics and politics to medicine and psychology, providing a practical solution that can be applied to various types of data and statistical problems. The proposed method is straightforward and easy to implement using standard statistical software, providing a cost-effective alternative to more complex Bayesian methods. We also explored alternative methods for estimating totals, such as utilizing the midpoint of rounded responses or the mode in specific ranges, which can be more accurate in certain situations. However, our primary contribution is the method that accounts for the ambiguity inherent in rounded responses, which has the advantage of handling a wide range of data and statistical problems. This research is an attempt to address a pervasive issue in research and data analysis, which is the impact of rounding on estimates and the resulting distortion of means and totals

To better understand the potential of this approach, a new theoretical framework is established to account for various sources of uncertainty in the field. From this framework, predictions are made for the discoverability of the 31 GeV dark matter spike in three different scenarios using statistical tools commonly used in particle physics. The predictions take into consideration the uncertainties associated with key factors, including the characteristics of dark matter particles, the composition of primordial gas, and the sensitivity of detection methods. In scenario III, where the detection techniques fall short of predictions, the discovery is likely to be in 2045.
