Machine learning models excel at revealing feature significance through varying techniques, but often, these methods are subjective and lack a clear, systematic approach. Despite the wealth of feature significance assessment methods, none account for another critical aspect - data reliability. Since data reliability and feature significance are intricately linked, it is essential to investigate the relationship between them. In this study, we introduce an innovative method centered on Mutual Information and Uncertainty Characteristic (MUC) to not only evaluate feature significance but also data reliability. Our proposed framework is versatile and applicable to any machine learning model. We specifically demonstrated MUC's utility with Random Forest, but its potential for use with other models exists. Our research demonstrates that data with high reliability, characterized by low uncertainty and strong feature relevance, contributes significantly to accurate classification. Conversely, data with low reliability, marked by high uncertainty and weak feature relevance, impairs classification performance. Our results show that our proposed framework is effective in filtering out unreliable data and features in a dataset. By leveraging our method, we discovered that ensembles of only the most reliable data, featuring strong significance, yield the most accurate classification results. Our research paves the way for further exploration of MUC and data reliability assessment methods in machine learning. Our findings on the importance of data reliability raise critical questions regarding the current understanding of feature significance and classification performance, which necessitate thorough investigation in future studies. Our results with Random Forest, obtained using 13 diverse classification datasets, demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed framework but indicate that the outcome is dataset-dependent. Re-identifying individuals across camera pairs without labels is a challenging task in unsupervised individual re-recognition. Existing methods typically rely on costly and impractical assumptions, such as needing multiple unsupervised re-identification sessions from each person across all cameras, in order to achieve good results. In contrast, our proposed approach assumes only a limited number of sessions from each person, without any need for re-identifying individuals within those sessions. By leveraging session-based unsupervised re-identification, our approach significantly outperforms the state of the art by 25.4% on the Market-1501 dataset and 12.9% on the MSMT17 dataset, demonstrating its ability to efficiently re-identify individuals across cameras even in the absence of supervised re-identification. In addition, our proposed method achieves real-world applicability by eliminating the requirement for artificially generated camera pairs, such as those with only a single image, in order to evaluate its performance on practical re-identification scenarios. Furthermore, experimental results show its ability to adapt to new, unseen cameras, without any need for further training, by extending the current state-of-the-art in evaluation of unsupervised individual re-recognition by 10.5% on the Market-1501 dataset and 5.5% on the MSMT17 dataset, in comparison to the method that introduced contrastive re-re-id loss but failed to report results on the Market-1501 dataset. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengxu95/URRCT. Furthermore, based on extensive experiments and analysis conducted on multiple datasets, including Market-1501 and MSMT17, a new evaluation protocol for unsupervised individual re-recognition is proposed, in order to assess the ability of re-identifying individuals across all available camera pairs without any need for supervised re-identification, by extending the current state-of-the-art in evaluation of unsupervised individual re-recognition by 12.5% on the Market-1501 dataset and 8.5% on the MSMT17 dataset. This paper presents a novel GARCH model that predicts tail risks using a Bayesian approach and achieves a notable improvement in performance over traditional GARCH variants, including a new method for estimating model parameters that produces more effective risk predictions at a lower cost. Unlike conventional GARCH models, which require arbitrary parameter settings and often produce misleading results due to model mispecification, the new framework seamlessly selects the optimal model parameters to minimize forecasting errors for large-scale macroeconomic tail risk data. Empirical studies confirm that the new framework significantly outperforms alternative GARCH models, including single and multi-factor GARCH models, and a recent GARCH model variation, and demonstrates robustness in predicting tail risks for a comprehensive set of global macroeconomic indices with high frequency data. Notably, the new framework shows a notable advantage in forecasting performance when compared to a recent state-of-the-art model, and its effectiveness is further validated through a cost-efficient analysis and a stress testing exercise. The new framework's parameters can be estimated using a relatively simple method that addresses the computational challenges associated with maximum likelihood estimation, and an extension of the model is also proposed to account for time-varying tail risk connectivity among asset returns. The proposed framework offers a groundbreaking solution to the persistent challenge of forecasting rare events and provides a valuable framework for policymakers and risk managers to make data-driven decisions. The framework's models and methods are implemented as an R package called BFGARCH, and the package's functionality is illustrated through a real-world application. The paper's results are also supported by a formal threshold measurement framework for tail risk forecasting, and the new framework's achievements are placed within the broader context of recent research on tail risk forecasting. The paper's results are further validated by a panel of leading experts in the field through a stress testing exercise. The Nambu-Goldstone boson with the lowest mass in a chiral $SU(3)$ symmetry breaking theory has properties similar to those of the pion. To understand the pion's low-energy behavior in detail, researchers are using lattice QCD to compute various pion quantities directly, but this process is very time-consuming. Instead of calculating each quantity individually, our study demonstrates that two-current correlations can be used to derive several important pion properties, including form factors, electromagnetic and strangeness fractions, decay constants, and meson-nucleon form factors, all with a significant reduction in computational costs. As a part of the "Physics Case" for an "exact lattice QCD" project, which aims to accurately determine the pion's properties on a lattice, our research is being performed with the collaboration of RBC and UKQCD on a 24-node 2.3-2.5 GHz IBM Blade System running 576-768 lattice processes on the IBM Blue Gene/Q at the KISTI in Korea. Our preliminary results show that two-current correlations are very precise, with errors typically below 1%, and our final results for the pion's electromagnetic form factor and strangeness fraction are in line with the global averages, while our decay constant and meson-nucleon form factor findings are somewhat higher than the global averages, and our results also indicate that the quark masses used in our calculations are consistent with those obtained through CHPT at the scale of the physical mass. Our research highlights the significance of two-current correlations in lattice QCD calculations and the value of having independent outputs from multiple processes, and our study has been submitted to Phys. Rev. D and is currently under review. Our research is also being presented at the Lattice 2014 meeting in Sifnos, Greece. Our study is an important step towards determining the pion's properties on a lattice, and our results demonstrate the significance of two-current correlations in lattice QCD calculations. Our previous research revealed an underrepresented category of T Tauri stars characterized by typically normal stellar parameters but abnormally high and frequent episodic accretion bursts in their light curves. We conducted in-depth analyses of light curves and spectra for one prototype of this group, XX Cha, using the latest versions of data and methods. The resulting high-cadence light curves from TESS and high-resolution spectra from AAT and 2dF/DARWIN revealed complex and non-stationary activity during the observed time period, featuring significant fluctuations in luminosity and net accretion rates exceeding 1 dex. These results demonstrated that high-mass fraction episodes can persist for weeks to months, accompanied by enhanced emission lines and variable rotation periods, likely induced by interplay between magnetic braking and material supply. We also discovered a significant correlation between the total integrated accretion history of the star and the duration of high-mass fraction episodes, which could have implications for the evolution of T Tauri stars. Furthermore, we found that XX Cha represents the most extreme example of its type and the largest deviation from the general trend of T Tauri stars when comparing their spectral and physical characteristics to the characteristics of their light curves and accretion rates. We also updated the empirical relationship between optical and near-infrared accretion rates and found that XX Cha is an outlier even when considering this relationship. We derived an updated range for the ratio of accretion rates in H-alpha and FUV, with a 95% confidence interval from 3.5 to 8.9, and a median value of 5.6, which can be useful for interpreting observational data in the H-alpha spectrum when the near-infrared accretion rate is not available. We also explored possible explanations for the unusual behavior of XX Cha, including an unstable disk, the presence of a star that is being stripped of its material, or an inner disk region dominated by jets, but we were unable to provide sufficient evidence to support any of these theories. We suggested that future research should focus on monitoring the spin-down of XX Cha and any resulting changes in its rotation period as well as any potential variations in its light curves and spectra once the light curve fluctuations cease. We also proposed that XX Cha and its time series light curves should be included in any training datasets for artificial neural networks used for the classification of T Tauri stars and their light curves. Chances and income play a crucial role in this dynamics, as they have a dual impact: can either concentrate to exacerbate disparities or diffuse to reduce them, depending on specific circumstances. The term "inequity of chance" refers to the situation that arises when there are initial disparities in chances, leading to varying income outcomes, regardless of whether this inequality is inherent or developed over time. This concept is the focus of this paper, which explores its implications through mathematical modeling and simulation. The results indicate that inequity of chance leads to income reallocation, resulting in increased overall variability, in addition to stimulating the development of new inequalities and causing existing ones to worsen, as seen in both stochastic and deterministic models, and particularly in their mean-field and Ising versions. These findings are particularly evident in the latter, as they allow for the emergence of multiple distinct inequality levels. The sensitivity of these phenomena to temperature, order, and interaction parameters was examined, and the observation made that certain parameter settings can give rise to situations where chances become less important than income in determining overall inequality, as well as the occurrence of ferrimagnetic behavior and the creation of new inequalities at higher temperatures. The potential applications of these results to policy decisions are also discussed, along with the need for further empirical research into how chances and income relate in different economic systems. The development of precise data debugging techniques is hindered by the absence of computational resources and detailed process information in large-scale, distributed systems used for machine learning. This study introduces an automated data debugging framework that leverages the Shannon entropy of models trained on subsets of data to determine the significance of individual data points. This framework is efficient because the data point significance computation, based on entropy, does not require access to underlying process information. Moreover, it is highly effective in identifying data points that are crucial for model performance because these points have a significant impact on model diversity. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through the debugging of high-performance machine learning models trained using Hadoop on synthetic and real-world datasets. The data points identified by this framework as important for model performance are, in some cases, inaccurately predicted but the actual inaccuracies are consistently found among the top-ranked data points identified as significant by the model. This framework offers superior performance compared to an alternative method based on computation time. It enables the development of more effective debugging tools that can identify data points based on their predicted significance, resulting in a significant improvement (up to 25%) in data points correctly identified in comparison to a baseline scenario. This framework is robust and is capable of correctly identifying data points in over 99% of cases across different machine learning models and datasets. This is the first study on the development of data debugging techniques that can handle large-scale, distributed machine learning workflows used in real-world applications. This framework is complementary to model debugging techniques that focus on fixing model errors and can be integrated with state-of-the-art debugging tools to accurately fix data points that need attention. This framework is applicable to a wide range of machine learning algorithms, including those used in deep learning, but the computation time for training models on subsets of data can be extensive. This framework is designed to be highly adaptable and its implementation is straightforward, making it suitable for use as a debugging tool in real-world applications. Our detailed studies of 23 clusters featuring extended radio emission, and interactions between stars and the cluster's core, light, and intermediate zones, have yielded notable results. We investigate a novel hypergraph restoration task, where a full-information hypergraph needs to be recovered from a sparse subgraph. This problem is distinct from standard graph completion, due to the absence of a central node in typical hypergraphs and the higher dimensional nature of hypergraphs. We establish a new objective function for this task, taking into account both the similarity between adjacent hyperedges and the structural properties of the hypergraph. To solve this problem, we develop an iterative algorithm that combines two optimization processes: a step of constrained minimization using Nesterov's acceleration, and a step of extrapolation. We also provide a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's convergence and a solution for an alternative representation of the problem. Experimental results demonstrate our method's effectiveness compared to alternative approaches. We further examine the application of hypergraph restoration in the context of hypergraph partitioning. Due to the relatively limited amount of labeled hypergraph data, we explore a framework that leverages a supervisor with limited labels, resulting in improved model generalizability. This framework enables the integration of hypergraph restoration with semi-supervised learning techniques. We observe potential advantages of our method over standard semi-supervised graph learning approaches. However, there are instances where our method fails to achieve better performance than standard semi-supervised graph learning approaches. We analyze these instances and identify certain characteristics of hypergraphs that contribute to these failures. We discuss these findings in the context of future research directions for hypergraph restoration. We present our results in the form of both rigorous experiments and qualitative hypergraph examples. These results are further illustrated through a demonstration of a hypergraph restoration application. The implementation of our method is accompanied by a demonstration of an interface for interacting with hypergraph learning models. This interface enables the exploration of hypergraph learning in an intuitive and visual manner. We provide a detailed description of both the hypergraph dataset we constructed and the interface we designed. This interface is an innovative tool for examining the effects of different hypergraph learning algorithms. We discuss the underlying theory of hypergraph restoration and clarify any confusing points. We also outline specific contributions of our work. Our analysis shows that the photons emitted from these atoms can exhibit unique, non-classical properties like bimodal distribution and anti-bunching, and that these properties are heavily reliant on the temperature of the atomic group. A critical temperature range, at which the superfect Casimir effect is most prominent, is identified and characterized by an unusual, double-humped structure in the photon correlation function. This specific temperature range cannot be achieved through cooling techniques that only consider individual atoms, making this finding's relevance being limited to scenarios where there is a substantial overlap between the atoms. Our research provides a foundation for investigating non-classical light in relation to thermal atoms in a broader context. Furthermore, it introduces a novel approach for measuring the temperature of overlapping atomic groups, offering a thermometer that goes beyond conventional methods. This is achieved by utilizing the unique, temperature-dependent photon correlation function, which serves as a temperature-proving indicator rather than a functional, usable temperature measurement tool. Our analysis also reveals that increasing the distance between the atoms has a significant, counter-intuitive effect: it initially decreases the anti-bunching phenomenon in a linear manner, but then suddenly increases it to a point where it is greater than its original, atomic individual value standard. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents has seen significant growth in interest due to its potential to create data-driven policy solutions for complex systems with multiple interacting entities. However, existing methods are limited by the requirement for labeled data from all possible trajectories, which is often impractically hard to obtain in real-world scenarios, especially when states and actions are high-dimensional. This study introduces a novel approach called Positive Trajectory Learning (PTL), which leverages unlabeled data from any source, including potentially biased datasets, and focuses on learning from identified successful trajectories. PTL develops a framework to learn a generalized policy using only data from positive experiences, without relying on comparisons with unsuccessful trajectories. This framework is based on an innovative multi-agent experience reweighting method that prioritizes high-quality experiences, giving them greater weight in the learning process. Theoretical analysis provides a dynamic weighting system that identifies successful experiences with the most value for learning, given the action spaces of the agents are collaborative. However, when the action spaces are competitive, the experience weights become dynamic and agent-specific, depending on the context, requiring a data-driven approach to determine them. This is demonstrated through energy management and mobility applications, showing significant improvement in learning efficiency and accuracy with only positive experiences, compared to established baselines, especially in challenging scenarios with high-dimensional states and actions. The findings highlight the potential for learning from any available offline data, regardless of its quality, which can be particularly beneficial for solving multi-agent problems in complex, real-world settings. The code for the proposed method, named Multi-Agent Reinforcement Education (MARE), is made available at https://github.com/andersonwatts/MARE, along with additional information at https://andersonwatts.github.io/project/MARE/. The study also presents an empirical evaluation of the performance of the method, titled Multi-Agent Reinforcement Education Challenges (MARECs), which is designed to assess the efficacy of offline multi-agent learning methods at scale, along with its results. The framework includes an innovative experience reweighting framework that prioritizes successful experiences in the learning process, giving them greater weight. This framework can be applied to any multi-agent experience reweighting method, including policy evaluation and value function estimation methods. The study explores the theoretical dynamics of the proposed experience reweighting framework, and demonstrates its benefits through energy management and mobility applications, showing significant improvement in learning efficiency and accuracy with only positive experiences, compared to established baselines, especially in challenging scenarios with high-dimensional states and actions. The study also introduces Multi-Agent Reinforcement Education Challenges

We developed a novel approach to align MV images from 2D and 3D, utilizing recent advancements in image processing using neural networks. Our technique utilizes a convolutional neural network, specifically the U-Net architecture, to produce a 3D MV image from a single 2D image, using a reference 3D image as a comparison standard. To improve alignment, we introduced a new method that directly assesses the 3D alignment, rather than relying on 2D alignment metrics, and implemented an efficient algorithm to perform 3D alignment in a series of 2D steps. Our system is fully automated and is capable of processing one 2D image every 5 seconds on a standard computer hardware. We tested our alignment technique on 10 3D datasets from MV images of the head and neck region, obtained from two different MV imaging modalities, and obtained satisfactory results with a mean 3D distance metric of 3.25 mm, indicating its potential for clinical use. Furthermore, our technique demonstrates robustness in handling various types of tumors. Additionally, our technique is more efficient, with an average time requirement of 5 seconds per 2D image, in contrast to the MPI protocol's time requirement of over one hour per 3D image. We believe that our technique has the potential to replace traditional MPI protocols in clinical settings, due to its higher accuracy and faster processing time. We demonstrate the relationship between single-particle entanglement and nonlocal effects in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer, utilizing a two-photon source that produces both entangled and unentangled single photons. Our findings show that genuine nonlocal effects, such as single-particle guidance, rely on single photons being entangled with their generation process, or with each other in the case of a source that produces entangled photons. This implies that any correlation existing between single photons, whether related to the generation process or each other, is sufficient for producing nonlocal effects with single particles. Our research also highlights the value of utilizing both entangled and unentangled single photons in the investigation of nonlocal phenomena in photon systems. As a result, the need for source characterization, typically required with entangled photon pairs, is eliminated when using unentangled single photons, obtained from an interferometer setup in a specific configuration. This specific configuration allows for the distinction between single photons that are entangled with each other, or with the generation process, or are not entangled with anything. This particular configuration enables the identification of any single-particle entanglement, or the entanglement of the source itself, or the lack thereof, based on the interference pattern obtained. Quantum error correction standards serve as indicators to measure whether a quantum computing system is functioning properly or not. We are investigating a new concept, "topological emitters," which could offer more precise control over photons interacting with matter through waveguide QED. To achieve this, we are developing a 2D model using a honeycomb lattice, where a strong interaction between atoms and photons is induced by coupling them through a photonic channel. We show that in this setup, we can create a one-way flow of photons between two distant points using a single control laser. Additionally, we find that by adjusting the strength of the atomic-photonic interaction, we can manipulate the emittance of photons from the source, even when there's no control over the direction of emission. We also discover that a strong reaction between atoms and photons is required to produce the desired topological properties. Finally, we propose a realistic experimental implementation using a diamond substrate and a laser-cooled ensemble of nitrogen-vacancy atoms. Shining a laser on these atoms could generate a variety of phenomena, including topological emission, using techniques similar to those that produced Bell-state emission and entanglement between two remote points. Despite significant research, enhancing learning with additional information in these scenarios has proven difficult and often leads to overfitting. 

This study deviates from the standard approach of evaluating model performance with labeled data and instead utilizes human judgments to assess the impact of various information types on model performance in three NLP tasks: sentence similarity, sentence paraphrase and sentiment analysis.

 
Key findings reveal that certain information can impede model performance even with high confidence and that the benefits of information vary significantly between types, with some yielding little gain even with low-confidence judgments that are more abundant than high-confidence ones.

 
A general framework emerges that certain information serves as a direct supplement to restricted data, another as a substitute for data and another as ineffective.

 
Interestingly, the benefits of information are highly setting- and model-agnostic, but the optimal amount of information is highly task- and model-dependent.

 
Lastly, our study demonstrates the efficacy of a simple data augmentation method that matches human judgment standards and finds that it is consistently outperformed by models that learn from human judgments with minimal data.

 
These discoveries provide valuable insights for the field and highlight the need for a more systematic approach to evaluating the effectiveness of information in NLP, with a proposed framework for future evaluation and a call for more rigorous human judgment standards in NLP.

In datasets, researchers often rely on handcrafted indicators to highlight significant sections of text for further analysis. However, creating and utilizing these indicators requires separate tools for both generation and data processing. Our proposed system, DiscSense, removes this dichotomy by offering a versatile interface for both automated indicator creation and guided exploration of marked text regions. Built on top of an indicator language and supported by advanced search algorithms, DiscSense provides an interactive environment for researchers to craft their own indicators or existing ones, and subsequently, perform targeted analyses on the associated text segments. We demonstrate the capabilities of DiscSense through a case study involving the development of thematic baskets in political discourse, showcasing both the capabilities of our system for both automated and guided approaches and the resulting statistical assessments of the indicators. Furthermore, DiscSense, coupled with an accompanying user manual, is available for public access at https://discsense.stanford.edu. Leveraging DiscSense, we invite the research community to contribute their own indicators, data sets, and analysis results to further the mission of the project: to provide an accessible framework for both the education and the advancement of text analysis in machine learning and natural language processing. Through this initiative, we aim to provide an extensive collection of indicators, marked data sets, and associated experiments to address the world's most pressing challenges and complex problems. In line with this vision, we invite researchers to collaborate with us in the development of DiscSense, encompassing both the system and the accompanying data sets and analysis results, to be collectively referred to as the DiscSense platform. As part of the launch of the system, we present an initial set of indicators for the community to build upon at https://discsense.stanford.edu/indices. These indicators, covering topics including sentiment, part-of-speech tags, named entities, and sentence similarity, among others, are designed to facilitate the exploration of a wide-ranging collection of text data, encompassing news articles, book chapters, and internet forums. As the first system of its kind to integrate indicator creation and data exploration, DiscSense is poised to revolutionize the field of text analysis by providing a unified framework for both automated indicator creation and guided exploration of marked text regions. With its versatile interface and advanced search algorithms, DiscSense is setting a new standard for the development of machine learning models and statistical analysis of text data. Furthermore, as a testament to its groundbreaking technology, DiscSense has been recognized as one of the top projects in the field of natural language processing at the Stanford University, where it was conceived and developed. Our study extends to temperatures as high as 400°C and reveals unique features of nitrogen-vacancy centers under these conditions, including a significant reduction of spin coherence likely caused by increased phonon activity from the diamond lattice, increased photon-induced spin flips due to absorption of emitted photons, and a marked decrease of spin lifetimes likely resulting from enhanced non-radiative phonon emission mediated by the diamond lattice. In the brain, neural networks are protected from harmful information by a functional equivalent of data protection, which is ensured through a highly complex interplay of neural systems. This research introduces a novel neural network designed to operate in an in vitro environment, which is comprised of a functional representation of a cortical microcircuit, along with a sensory input system and a memory function similar to the hippocampus. The network is capable of self-regulation, rejecting the abnormal stimulation it receives during an upstate sleep phase, while actively learning normal stimulation during an awake phase. The network also displays an ability to recognize and recall sensory stimuli, as well as exhibit advanced computational capabilities such as pattern recognition and the generation of complex movement patterns. The code for this network is highly versatile and can be easily adapted for use in both in vitro and in vivo experiments. The neural network presented here provides valuable insights into the basic principles that any data protection system operating within the brain must adhere to, as demonstrated through the observation that the network's ability to regulate itself is dependent on both its internal workings and its memory function. Furthermore, this research offers the possibility to experimentally validate theoretical hypotheses regarding the brain's data protection system in vitro. The network's capacity to regulate itself also raises the possibility that certain abnormal brain patterns observed in individuals with psychiatric disorders could potentially be the result of an underlying issue with data protection, as suggested by the fact that some of these patterns, such as schizophrenia-related deficits in sensory processing, are also observable in in vitro recordings of these neural networks. The data protection system described in this research is unique in its ability to oversee neural connections at all levels, as it accomplishes this through a non-selective form of regulation known as homeostatic regulation, as opposed to the more targeted form of regulation employed by systems such as the prefrontal cortex's default mode network. The distinct characteristics of this data protection system make it better suited to managing the brain's complex interplay between neural systems, as it is capable of handling both the brain's highly active and constantly changing state during wakefulness, as well as the more stable and less active state during sleep. The unique properties of this data protection system also provide a solution to the long-standing brain function paradox, as it shows that the brain's data protection system is actually more active during wakefulness than during sleep. The novel neural network presented here has the potential to be used in a wide range of applications, including the development of more sophisticated brain computer interfaces, as well as the creation of highly realistic simulations of the brain's data

Using large-scale Monte Carlo simulations in the context of the chiral sigma-model, we investigate whether Néel and Veselectri moments can be stabilized on a triangular lattice with three-fold symmetry for $SU(3)$ spin systems at low temperatures. Our research reveals that in antiferromagnetic arrangements for both Néel and Veselectri orders, a significant reduction in free energy occurs when the triplon's wavelength is around $6$, a phenomenon that is independent of spin representation. Moreover, a $SU(3)$-representation with Néel order exhibits robustness even in the presence of weak ferromagnetic interactions, a characteristic that is not observable in higher-spin systems. A $SU(3)$-triplon's hamiltonian in the Veselectri phase is comparably more susceptible to disorder, however we have established a relationship between this disorder and a $SU(3)$-triplon's hamiltonian in the Néel phase, where the latter can be understood via a SU(3) trimer rotation symmetry. Ultimately, our research establishes a method to determine a system's free energy using a $SU(3)$-triplon's hamiltonian in the Néel phase, a technique that can be applied to any spin representation. Finally, in both antiferromagnetic arrangements, we have identified a common critical exponent for triplon's wavelength $\nu \approx 0.66$ and have confirmed that both Veselectri and Néel moments can be stabilized at low temperatures on a triangular lattice with three-fold symmetry for $SU(3)$ spin systems. Additionally, our research provides a comparison with nematic moments on a triangular lattice with six-fold symmetry, a system that is closely related to the one studied here. Ultimately, our research provides a theoretical justification for experimental observations reported on $SU(N)$ triangular lattice compounds, specifically the $SU(3)$ compound with the chemical formula Yb$_3$Ti$_2$O$_{7}(SO_4)^{3-}$.2H$_2$O, where the measured reduction in free energy is consistent with our simulation results for both Veselectri and Néel orders. This new approach offers a consistent framework for studying both bounded and infinite systems through a uniform and logical extension of B-spline variation after Esposito, where the mean-field potential is represented by a linear combination of basis functions with locally resolved properties. As a critical phenomenon in this interplay, explosive synchronization (ES) has been extensively studied in various contexts and under different conditions in recent years. However, a fundamental issue with these studies is that they were conducted in isolation, without a common standard for comparison. To address this limitation, a set of reference criteria was developed to homogenize the methods used to investigate ES in network dynamics. A comprehensive analysis of multiple variables networks was performed to evaluate the effects of distinct network topologies, different types of coupling, and various disordering mechanisms on the occurrence of ES. These effects were categorized into three categories: explosive, transitional, and non-explosive, and were represented in a standardized form, such as in the form of a heat map or a surface plot. A user-friendly online platform was developed to enable users to assess the exponential growth of their own network by calculating the second exponential growth factor. The research demonstrated that there are robust features in network dynamics that remain unchanged with respect to the chosen variables, and a discussion on the implications of these findings in relation to network dynamics and the effects of epidemics in complex networks is also presented. Additionally, the research provides a framework for investigating other critical phenomena in complex networks. We begin by presenting a novel perspective on matrix optimization that is well-maintained for an extensive class of nonconvex and low-rank matrix optimization problems. This perspective is founded on a specific type of geometric concept called geodesic convexity, which is a more intricate property than the standard concept of convexity. From this viewpoint, we conduct an in-depth examination of an extensive class of fixed-rank matrix optimization problems with trace-based objective functions subject to general constraints that can be interpreted as geodesically convex when the matrix manifold is equipped with a specific metric. A significant highlight of our contribution is the formulation of an analytical framework for assessing the isolation of optimal solutions for a broad class of nonconvex matrix optimization problems. Furthermore, we derive a general algorithm that can be viewed as a combination of convex approximation and trust region techniques within a specific matrix manifold. We apply this viewpoint to fixed-rank matrix optimization problems involving Euclidean space, where we provide an alternative perspective on existing results that demonstrate the convexity of these problems. We also investigate rotationally invariant matrix optimization problems, which do not have a known analytical solution. From our geometric viewpoint, we are able to derive an in-depth examination of these problems as well as a general solution to a specific instance of this type of problem. Finally, we introduce a novel algorithm that integrates our understanding with the aim of solving a specific fixed-rank matrix optimization problem involving Euclidean space. We support our theoretical findings with numerical results that provide a comprehensive comparison of our proposed algorithm with existing methods for a broad class of matrix optimization problems. Collective solutions derived from our experiments are made available under an open-source license. Our work is also accompanied by an in-depth analysis of the challenges and potential solutions for a substantial class of fixed-rank matrix optimization problems within a specific matrix manifold. This analysis is presented in the form of an international survey on fixed-rank matrix optimization problems. We conclude our work by presenting an overview of emerging trends, potential solutions, and open issues in fixed-rank matrix optimization within a specific matrix manifold, along with a comprehensive glossary of terms used throughout our contributions. Collective code used in our experiments is made available under an open-source license. We hope that our work will contribute to the advancement of fixed-rank matrix optimization within a specific matrix manifold through the provision of analytical solutions, general algorithms, and novel perspectives on this type of problem as well as a comprehensive survey on fixed-rank matrix optimization within a specific matrix manifold. Currently, there is a widely accepted conjecture that any cubic bipartite graph can be tinted with four vertices. However, this study presents a well-trusted edge-tinting method when there are three vertices; however, it identifies a specific instance, referred to as the "N0 configuration," where the method fails when trying to apply it from an alternate perspective. By utilizing an approach that utilizes the N0 configuration, an instance is created that cannot be edge-tinted with just three vertices. This new instance or edge-tinting counterexample has the smallest number of vertices compared to any previously documented counterexamples. It is notable that all its vertices have an identical degree of three. This discovery forces an update to the widely accepted conjecture, which now states that any cubic bipartite graph can be edge-tinted with at least five vertices for all possible configurations except for the N0 configuration. This newly created counterexample is essentially irremovable, as it cannot be edge-tined even with the removal of one of its vertices. This study also investigates the characteristics of a smaller subset of a counterexample that also cannot be edge-tinted, but it cannot be removed. This subset or edge-tinting excluded area has the smallest number of vertices compared to any previously documented excluded areas. We investigated the Nash Equilibrium in a static Cournot game using a coevolutionary genetic model and found that several variations of this approach produce similar outcomes. Our research revealed that coevolutionary genetic methods can effectively identify the game's Nash Equilibrium at various population sizes and in environments with both low and high mutation rates. We observed that some methods yielded more stable results than others. Interestingly, a smaller population size in one dimension can, in fact, produce results as accurate as those obtained with larger population sizes. Notably, all methods demonstrated the ability to reach Nash Equilibria even in a scenario without any initial random variation. Our research contributes to the ongoing exploration of how coevolutionary genetic models can be applied to establish Nash Equilibria in a static Cournot game. Furthermore, our findings provide valuable insights for future research on dynamic versions of this game. Large-scale ontologies with limited updates can benefit from incorporating recent, relevant information from vast amounts of available text. While current NLP techniques excelled in individual tasks like text classification and knowledge base population, they struggle with comprehensive, systematic searches for information to support ontology enrichment. To address this challenge, we developed an original end-to-end approach that leverages both deep learning and graph-based methods to efficiently locate and extract information from unstructured text to enhance ontologies. By combining a search module with a extraction module, we enable targeted discovery of information related to specific ontology entities, followed by the extraction of additional, relevant data from the search results. To validate our approach, we conducted both rigorous search and extraction experiments, utilizing 1500 questions as both evaluation and training tools. Our results demonstrate superior performance compared to existing methods and showcase our model's capacity to enhance ontologies with newly discovered relationships and new entity additions. To illustrate the practical applications of our model, we employed it to update the YAGO3 ontology, incorporating 133 new entity pairs and 385 new property pairs from search results, carefully reviewed and validated by human assessors. Our approach and associated data and code are available for public use and distribution. Additionally, we provide early findings and methodologies for guided text searches to further expand and enrich ontologies. By incorporating both taxonomy and entity information, we successfully executed both structured and unstructured searches for information to enhance ontologies, exploring novel paths in the graph-based search for entities that, in turn, lead to additional discoveries. As a result, our approach has far-reaching implications for the extension of richly taxonomized ontologies via search, uncovering new entities and relationships and paving the way for the systematic exploration of complex graphs using guided text searches. To further improve our model, we are currently exploring the integration of alternative search and extraction methods as well as the addition of ranking and evaluation components to prioritize and assess the extracted information more effectively. To facilitate this integration, we plan to extend our evaluation experiments to encompass a broader range of tasks and to explore both weak and human-in-the-loop supervision methods to guide our model in the future. By incorporating both deep learning and graph-based methods, we are confident that our approach provides a more comprehensive and robust framework for the systematic search for information to support the enrichment of large-scale ontologies. We investigate how different weather factors contribute to the spread of airborne viruses through suspension in the atmosphere, specifically within urban areas with densely populated streets. This examination is mathematically represented by solving a system of partial differential equations that account for the movement of viruses, the cooling effect of wind on aerosols, and the impact of thermal and mixing instabilities. Our analysis, conducted under stable and stratified conditions, reveals that viruses can disseminate up to 170 times their original distance in a day, with wind speed playing a significant role. Notably, our findings indicate that viruses can spread further in stable conditions than in stratified ones, with some discrepancies arising from the destruction of virus stability in areas with strong thermal gradients. Moreover, our research shows that aerosol spread is significantly influenced by the size of the area in question, with viruses covering a greater proportion of that area in stable conditions. Our results also highlight the importance of wind speed in aerosol dissemination, with a greater proportion of the spread attributed to this factor in stable conditions, and demonstrate that submicron viruses can maintain stability in both weather conditions, whereas larger viruses can also maintain stability in stratified conditions. Our analysis also includes the examination of how the dispersion of viruses is distributed, with a focus on how it relates to the spread of diseases. Ultimately, our research provides the basis for further exploration into the complex interplay between weather conditions and the dissemination of airborne viruses. With the increasing prevalence of stable conditions in many urban areas, our findings suggest that there is a growing need for public health officials to consider the impact of weather on disease spread and the potential benefits of public health policies that take this factor into account. Building on our analysis, our results also raise questions about the role of environmental factors in the spread of diseases, with implications for our understanding of the underlying mechanisms that drive this process. Modern machine learning models, particularly those producing continuous output, often engage in scientific competitions to assess their performance. This study focuses on a specific aspect of this evaluation – input data ambiguity – examining existing measures and proposing a comprehensive framework for reference points. The framework consists of three primary components: (1) ambiguity metrics, defined as self-evaluation functions that assess the output's variability; (2) calculation methods for these metrics, including theoretical formulas and data-driven approaches; and (3) standards for measuring ambiguity in relation to performance indicators. The study evaluates eight machine learning models for classification and regression tasks, applying 15 different ambiguity measures and standards to gather 1440 data sets. The evaluation reveals the measures' variability depends on the model and is influenced by problem difficulties, while model performance is often correlated with ambiguity in some cases. The study also explores the connection between ambiguity and model diversity, along with the effects of model ensembling. The evaluation results are made available through comprehensive confusion matrices and detailed model performance rankings for each task. The study is a foundational exploration of ambiguity in machine learning, and future research is expected to build upon its findings and framework. The study is a collaboration between researchers from the University of Oxford, the University of Edinburgh, the University of Cambridge, the University of London, and the University of California, Berkeley. The study is an extension of a previous conference paper presented at the 2019 IJCA special session, while the experiment replication guidelines can be found at this link https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.05117, and the code is available at this link https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.05117.

Building upon the foundational work of Berman in 2003, our research expands upon the Jordanian twist concept. We have derived a comprehensive set of modified B-type superintegrals utilizing a one-parameter collection of Jordanian twists. These integrals are remarkably adaptive, as they seamlessly incorporate various Hamltonian configurations, including both solvable and non-solvable systems. Our novel integrals exhibit an intriguing property, where they transform into bi-Hamiltonian superintegrables upon combining with the original Hamiltonian, demonstrating a distinct separation into two independent components that each possess individual hamiltonian properties. Additionally, our research introduces an innovative three-dimensional representation of Poisson subalgebras, enabling a clearer understanding of the modified superintegrals' behavior. Our specific examples explore both monogenic and bigenic Jordanian twist combinations, revealing new potential applications in both discrete and continuous quantum mechanics systems. Our research also delves into establishing relationships between 2D and 3D systems via bigenic Jordanian twists, exposing novel bi-Hamiltonian connections between previously separate monogenic systems. Our findings also uncover new bi-Hamiltonian structures hidden within 3D solvable potentials, providing avenues for extending non-solvable potentials into superintegrable form. Our research in this field is still in its nascent stages, and future studies will further investigate both discrete and continuous quantum mechanics through three-dimensional Schrödinger equations, as well as examine new bi-Hamiltonian structures in 2D Lie algebras, such as nilpotent and semi-simple algebras, in subsequent papers. Conversational State Tracking (CST) is a key technology for enabling multi-turn conversations with limited human involvement, but a significant hurdle in its development is the challenge of handling label uncertainty. To address this, we propose a method to incorporate uncertainty into CST, which is designed to facilitate the creation of data sets that account for label uncertainty. We evaluated our approach using a pre-existing dataset called DSTC3 Task 1 Data, which involves tracking the conversation state in a real-world human-service interaction platform. Our approach demonstrated superior performance compared to standard methods, to which we added uncertainty-aware components, resulting in a 9.4% reduction in unknown entities, a 7.5% reduction in missing slots, and a 12.5% reduction in contradictory slots. Our approach also yielded a 19% increase in the mean of the negative log-likelihood and 0.34 in the overall score when evaluated by multiple metrics. We made several modifications to the dataset as a result of our evaluation, which included removing data with conversation state errors and introduced an uncertainty-aware dataset cleaning process, along with a method for data set balancing. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/zhengyang-wu/ASSIST. In late October 2019, violent demonstrations and widespread unrest erupted in Chile, quickly spreading across the country within 48 hours. To understand this rapid dissemination, we developed a statistical model to forecast disease-like patterns of behavior, with the goal of identifying timeframes and population segments that drove the contagion and fuelled the unrest, ultimately informing policymakers on areas and periods that required targeted intervention. Our epidemiological simulation, based on local non-global proximity metrics, successfully replicated and predicted behavior across 25 Chilean regions, demonstrating the utility of this approach in capturing and predicting the underlying dynamics of complex contagions, and highlighting the value of region-specific policy solutions. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that urban areas and certain demographic groups exhibited higher levels of unrest, as well as distinct temporal patterns, with some regions experiencing peak unrest before the overall epidemic curve peaked, suggesting targeted interventions can have a positive impact on public health and safety. In the aftermath of the protests, our simulation showed that regional epidemics began to recede at different times, with some areas exhibiting post-outbreak increases in unrest, potentially indicating underlying social issues in those regions. Building on this success, we believe this approach can be applied to model other complex contagions and unrest in Chile and worldwide. Due to varying data availability, further research is needed in other countries and in Chile for specific regions and demographics, with potential applications across multiple fields. Our code is freely available on an established repository, providing an invaluable resource for both academic and practical communities, along with detailed guidelines for both theoretical and methodological use cases. With the current global pandemic serving as a timely reminder of the critical importance of public health, our simulation underscores the value of data-driven policy solutions, with a strong case for their consideration in both emergency response planning and day-to-day decision-making. As a result, we recommend that policymakers, in collaboration with researchers and scientists, incorporate epidemiological models into their decision-making framework, with a view to addressing not only the current pandemic but also other social contagions and unrest in Chile and worldwide. With this approach, we can collectively develop targeted, effective, and compassionate solutions to these complex, pressing issues. By comparing various methods of measuring star formation rates (SFRs), researchers discovered a notable correlation between these measures and the mass of the galaxy. However, a significant challenge lies in selecting a reliable and unbiased indicator of SFR, especially across different galaxy types and mass ranges. A study discovered a previously overlooked line, Brackett-$\gamma$, that serves as a robust indicator of ongoing star formation, unconnected to molecular gas mass or galaxy type. Using data from the CALIFA spectroscopic database, a team of scientists established a clear, distinct relationship between Brackett-$\gamma$ emission and estimated star formation rates, despite some scatter. Notably, this relationship held true for a broad spectrum of galaxies, from Mrk 331 to NGC 4555. A comparison of various SFR indicators with those derived from Brackett-$\gamma$ emission revealed a notable discrepancy, with SFR(BR$\gamma$) generally exceeding other measures by 50-100% in low-mass galaxies and 5-50% in massive galaxies. A key consideration is that Brackett-$\gamma$ is a direct, unfiltered emission line, unencumbered by optical distortions which may skew other SFR estimates. As such, this study advocates for the use of Brackett-$\gamma$ as a benchmark to evaluate other SFR indicators, with a warning that some methods may overestimate or underestimate star formation rates in certain galaxy types or mass ranges due to optical selection effects. Ultimately, this study suggests that a thorough examination of SFR derivation methods is essential to ensure accurate measurements, with Brackett-$\gamma$ as a reliable standard against which to compare and contrast other indicators. As such, it is crucial to consider the method of SFR estimation when comparing SFR among different galaxies or within a single galaxy across different R-band equivalent passbands. With the advent of integral field units (IFUs) that can observe Brackett-$\gamma$ in a broader range of galaxies and galaxy types, a reevaluation of existing and new SFR indicators in relation to Brackett-$\gamma$ is both feasible and necessary, with a study suggesting a comparison of SFR(BR$\gamma$) with other indicators for each galaxy individually. We are given a function $f\in C^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ that is positive and has global minimizers. Our main objective is to examine its relationship with the SOS cone, specifically to determine if $f$ can be represented as a sum of squares in a neighborhood of any point within its effective domain. Our findings indicate that if $f$ can be represented as a sum of squares in a neighborhood of a given point within its effective domain, then that point must be an interior point. Conversely, if $f$ can be represented as a sum of squares in a neighborhood of all points within its effective domain, then those points must be strictly positive and form an irreducible variety. We also demonstrate that if $f$ is convex and self-determined in its effective domain, then it can be represented as a sum of squares in a neighborhood of all points within its effective domain if and only if it is a member of the Kummer surface defined by $u^2=v^4$. In the context of federated learning, various methods are being explored to tackle the challenge of integrating diverse data without exchanging information. Our proposed approach, Federated Discriminative Aggregation, is centered on leveraging a discriminative model for aggregation. Initially, multiple independent models are trained within their respective data sets and then, without data exchange, our approach discriminates between the models based on their performance and selects the most suitable one for combining their predictions. Our selected model is chosen through a systematic evaluation process that assesses its performance on a common task across all participating networks. Our method showcases superior performance integration results compared to other methods, including non-federated baseline, in two substantial experiments for sparse and dense graph classification. However, this assumption may change if we account for rotational changes in these stars over time. If differential rotation in these stars is opposite to the typical (anti-solar), we investigated its potential to generate a poloidal field and contribute to magnetic field evolution. In a simulated environment with a low magnetic energy compared to kinetic energy, a solar-type dynamo can only maintain an axial dipole field if the toroidal field is restricted to specific intensity ranges. In contrast, an anti-solar differential rotation can support higher toroidal field intensities, resulting in the natural generation of a poloidal field through flux transport. This can lead to a dynamos cycle even in stars with gradually decreasing rotation rates. Notably, this cycle is self-sustaining without external influences, demonstrating the importance of an anti-solar differential rotation in potential magnetic cycles in these stars. The results also show that an anti-solar rotation is more likely to produce magnetic cycles in stars with rotation rates below 1.5 times the present solar rate. The findings further indicate that an anti-solar differential rotation can generate magnetic cycles even in stars with rotation rates as low as 0.7 times the present solar rate, in contrast to the widely accepted threshold of 0.4. Researchers in motivic homotopy theory are seeking a universal K-theory functor that extends to curved simplicial schemes and captures the classical algebraic K-theory of Quillen. This paper explores alternatives to the classical functor of Quillen, while also examining a potential replacement for the simplicial Yoneda embedding that could be used to compute the universal K-theory functor. By demonstrating connections between the motivic homotopy theory of simplicial schemes with the Grothendieck topology defined by Neron descent, the paper provides a framework for studying the universal K-theory functor and its relationship to geometric K-theory. This research includes a definition of curved algebraic K-theory for simplicial schemes with flat connections and a description of geometric K-theory as a broad category that includes curved algebraic K-theory as a subcategory. Ultimately, the findings of the research imply that a universal K-theory functor exists but is not unique, and this non-uniqueness is rooted in the ambiguities present in the motivic homotopy theory of simplicial schemes with flat connections. This study investigates the performance of the Rapid Multipole Technique in integrating
the force and potential contributions for particles with large angular momenta. To
validate RMT, we employ three test scenarios with particles possessing substantial
angular momenta, ranging from 10 to 100 times their computational cell size.
Additionally, our analysis examines how RMT's accuracy and efficiency compare to
those of the standard Particle-Particle Particle-Mesh (PPPM) solver for the first
time. Our findings indicate that RMT is more efficient, though it introduces an
error in angular momentum conservation, ultimately leading to circular rather than
elliptical orbits. In contrast, the traditional PPPM method precisely conserves
angular momentum but is significantly slower than RMT. To rectify RMT's inaccuracy
in angular momentum conservation, we propose a hybrid approach, combining it
with the Burkow-Hockenbury force correction for particles exhibiting large
angular momenta. Notably, this modified RMT method boasts a higher efficiency
rating than the standard PPPM solver, while precisely conserving angular momentum
and maintaining fast computation times. As a demonstration of its effectiveness,

Although deep learning-based medical image segmentation has achieved remarkable results in recent years, it still faces a significant challenge when applying its knowledge across similar anatomical structures in various images. This research introduces a contrastive semi-supervised learning method called Contrastive Semi-supervised Education (CSE) to overcome this challenge. By leveraging a limited number of labeled samples and a vast amount of unlabeled medical images, CSE learns to extract universal features from the data and discovers a way to transfer this knowledge to new images and targets. This is accomplished through inter-domain and intra-domain contrastive learning, which enables the network to adapt to new targets by exploring the existing data's rich domain information and preventing the model from drifting away from the target's annotations during the training process. This paper challenges that notion by demonstrating that the 1.5 order BRS formalism, a widely accepted extension of the BRS formalism from 1-dimensional supergravity to conformal supergravity, actually violates algebraic consistency which has seemingly been masked by a non-trivial identity. A simple transformation was devised to transform the consistent 3.0 formalism from D=1 supergravity to the 1.5 order formalism of D=11 supergravity and its relationship with conformal supergravity was explored. This transformation was applied to the 3.0 formalism from D=1 supergravity to derive the 1.5 order BRS transformation for conformal supergravity which was found to break algebraic consistency. The check of algebraic consistency for the 1.5 order formalism from D=11 supergravity failed due to a non-vanishing anticommutator of supercharges which is a novel feature that does not occur at 3.0 order. The analysis also uncovered the underlying reason for this failure which is the absence of a legible 3.0 order BRS transformation for conformal supergravity. The 1.5 order check of algebraic consistency was bypassed in the past due to the unique properties of the superalgebras in 1-dimensional supersymmetric theories which do not conform to the common perception that the check of supercharge stability is ensured by the closure of the superalgebra. The failure of the 1.5 order BRS formalism to pass the check of algebraic consistency has significant implications for the consistency of conformal supergravity in the absence of matter multiplets. It has been proven that conformal supergravity is inconsistent in the absence of matter multiplets which contradicts the findings of various studies that demonstrated the renormalizability of conformal supergravity coupled to fermion and scalar matter multiplets in 1-dimensional space-time. The discrepancy was resolved by showing that the consistency of these theories relies on modifying the 3.0 formalism from D=1 supergravity rather than adopting the 1.5 order BRS formalism from D=11 supergravity. The analysis demonstrated that the 1.5 order BRS formalism does not produce a legitimate BRS transformation for conformal supergravity in 1-dimensional space-time. Quantum systems, like any other technology, are prone to environmental disturbances which can result in the degradation of processed information. This threat becomes particularly menacing when sensitive data, such as cryptographic keys or encoded messages, is subject to error-prone storage or dissemination. A critical aspect of any quantum communication network is its data storage, and it is, therefore, essential to implement efficient and reliable decoding protocols for protecting information against rank-one measurement errors, which are induced by specific coherent attacks. Although, over a single use, these errors can be corrected with quantum error correction codes, such errors can escalate to more destructive forms, such as phase damping or bit flip errors, with each storage period, ultimately threatening the integrity of the stored information. In this work, we introduce a decoding protocol that is specifically designed to counter symmetric rank-one measurement errors in any-dimensional Hilbert space, and we demonstrate its effectiveness in protecting data against this type of error through an extended period of storage. We show that certain protocols based on our decoding method can achieve a storage duration several times greater than that achieved by applying quantum error correction codes over the same number of repetitions, or, alternatively, provide the same level of storage durability as codes that require significantly more measurements. Notably, we found that using a simple decoding protocol in combination with the storage of only a few qubits can offer a several-fold increase in storage capacity compared to applying quantum error correction codes over the same number of repetitions. This indicates that, in certain scenarios, our decoding method can provide enhanced performance, either in terms of prolonged data storage or increased storage capacity for a given storage period, either in scenarios involving coherent qubits or those involving mixed states with a high degree of entanglement, thus rendering it an attractive solution for safeguarding quantum information. This breakthrough could serve as a viable alternative to extensive rank-one measurement, such as coherent parabolic, projection, or amplitude modulation attacks, which all share similar effects, allowing it to protect quantum information effectively against a wide array of environmental threats. This finding holds significant implications for the secure dissemination of quantum information through storage and transmission, enabling the safeguarding of sensitive data, such as cryptographic keys or encoded messages, over extended periods of time, thus paving the way for robust quantum communication networks to become a reality. We've derived a novel closed-form expression for the correlation functions of a specific family of rotating operators in CFT$_2$, which are located at distinct points and separated by an OPE segment within a Lorentzian AdS$_3$. These results can be applied to compute the imaginary parts of conformal blocks when combined with the AdS/CFT approach. Notably, our findings reveal that rotating OPE segments behave as sources of semi-local symmetries that govern conformal field theories, which is supported by explicit examples from free CFT and a conformal field theory featuring a Kleinian surface group. The relationship between rotating OPE segments and monodromy symmetries within CFT is also highlighted. Our analysis indicates that the presence of these semi-local symmetries ensures that cross-ratio independence is maintained for specific correlation functions even when the OPE segments are rotating. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the semi-local symmetries that arise from AdS$_3$ and the Nambu-Goto string's monodromy constraints in flat spacetime. This discovery enables us to predict the behavior of rotating OPE segments in CFT$_d$ for $d\geq 3$. The associated field theory action is presented, along with supporting evidence derived from a simple conformally invariant massless scalar field theory in 1+1 dimensions. The associated field theory action is also shown to result in the imposition of monodromy constraints on string theory action in flat spacetime, which can be achieved by incorporating a Wess-Zumino term into the Lagrangian. The Wess-Zumino term has a unique coefficient that is determined by a surface group's Lie algebra, allowing for the recovery of the Nambu-Goto string's monodromy constraints when this term is chosen to correspond to a Kleinian surface group. The relationship between semi-local symmetries in CFT and the monodromy constraints of string theory represents a novel application of the AdS/CFT correspondence. Our analysis also reveals that rotating OPE segments give rise to a new, overarching symmetry that combines both conformal and AdS symmetries, which we refer to as the semi-local conformal AdS symmetry. This new symmetry must be adhered to in any conformally invariant field theories that incorporate OPE segments within a Lorentzian AdS$_3$. We propose that the presence of this new combined symmetry will result in the imposition of monodromy constraints on the associated string theories

We obtained early and late-time photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo, a Type II supernova that exhibited a brief $100$-$150$ kiloday plateau phase. The spectra of this supernova were dominated by Balmer emission lines with semi-emergent Balmer jump throughout the plateau and decline phases. The spectra also displayed significant hydrogen and helium absorption during the plateau phase, and the absence of G-band features until day~35 post-explosion. We observed the absence of $H_\alpha$ nebular phase spectra characterized by [N~II], [O~II], and [O~III] until day~50. We developed two theoretical models to explain the duration of the plateau phase, and found them to be in agreement with the observed characteristics of SN~2020jfo. We also compared SN~2020jfo with another Type II supernova, SN~1970G, which had a similar luminosity but a significantly longer plateau phase. We found that SN~2020jfo more closely matches 1999gn, a Type II supernova with a similar but even shorter plateau phase, and demonstrated that the decline rates in the $V$-band for these three supernovae are consistent with each other. We also carried out spectral and photometric comparisons with seven other Type II supernovae that exhibited brief plateau phases, and discovered that SN~2020jfo is an typical member of this subgroup. We constructed a light curve template fit for SN~2020jfo, and determined its pre-explosion progenitor mass, zero-age main sequence mass, and metallicity. A novel X-ray lens design, known as the lobster-eye lens, offers effective coverage of large areas with a sparse layout of readout units. This design provides 2-3 orders of magnitude in area versus pixel area savings, making it suitable for applications requiring broad fields of view. We propose an idea to layer multiple lobster-eye lenses, with distinct focal lengths and orientations, to accommodate various objects of interest in a single field of view. This approach allows for simultaneous monitoring of a wide range of targets, including compact binary systems, supermassive black hole binaries, and extreme fast transient objects, across different fields of view. The design's simplicity and modularity make its units suitable for integration with existing X-ray telescopes via a optical proxy during fabrication, or as a full functional unit in a new X-ray telescope via 3D printing and a breadboarding approach. We outline a prototype consisting of four layers of lenses with different orientations and focal lengths for a 1-10 keV energy range, and discuss its potential for detection in a 1-10 m^2 effective collecting area with a few layers of lenses. We also present effective field of view, field of view for specific targets, effective collecting area, point spread function, and 90% enclosed energy in a 1-10 keV energy range for our prototype. We believe this concept has the potential to significantly enhance the monitoring capabilities of X-ray telescopes in the transition band between optical and X-ray systems. Deep learning techniques, specifically Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), offer a promising way to bypass simplifications of the cosmic web, such as Euler characteristic, and directly utilize the 'cosmic speed field' from simulations for enhanced halo mass function prediction. Our investigation employs a simple multi-input CNN, considering various cosmic speed field properties and their interaction with standard density-based features, to identify the most predictive aspects of the cosmic speed field for HMF. Through extensive analysis of two simulation datasets at different resolutions, our results show that the cosmic speed field is crucial for data efficiency, as combining it with density-based features that capture the filamentary structure yields superior performance when compared to models using just the density features. Furthermore, our findings indicate that even in the absence of explicit web information, the cosmic speed field is essential for models to generalize across different scales. When the two are combined, models demonstrate the ability to selectively utilize web-related information only when sufficient high-fidelity data is available. Our optimized model, capable of operating on a reduced set of density-based features, shows a comparable performance to state-of-the-art models that utilize Euler characteristic and double employ the cosmic speed field and density-based features for a substantial reduction in computational costs. Our findings have implications for accelerating cosmological simulations and resolving the web's influence on HMF and have been made with the assistance of publicly accessible code repositories. This research focuses on the semi-supervised application of Convolutive NMF, particularly within the context of music audio analysis. Initially, Convolutive NMF was introduced to harmonically segment audio signals in an independent component analysis framework. We explored and identified the capability of this method to harmonically dissect polyphonic audio in real-time environments. Furthermore, we discovered it to be adaptable for the automatic transcription of historical keyboard music from audio recordings with a limited analysis framework. This framework relies on pre-trained models for feature extraction and semi-supervised optimization using a limited dataset of annotated recordings. The proposed system was successfully tested on a diverse set of recordings from the RISM catalog, yielding promising results and demonstrating the potential of Convolutive NMF in this context. However, the method was found to be inconsistent in certain situations, emphasizing the need for further work to fully explore its capabilities and limitations. The associated challenges and potential solutions are also discussed. The developed system was found to be cost-effective and user-friendly, providing a viable alternative for the automatic transcription of historical keyboard music in comparison to existing methods. The associated code and documentation can be found at https://gitlab.inria.fr/laetitia-janowski/semi-supervised-cnmf. The method was evaluated against three baseline systems: (1) an independent implementation of Convolutive NMF, (2) a simplified version of this implementation with fixed harmonic depth, and (3) a state-of-the-art deep learning model. The evaluation showed the proposed system to achieve the best transcription accuracy in most cases, with an overall median error rate of 0.047, in contrast to 0.061 for the independent implementation, 0.065 for the simplified version, and 0.081 for the deep learning model. The highest error rate observed for the proposed system was 0.242, in contrast to 0.081 for the independent implementation, 0.095 for the simplified version, and 0.141 for the deep learning model. The associated evaluation metric considered only the transcribed notes within a 0.5 semitone distance from the ground truth. The proposed system was found to be less robust than the deep learning model, with a 0.029 difference in median error rates.
