This research focuses on enhancing the scalability of document processing frameworks that rely heavily on visual data and have been proven to be accurate in various applications. Although these frameworks excel in performance, they require significant amounts of labeled data for training, making them impractical for use with large datasets due to the excessive cost of data labeling. In response to this limitation, our approach develops a system that with minimal human guidance, at approximately 1/10th the cost, effectively labels a large dataset of documents for training purposes without compromising the model's performance. Our solution leverages a combination of semi-supervised learning, human-in-the-loop labeling, and system-led labeling to achieve this level of efficiency. Our experiments involving real-world data and diverse document types demonstrate that our system-led labeling approach, with some human oversight, reduces data-labeling expenses by tenfold without any compromise on model performance. Our system's code is available at https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/main/efficient_document_data. Datasets used in this research are available at https://drive.google.

The discovery of gravitational waves by LIGO and Virgo collaboration in 2015 opens up a new area of astronomy, allowing for the examination of high-gravity events like the merging of neutron stars and black holes. However, identifying the components of these events is a complex problem due to the richness of their signals and limited information available. Expert systems and machine learning algorithms have shown promise in assigning categories to events, but they are often constrained by their reliance on signal features that are manually selected. This study introduces a deep learning approach called the Category Identifier Network (CIN), which is trained directly on raw gravitational wave signals to predict their properties, such as mass and spin, and assigns them to predefined categories based on physical characteristics of compact objects. When tested on a diverse set of signals from binary black hole and neutron star mergers, the CIN demonstrated excellent performance in predicting mass, spin, and merger dynamics, as well as distinguishing between different types of events and identifying unique features of certain events. This innovative approach has the potential to enhance our understanding of these events and guide future observations with improved feature extraction, enabling it to prioritize specific types of events based on their predicted characteristics. This research was conducted in collaboration with the LIGO Scientific Collaboration and the Virgo Collaboration, and the code developed is openly available for further development and use by the gravitational wave community. Understanding the complex interplay between social factors and health requires text-based information that varies by region and needs to be extracted from diverse sources such as newspaper articles and health websites. To accomplish this, we've developed a token-based neural network to be region-specific and tailored to specific domains for the simultaneous task of identifying relevant sentences and extracting related information from those sentences. Our model includes a sentence representation component using a sentence-level classification with a tokenized mask representation and a text classification component using a tokenized mask representation. We've tested this model on a dataset derived from newspaper articles related to cancer and have achieved notable performance improvements compared to standard neural network baselines. To facilitate large-scale data extraction on a broad range of topics and regions, we've developed an open-source framework called NeuroMine that enables efficient, streamlined selection of feature tokens and efficient model training in multiple regions without the need for explicit feature engineering. This framework allows for the extraction of a wide range of topics and social factors from text data. To demonstrate the capabilities of this framework, we've conducted an in-depth analysis of the social factors of cancer from a regional and domain-specific perspective using 10 million journal articles and have made the derived feature models openly available for further cancer studies in various regions and domains at https://nlp.stanford.edu/software/token-bert-features/. This work represents an important step towards the large-scale extraction of social factors of health from text-based information that varies by region and domain. To build on this research, we invite other researchers to join us in further advancing the field of neuro-based feature extraction from neural language models. To facilitate this, we've issued a call to action to formulate a set of best practices for the development and evaluation of token-based neural network features that can be used to derive insights from text data in the presence of diverse topics, regions, and domains. This call to action includes a set of metrics and a sample dataset for the simultaneous task of identifying relevant sentences and extracting related information from those sentences. This work has been presented at the 2021 IEEE BHI conference and an updated version can be found at https://www.dropbox.com/s/6x6s5g0g0mfyf5m/20211115-BHI-Revision.pdf. This work has been supported in part by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) and the National Science Foundation (NSF). This research has been conducted in part by the Stanford NLP Group and the University of Virginia. This work has been performed in part by the authors at multiple research institutions

Our data showed that interactions among urban residents from different income levels displayed distinct variations in several key indicators, including daily encounter rates, encounter intensity, and encounter frequency. The formation of O-type protostars remains an area where model and observation collide, with recent research suggesting that these stars often emerge from the collapse of rotating low-density molecular clouds rather than the collapse of dense, non-rotating gas. One key aspect of O-type star formation that needs explanation is the presence of dense, star-forming filaments in their surrounding environment. Using a highly advanced computational model that incorporates the effects of gravity, magnetohydro dynamics, and the development of an optically thick gas, we simulated the development of massive protostars in a manner that accounts for the growth of their magnetic fields. Our simulations, covering a mass range from 1 to 60 M_sun, consistently showed that when the mass of the protostar exceeds 10 M_sun, a portion of the collapsing gas is diverted from direct accretion and instead collects in nearby regions under the influence of magnetic loops, eventually coalescing into distinct clumps. As the protostar continues to develop, these clumps become increasingly dense and break apart into smaller fragments that then merge with the main body of gas accreting onto the protostar. This process creates a continuous stream of dense, star-forming filaments that are then disrupted as they are stretched and compressed by the expanding gravitational influence of the developing protostar. Ultimately, fragments of these filaments then accumulate into distinct clumps that then merge with the main body of gas accreting onto the protostar, repeating the cycle that produces dense, star-forming filaments in the surroundings of massive protostars. This finding provides a plausible explanation for the presence of dense, star-forming filaments in the environments of massive protostars. It also suggests that massive protostars like O-type stars have a significant chance of being formed through the merger of low-mass fragments in a filament that then collapses under its own gravity, a process that is supported by recent research on the development of massive protostars that involved computational modeling and observations that went beyond traditional diagnostics. This new understanding of the development of massive protostars also raises the possibility that massive protostars that are born through the merger of low-mass fragments in a filament that then collapses under its own gravity could leave behind a massive black hole that has an extremely low mass-to-light ratio, a type of object that has been identified through recent research and is referred to as an overmassive narrow-line system. These equations can be seen as a variant of the Dysthe model, which is commonly used to study weakly nonlinear surface waves. We obtained an approximate solution for our problem by applying a Hamiltonian version of the Dysthe method, which is essentially a perturbation technique. We based our analysis on both theoretical and numerical aspects. Our research focuses on enhancing the navigation capabilities of an unmanned ground vehicle in outdoor environments with varying plant life by leveraging a combination of sensor technologies. We are using a sonar sensor, which provides crucial data for the vehicle's altitude control and terrain detection, and incorporating it into our Stratified Navigation Controller system. Implementing real-time sonar data processing will enable more precise terrain classification, leading to improved vehicle stability and preventing potential collisions. We have successfully integrated the sonar sensor with the controller system and conducted experiments to validate its performance. The proliferation of false news has become a critical issue in today's fast-paced, heavily interconnected news dissemination platforms. With the constant influx of news, individuals are finding it increasingly difficult to identify credible information, and as a result, there's a growing need for false news to be efficiently pinpointed. Presently, system-driven false news identification frameworks struggle to keep pace with the rapid publication of news, largely due to their excessive reliance on convolutional neural network architecture for picture and symbolic representation learning. To address this challenge, our proposed method leverages automated text condensation, allowing our model to balance the desire for complex feature extraction with the need for extensive language model training data. By reducing the degree of representation learning and condensing the training data, we successfully developed a false news identification system with improved efficiency and accuracy. Experimental results indicate that our proposed framework achieves superior performance when compared to traditional false news baseline models, demonstrating the effectiveness of automated text condensation in false news identification. Furthermore, our study reveals that employing condensation has the added advantage of enabling false news identification using only a limited amount of annotated training data, representing a significant breakthrough in this domain. Consequently, we believe that my method may also be applicable to other complex text classification tasks requiring substantial training data. Nonetheless, there remains scope for further improvement in our model's simplicity, reliability, and overall performance, especially when compared to cutting-edge transformer-based models. With these considerations in mind, we have made our model's code and configuration publicly available on GitHub at the address listed in the reference section. Despite the fact that false news pose a significant threat to the information ecosystem, little research has been conducted on our proposed framework or related methods incorporating automated text condensation in deep learning models. Consequently, there is a pressing need for further exploration of the condensation technique in neural network architectures, along with open issues and potential research directions outlined in the conclusion section. Furthermore, we have investigated the role of data quality in our model's performance, along with potential areas for query-based false news identification, along with an examination of the impact of the condensation hyperparameters on our model's results. Additionally, we have examined the application of our proposed framework to the detection of hate speech and have made our model's statistics and additional experimental results available in the supplementary materials section. This paper introduces an iterative algorithm for identifying rotationally symmetric principal components in 3D point clouds by minimizing the $\ell_1$-norm. The proposed method is linearly convergent and yields a direct solution, in contrast to non-convergent iterative methods commonly used in 3D computer vision. Our analysis shows that employing a specific starting point results in a unique solution at the next iteration, which shares the same symmetry as the point cloud. We further develop an efficient starting point that facilitates a significant reduction in the number of iterations. In experiments, our method achieves a similar performance to SVD on 2D datasets but exhibits a notable improvement in 3D datasets, particularly under occlusions and when modelled as spherical $\ell_1$-norm PCA. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhengyangwang/rotationally-symmetric-pca. To improve the performance of intelligent personal assistants in understanding user emotions, we propose a method that leverages pre-trained language models to systematically identify and annotate the underlying semantics of questions related to emotions. We employ BERT, a state-of-the-art neural network, to develop a tagging system that captures the essential information in each question. We collect and annotate a comprehensive dataset consisting of 36,421 questions categorized into 11 semantic groups. Our proposed system, built using BERT, significantly outperforms a baseline model and matches the performance of human annotators, with an overall F1 score of 65.32%. We demonstrate that our model's ability to recognize the underlying semantics of questions leads to a more accurate classification than traditional methods. Our dataset and BERT-supported tagging system provide a valuable resource for developing emotion-aware intelligent personal assistants. We anticipate that our method will contribute positively to the industry by facilitating the production of high-quality, semantically-tagged data at a substantial reduction in production costs (below $0.01 per sample). Our data and tagging system framework can be accessed at https://github.com/oppo-platform/emotion-semantic-tagging. With the rise of increasing amounts of user data, we anticipate that our method will contribute to the development of more sophisticated emotion-aware systems. Our model's performance has reached human-level standards, with potential applications extending beyond intelligent personal assistants, such as in the classification of user feedback and question-answer pairs. Our model has been integrated into the Alipay mobile assistant, one of the most widely-used mobile assistants in China, with a team of seven employees working on its emotion-aware system. Our method has allowed the company to process over one million samples per day. Our solution has addressed the industry's long-standing challenge of developing emotion-aware systems by solving two critical problems: the absence of a unified semantic tagging system and the limited scope of current datasets. Through a collaborative effort, researchers from multiple countries participated in the "Power Graphs and Polynomials" workshop, held in Slovenia in 2019. This special issue is a compilation of a diverse range of research topics related to power graphs, including new insights into existing areas such as matrix theory, order theory, and politics, among others. One notable area explored is the relationship between groups and graphs, specifically focusing on complete order groups and its associated game graphs, from a theoretical and computational perspective. Additionally, this study extends the concept of power graphs to a theoretical framework known as "power games" and explores some of its inherent properties. Some "power games" properties are universally applicable as they align with general graph principles, whereas others are distinct to specific graph types, such as complete order groups, whose game graphs are isomorphic to the original group for certain abelian groups, such as Z_n, Sn, and Zn×m.zn, although this is not the case for non-abelian groups like A_n and S3. Furthermore, this study delves into "power games" through a computational perspective, utilizing software designed to analyze and verify "power games" properties for different groups and graph types. A subclass of magnetic binaries known as Polars relies on cyclotron radiation to shine.  Research indicates that about half of all Polars within the Milky Way remain undiscovered.  Recent studies utilizing X-rays to identify additional low-mass binaries were the basis for discovering three new Polars and one more is announced here from X-ray data with high energy resolution.  This new discovery, known as HU Comae Gabrieli, exhibits hard X-ray spectra and irregular light curve patterns, and is found to be an asynchronous binary with an unusual 0.68-d syncronization period and an X-ray "toughness" ratio significantly greater than average, suggesting a link between synchronous and non-synchronous binaries and their respective X-ray hardness ratios.  Future research opportunities with X-ray telescopes are also outlined to discover more of these low-mass binaries.  A chart of X-ray hardness ratios against synchronization periods for all low-mass binary Polars is provided, including notes on the detection methods used for each system.  A theoretical magnetic field strength is also calculated for each binary using two methods, both of which are found to be generally consistent with previous measurements, and are made available in a compiled database of all low-mass binary Polars.  Two of these systems are also for the first time reported as asynchronous, along with an X-ray "toughness" ratio for each, and are found to exhibit a similar ratio to HU Comae Gabrieli, and are all included in a revised diagram with all discovered low-mass binary Polars, along with an updated analysis of their spectral types, masses, radii, and other key properties.  A revised diagram of all discovered low-mass binary Polars is provided in a format suitable for viewing with an e-book reader, along with all data used to create it in a compiled database format suitable for viewing with a spreadsheet program.  A new method for predicting the discovery probability of these systems based on their X-ray colors and light curve patterns is also introduced and tested, and is found to be highly accurate, and is used to identify several more candidates, including one more discovered Polar, and is outlined as a potential tool for new research opportunities with X-ray telescopes.  A new term "X-ray toughness" is also introduced and defined, and is proposed along with two new sub-classes of low-mass binaries, along with a revised definition for synchronous and non-synchronous systems, and are all included in a compiled database of all low-mass binary Polars

This paper focuses on the development of a novel strategy that integrates the Reduced Basis method with both localized and non-localized techniques for the time-dependent Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) problems, characterized by a dynamic membrane and an unsteady fluid. The purpose of this approach is to create a multi-scale solution method that leverages the general and the localized reduced order models, both being derived from the same isogeometric boundary variational formulation. A localized technique, such as a boundary layer approach, can generate a localized fine mesh in specific regions with significant impacts on both the fluid and structure behaviors. A unified and a segmented reduced basis approach were developed and tested on two sample problems: an aeroelastic beam with a narrow boundary layer region and a beam subject to shear flow with membrane flutter. The results from these experiments demonstrate the ability of a unified approach to deliver general and a segmented approach to deliver localized dimensional-reduced solutions for both the structure and fluid components. All of the developed solutions were generated using the same solution techniques, including a segregated implicit method, and a hybrid dimensional-reduced form for both the fluid and structure components. The results from these experiments were in good agreement with those obtained from a fully modal approach and an enriched POD approach. The results also indicate that both the unified and a segmented approach have the potential to deliver significant reductions in both the number of degrees of freedom and the computational cost for solving time-dependent FSI problems. For agents to effectively navigate through unfamiliar areas with obstacles, it's crucial for them to maintain a clear understanding of the surroundings and their position within. Current localization techniques rely on line-based representations of spaces, which can become confusing for the agent if it encounters a significant turn or a complex intersection. To address this issue, we propose HiTMap, a novel topological map based on a hierarchical structure, comprising interconnected areas divided by natural boundaries. Each section receives a unique identifier and a simplified description of the surroundings, enabling the agent to compare and navigate between areas. Building upon this robust map, we develop an algorithm to update the hierarchy as the agent moves, allowing it to accurately pinpoint its location within the environment. Through extensive simulations, our HiTMap system demonstrates its capacity to facilitate efficient and precise navigation in complex, uncharted spaces with obstacles, outperforming line-based map navigation in the agent's understanding and localization in all scenarios. System details are shared in the paper, along with a thorough comparison of its performance against a line-based map navigation system, along with key code is made available online. Furthermore, the paper introduces a novel evaluation metric called HiTMap score, designed to assess the agent's understanding of its environment and its position within it, and this metric is used to analyze the results from the simulations. The paper also explores the effect of various obstacle placements within the environment on the agent's understanding and localization, and it identifies several interesting insights from the data, along with all the simulation data that is available online. Building upon the line-based representations of spaces, we believe that our proposed HiTMap system offers a more suitable map structure for line-based localisation systems, and this structure is highly adaptable to various line-based localization algorithms, and this is further confirmed by the good navigation performance observed in all scenarios and environments used in the experiments. Type theory's combination process is notoriously challenging, largely because it necessitates the incorporation of a well-behaved normalization technique. Our research proposes an innovative normalization approach, called robust normalization, which is inherently agnostic to syntax and instead operates on types as topological spaces. This framework is particularly well-suited for the Calculus of Constructions, allowing us to seamlessly integrate it with existing proofs and computational content while maintaining normalization's reliability. Our key innovation is the identification of a specific topological space, referred to as the "generic universe," which serves as a universal carrier for all types and serves as the primary arena in which normalization takes place. Within this framework, every computable type is homeomorphic to a subspace of the generic universe, thereby providing a systematic path to achieving normalization for an infinite number of types through the application of topological principles rather than syntactic rules. Our research also introduces an innovative type constructor, referred to as robust dependent sum, which upholds integrity and normalizability while offering a level of expressiveness comparable to that of the Calculus of Constructions. Our research's soundness and efficiency are demonstrated through a configuration-recursive implementation of closure for the generic universe, along with the inclusion of an executable specification of robust dependent sum's constructor in Coq. Our research's findings are presented in an informal setting utilizing an abstract model of typing, coupled with diagrams to illustrate key concepts like types, subtypes, and normalization. Our research's core results, including robust normalization and closure, are made available through an open-source repository along with an accompanying non-technical overview available at https://norm-coc.github.io/. We encourage academics to utilize simple, educational representations to explain complex ideas from topological quantum phenomena. Through interactive simulations, we explore the one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, making its underlying physics accessible to everyone from beginners to advanced professionals. By leveraging Dirac notation and matrix calculus, we break down the model's fundamental aspects, including wavefunction purification, Hamiltonian transformation, and gap engineering. We derived a precise two-loop correlation function for two graviton excitations in AdS_5, resulting from the interaction of two gluon operators in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory at strong coupling, laminarized in a null direction. Building upon the AdS/CFT correspondence, this yields a generalized holographic function for two graviton modes in AdS_5 and its mirror in S^5, also determined at the two-loop level for certain configurations in a null direction. This new finding extends the scope of our prior work with C. Kristof, where we found a one-loop correlation function, now expanded to the two-loop level in that specific direction. With this improvement, the AdS/QFT correspondence allows us to define two-loop cross sections for two gluon scattering in QCD and N=4 super Yang-Mills theory in 1+1 dimensions, providing a bridge between the AdS_5$\times$S^5 supergravity approach and the QFT method of C. d'Addin et al. and S. d'Addin et al., who derived one-loop QCD cross sections from this data. However, due to the presence of an infrared divergence at certain energies, the two-loop QCD cross section cannot be directly obtained from supergravity in AdS_5$\times$S^5. Building upon our findings, we derived two-loop correction factors for the on-shell positivity constraints of certain scattering amplitudes in QCD and N=4 super Yang-Mills theory in 3+1 dimensions, using the general two-loop AdS/QFT correlation function in its laminarized form. This new understanding extends the scope of our prior work with J. Hennig and C. d'Addin, where we identified one-loop positivity constraints in a specific direction, now generalized to the two-loop level in all directions. Due to the influence of all positive directions, the two-loop constraints cannot be replicated by the QFT method of S. d'Addin et al., resulting in constraints that are more stringent than those of the QFT approach, leading to potential applications for the study of scattering amplitudes in QCD and N=4 super Yang-Mills theory in 3+1 dimensions. We introduce DynaSOAr, a concurrent memory allocator designed for object-based programming on GPUs. This memory allocator achieves optimal memory access by utilizing coalescing memory transactions that align with GPU memory architecture requirements. DynaSOAr enables the creation of various data structures like linked lists, stacks, and trees, facilitating object-based programming on GPUs. Its high-performance capabilities are exemplified through benchmarking of a K-means clustering application, showcasing speedups of up to 5 times over naive serial memory access and 2 times over an existing GPU memory allocator when running on a NVIDIA A100 GPU. Furthermore, DynaSOAr supports the development of parallel applications, as evidenced by a reduction in memory allocation overhead of at least 5 times over an existing GPU memory allocator in an image processing application. This, in turn, enables the creation of larger data structures and facilitates the development of practical, parallel object-based programs on GPUs. DynaSOAr is an open-source project, and its source code is available on GitHub under the MIT License. This research is an extension of our earlier work presented at ASPLOS 2020, DynSOAr: A Concurrent Memory Allocator for Object-based Programming on GPUs, published in the ACM SIGPLAN Conference on Programming Language Design and Implementation (PLDI). This paper provides a more in-depth analysis of DynaSOAr's design, its evaluation, and its extension over DynSOAr. Additionally, this research is an outcome of collaborative research between the University of California, Irvine and the University of Texas at San Antonio. Our proposal, FourierMask, aims to integrate Fourier analysis with implicit neural networks to tackle instance segmentation. FourierMask employs an implicit representation for both object masks and bounding box predictions, which are then linked through a shared implicit function that considers point coordinates and relative frequencies. To train this system, FourierMask uses a Fourier extension of mask IoU loss to optimize the implicit mask representation, leveraging the properties of Fourier transforms to significantly reduce the required sample points by approximately 5 times, compared to the original Fourier IoU loss. Moreover, FourierMask introduces a novel implicit bounding box regression framework that considers frequency information, enabling the use of frequency-aware IoU loss and leading to improved precision in box predictions. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on the MS COCO dataset for instance segmentation, achieving a 52.7% AP with FourierMask (mask-only), surpassing previous work utilizing Fourier transforms and implicit architectures, and a 55.1% AP with FourierMask (complete), setting a new standard for the field. The project is open-sourced at https://github.com/leopeng88/FourierMask. Leveraging frequency domain knowledge in implicit networks paves the way for more innovative applications and we anticipate FourierMask to inspire further breakthroughs in deep learning for segmentation and beyond. Although implicit networks offer numerous benefits, their primary limitation lies in the difficulty of optimizing their absolute positions due to the absence of absolute reference points. Our solution to this challenge is to introduce a novel implicit bounding box regression framework that considers frequency information, expanding the scope of instance segmentation beyond mask-only IoU loss. Building upon this success, we anticipate future work to further explore the interplay between frequency domains and deep learning architectures, with potential applications extending to source code repositories and citation networks available at https://github.com/leopeng88/FourierMask-Extensions, prompting a call for researchers to contribute novel frequency-aware implicit network architectures. This research investigates the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon or nitrogen atoms substituted into the (O$_{2}$ x C/N) rutile TiO$_{3}$S$_{1-x}$ framework. By employing spin-polarized density functional theory with a hybrid DFT method, we examined how the elemental substitution at various sites within TiO$_{2}$ influences the arrangement of electrons and magnetism. The results show that infusing a p-electron in a substitutive or interstitial position significantly impacts the local spin arrangement and can lead to localized or delocalized magnetic properties. When the p-electron is shared among Ti and O ions, we observed localized spin with various orientations, while an unshared p-electron results in delocalized spin with a net spin of one, comparable to a free electron. This property makes TiO$_{3}$S$_{1-x}$ suitable for developing stable and soluble TiO$_{2}$-based spintronics and catalytic materials. Furthermore, these findings suggest that modifying the TiO$_{2}$ lattice with carbon or nitrogen can facilitate magnetic properties without the need for oxidation extension, providing a more stable and robust alternative to conventional magnetic materials. Additionally, we discovered that these materials exhibit unique optical and magnetic properties that can be modulated by varying the location of the infused p-electron within the lattice. This knowledge can be utilized to design and optimize the magnetic and optical characteristics of TiO$_{2}$-based materials through controlled infusion of carbon or nitrogen at different sites within the lattice. Experimental verification of these theoretical predictions is also presented, involving X-ray photoelectron and absorption spectroscopy, EPR, and SQUID magnetometry, which support our computational findings. A notable outcome of this research is the synthesis of a 2.5-nm TiO$_{2}$ nanocrystal doped with a single nitrogen atom, which exhibits unique optical and magnetic properties, demonstrating the ability to replicate the complex electronic arrangement and magnetism of small molecules within the confined space of a nanocrystal. This achievement opens up possibilities for further exploration of the unique chemical and physical properties of nanomaterials in confined spaces. A new concept of proximal doping is also introduced, which allows for the controlled infusion of a p-electron into a small molecule within a nanocrystal by utilizing an excess of an electron in a nearby molecule. We employed eye-tracking technology to gather data on how viewers respond to videos featuring patients with Bell's Palsy. Our analysis indicates that, unlike standard metrics such as viewing duration and click-through rates, eye movement patterns provide a more accurate and reliable indicator of the condition. Our findings suggest that patients with Bell's Palsy are easily distinguishable from healthy individuals simply by analyzing eye movement patterns in video clips. We discovered that certain features in eye movement patterns correlate with Bell's Palsy and can serve as a benchmark for medical professionals to assess the severity of the condition through eye-tracking technology in a non-invasive manner. Our eye-based methodology achieved a 91% accuracy rate in identifying Bell's Palsy and a 95% accuracy rate in quantifying the condition's severity in a dataset comprising 5,000 5-second video clips. Our eye-tracking system demonstrated exceptional efficiency, real-time processing, and minimal reliance on eye-tracking data, making it an exceptionally robust solution. We are confident that our eye-tracking method provides a groundbreaking solution for diagnosing and assessing Bell's Palsy and has vast potential for diagnosing other facial paralysis conditions with similar symptoms. Our research validates the effectiveness of eye-tracking technology in a real-world setting and paves the way for further exploration of its applications in medical diagnosis and assessment through eye movement patterns in response to visual stimuli. We are excited to share our findings with the medical community and eye-tracking experts and are willing to collaborate and provide access to our dataset in full compliance with data protection regulations. Furthermore, quantum simulations with qutrits allow for the reproduction of scalar QED sound data, enabling mass calculations even when sound modes are entangled. Calculations considering the system's temperature reveal that using qutrits enhances the fidelity of quantum simulations at higher temperatures and aids in mass calculation when the system is in thermal equilibrium. Notably, the benefits of employing qutrits are most pronounced in regions of the mass spectrum that cannot be reached with qubits. To study Bremsstrahlung radiation from the interaction of positrons with a highly polarized electron cloud, as expected in future linear colliders operating in the QED regime, researchers propose a novel positron source utilizing a laser-irradiated thin foil target. The proposed setup, consisting of a macropulse positron source combined with a cathode modulated by an intense laser, produces a thin, highly polarized positron beam. Calculations indicate that approximately 10% of the positron yield, approximately 10^9 per second at a polarizaton of 10^-4, are highly polarized, with an estimated 10^-7 radiation polarization. To achieve this, a simulation of the interaction between an ultrapolarized electron cloud and Bremsstrahlung positrons was performed, resulting in a source with a large polarization potential. It was found that increasing the intensity of the laser or the number of macro pulses would significantly enhance the positron yield while maintaining a high polarization ratio. To produce such a source, consideration must be given to the interaction between the positrons and the electron cloud in the final focusing magnet, which could impact the final polarization of the positron beam. Systematic studies of the proposed source are being conducted with a full-scale simulation of the Breit-Wigner distribution that characterizes the distribution of Bremsstrahlung photons, taking into account their energy, polarization, and production probability. Long-lasting stability of poloidal magnetic fields in stars is assumed under the premise that they maintain their initial symmetry. However, in reality, any magnetic field within a star will inevitably become non-symmetric over time due to various dynamic processes. This study focuses on conducting a comprehensive and in-depth analysis of the long-term stability of stars featuring non-symmetric, axisymmetric magnetic fields. Such fields consist of two primary components: a stable, symmetric (poloidal) component and an unstable, asymmetric (toroidal) component, generated by nonlinear force balance in the star's interior. The interaction between these components is governed by a linear hydrodynamic stability approach, where non-symmetric perturbations are applied to an ideal hydrodynamic stability framework in stars. This research specifically explores the stability of each magnetic field component in various stellar environments, including in rotating solar-type stars, in addition to pre-main sequence and magnetically active low-mass stars. The findings indicate that the unstable, non-symmetric component of a star's magnetic field is generally more susceptible to instability than the stable, symmetric component, with local growth rates reaching up to 10-100 times greater in certain regions of magnetically active low-mass stars. The discovery of unstable modes in stars featuring non-symmetric magnetic fields raises new concerns and implies that such fields will inevitably undergo changes over time, ultimately leading to magnetic rearrangement and possible ejection of magnetic flux, with potential implications for magnetic field evolution in stars and in galaxies. This thesis also proposes a theoretical framework for predicting unstable modes in magnetic stars based on their global magnetic properties and structure, paving the way for more detailed, numerical simulations of magnetic field evolution in stars. This research is a fundamental step towards a greater understanding of magnetic field stability in the dynamic environments that exist within stars, and as such, it has significant implications for the broader field of astrophysics. Furthermore, this study highlights the importance of exploring magnetic stability in stars across a broad mass range, from low-mass stars to massive O-type stars, as well as in other complex magnetic objects, such as white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes, in order to gain a deeper understanding of magnetic field evolution and stability in the universe. Additionally, this study suggests potential applications for the development of early warning systems for magnetic instability in stars, such as supernovae and magnetar births, which could provide valuable insights for astronomers in identifying these phenomena, as well as contributing to a better comprehension of the relationships between magnetic fields, rotation, and stellar evolution. To address this need, our proposal presents Pied Piper, a cutting-edge meta search engine tailored to the world of music. It achieves this by aggregating the results from three key components: a vast database of song features, a robust database of music metadata, and a powerful API for searching through vast collections of audio spectra. To illustrate the effectiveness of Pied Piper, we present two novel experiments showcasing its capabilities. Firstly, we design a demonstration of a cutting-edge music recommendation system built using Pied Piper, which demonstrates its superiority over rival methods. Secondly, we develop an innovative algorithm to classify music genres through a collaborative approach between the search engine and machine learning experts, resulting in remarkable improvements in both efficiency and accuracy. Consequently, our findings provide a compelling case for Pied Piper to become the go-to standard for music search engines, with potential applications in various areas such as audio analysis, genre classification, and composition, thereby propelling the field forward. To create this connection, we utilize the relationship between stacks and certain geometric structures as described by a theoretical framework developed by Prellberg and Rivasseau. Furthermore, we derive a link between the local properties of certain abelian varieties and the geometric objects on specific Deligne-Mumford stacks, particularly those associated with 2-dimensional Fano varieties. Our findings also reveal a link between the configurations in the broader context of differential geometry and the study of modular forms in number theory. To establish this connection, we use the relationship between the Betti numbers of certain singular complexes and the values of modular forms, along with an open problem regarding the representations of Lie groupoids and smooth stacks as geometric objects on non-compact spaces. Our findings resolve a previously known result and provide a correction to it. We present an analysis of the infrared continuum within the dark nebula Dragon using the SHARPs method to analyze textures, and find that a central region exhibiting emission at 8 $\mu$m, likely indicative of embedded young stars, is surrounded by a larger area emitting at 24 $\mu$m, suggesting the presence of a molecular core. SHARPs analysis of this core at 24 $\mu$m, here referred to as SHARPs-24, shows a non-axisymmetric morphology, with enhanced emission along its minor axis, at a level greater than twice the noise, and is consistent with a model featuring a dense infrared-bright filamentary structure, likely a precursor to massive star formation. A proposed equilibrium density within this filament, when applied to a 2D map, suggests a peak density of approximately 10^4 $cms^{-3}$. SHARPs-24 extracts previously obscured information regarding the structure and composition of this core, and its non-axisymmetric shape may be the result of gravitational forces, contributing to its potential for massive star formation. Optical depth estimates derived from SHARPs at 8 $\mu$m and 24 $\mu$m, indicate a core that is only partially transparent at 8 $\mu$m, and support the presence of a dense infrared-bright filamentary structure, while also suggesting that the dust temperature within this region is around 20K. A comparison of optical depth estimates to a model of density, reveals a positive correlation, and a core radius based on this model, along with the density within the filament, suggests a dimension for this structure, potentially a precursor to massive star formation, here referred to as the "Dragon Core". A proposed mass for this core, when applied to a 2D map, suggests a peak mass of approximately 340 $M_\odot$. A comparison of this map to models of molecular cores, using the "Core-Column Density Diagram", reveals that the "Dragon Core" is in an advanced stage of evolution, likely on the path to massive star formation, and is in a state of gravitational collapse, with optical depth and density both playing a crucial role in this process. We investigate the combination of Godel's axioms with normal modal logics, considering their applications to complex systems like cyber physical systems. Due to the coexistence of discrete and continuous elements in such systems, reasoning about their behavior requires a blend of digital and metric reasoning. We explore how adding modal operators enhances the ability to reason about the relationships within these systems' variables, potentially leading to higher levels of complexity in available reasoning tools. As a result, we examine various extensions of Godel's algebras and structures, incorporating Godel's algebras with modal operators defined through relations within a last model approach, as proposed by Humberstone. Specifically, we explore four such extensions: (1) defined using a natural interpretation method, (2) based on prioritized operators, (3) with preemption, and (4) with fragile propositions. For each of these extensions, we assess its theoretical properties and demonstrate its practical utility through a case study involving the scheduling of tasks for a continuous cyber physical process. Further research opportunities within this field are also discussed. Finally, a survey with nine experts on the topic has yielded valuable feedback and guidance. This work is being presented in its current form at the IJCA special sessions on many-valued and fuzzy logic at CAEPIA 2023. Additionally, a link to the associated technical report is provided. To achieve effective control over cyber physical systems, we propose the use of a combination of their physical properties and control laws, doing so in a manner that accounts for H. F. Weber's and E. V. Martin's laws of physics. This control method, utilizing a continuous variable for the system's state and a Boolean variable to indicate if the system is in an equilibrium state, enables the derivation of preconditions for both continuous and discrete changes in the system's state. By incorporating modal operators into this framework, we can express and prove theorems related to the system's behavior over time, including those related to the occurrence of events and the satisfaction of formulas at different time points. This approach is shown to be representable using a modal Godel algebra with a cyclic relation, an interpretation method, prioritized operators, preemption, and fragile propositions. Within this framework, we can apply and extend existing results from modal logic, such as those regarding the existence of maximal consistent sets or the application of the fundamental theorem of algebra, by adapting them to the properties of a cyclic relation. LiDAR technology, considered a safety standard in vehicle systems, relies on 3D point clouds to operate, and their underlying infrastructure is primarily built using 2D map data from companies like Ouster, Velodyne, and Luminar. These point clouds are generated to estimate mileage, detect obstacles and map areas, and are critical for advanced safety features in vehicles. In this work, we introduce a well-explained evaluation framework that assesses the capabilities of machine learning models in interpreting LiDAR point clouds, with a focus on producing reliable predictions on real-world datasets. Our results show that despite significant progress in other computer vision domains, the current state-of-the-art models are only modestly better than simple baselines at interpreting LiDAR data, and that there are several key challenges and potential improvements in this domain. We have created an open-source repository containing all the data, experiments, and results discussed in this study, and it is available for exploration by the broader community. In particular, we believe our results indicate that further research is needed to fully leverage the capabilities of LiDAR technology, and we are eager to collaborate with other researchers in this area. With the continuous growth in available computing power and the development of more sophisticated machine learning models, it is now feasible to explore more complex systems that are capable of interpreting LiDAR point clouds in a more human-like manner. In contrast to other computer vision domains, such as image classification and segmentation, relatively little research has been conducted on understanding LiDAR point clouds, despite their critical role in ensuring the safety of vehicle systems. The discovery of high-energy cosmic neutrinos in 2013 marked a historical turning point, opening up a path to investigate extreme astrophysical phenomena using multi-messenger approaches. By combining neutrino data with ultra-high-energy cosmic particles, namely cosmic rays above 100 billion electron volts, we performed a comprehensive statistical analysis to identify associations between these two types of high-energy phenomena. Our research revealed four potential connections between neutrinos and ultra-high-energy cosmic rays, with only one association holding up under strict criteria. Although only one strong link was found, the rate of observed connections exceeded theoretical predictions by more than five times, indicating a significant probability density of $34.9\%$ that they arise from random occurrences. These findings provide initial clues for understanding the sources of ultra-high-energy cosmic particles and neutrinos, and will serve as a foundation for future research with expanded data sets. These values will be used to make predictions for the detection of optical and radio counterparts in associated events. A liquid foam's resistance to flow is determined by two opposing forces: the pressure required to move grains of foam and the pressure needed to deform its surface. Researchers have extensively studied the former but the latter has remained under-explored. This study focuses on the latter by measuring the viscosity of pure surface films under various levels of tension. It shows that a film with low surface tension behaves like a viscous liquid even if it is pinched off from the rest of the foam. Researchers have long been fascinated by the intricate patterns that emerge from viscous fluids undergoing sudden changes of state, as seen in Rayleigh--B\'enard and Hele--Shaw cell experiments. In a new study, a novel type of pattern known as a quasi-periodic 'fingerprint' pattern is discovered in a rotating Hele--Shaw cell containing two immiscible fluids with significantly different viscosities. This distinctive pattern forms when an inner, less viscous drop is placed within the outer layer and subjected to an oscillating boundary. As the outer layer is made increasingly thin, the fingerprint pattern transforms into a series of curved waves and eventually a circular wave pattern. These discoveries are confirmed by numerical simulations and are found to align with a proposed theory that explains fingerprint patterns as a combination of circular waves and aspherical bubbles. When the outer layer is thin enough, the pressure differences between the two fluids become equalized, resulting in patterns of circular waves. In response to an oscillating boundary, an inward flow occurs within the outer layer, giving rise to curved wave patterns. This inward flow is caused by the conservation of mass within the Hele--Shaw cell, as the outer layer's thinness restricts its ability to expand laterally. In an attempt to break free from these constraints, the drop then deforms into an aspherical shape, as the pressure exerted by the less viscous fluid at its center drives its own flow. As a result of these interactions, an instability develops within the drop's boundary, ultimately contributing to the development of the fingerprint pattern. This complex interplay of forces and fluid dynamics gives rise to unique patterns that hold the potential for applications in fields such as medicine, where the dispersal of oils within biological fluids can be better understood through the study of these patterns. In addition, the discovery of these patterns may also contribute to the development of novel sensing technologies, as they exhibit a unique property of responding to changes in the boundary conditions of a given medium. Furthermore, the unique characteristics of these patterns could also enable them to function as markers that indicate changes in the boundary conditions of a given medium, as they exhibit a distinct feature that differentiates them from other patterns that form in similar experimental conditions. We have performed a thorough examination of the 13C and 14N hyperfine structure in ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H4CCH) and cyano cyclopentadiene (C5H4CN) emissions from TMC-1. Ethynyl cyclopentadiene emissions reveal double peak structure for both the K.F=0 and K.F=1b transitions, allowing us to conclude these are the rotations of two isomers of ethynyl cyclopentadiene. Our modelling indicates that the major isomer is cyano cyclopentadiene, while the more rare isomer has a relative abundance of approximately 0.07. Cyano cyclopentadiene emissions, however, only show a single peak for both the K.F=0 and K.F=1b transitions, indicating that this form dominates under observational conditions. We estimate the column density of ethynyl cyclopentadiene to be 1.0±0.2*10^12 cm^-2 for both the majority and minority isomers, while cyano cyclopentadiene has a column density of 1.3±0.2*10^12 cm^-2. The gas temperatures in both cases are around 7 K, while the molecular abundances are in line with previous observations of TMC-1, at an overall chemical age that is considered moderate to high. Our modelling of ethynyl cyclopentadiene emissions also provides the first direct evidence for the presence of two cyclopentadiene variants, CCH and CN, which are both likely to be ring forms. We estimate their relative abundances to be around 0.07 for the minority isomer and 1 for the majority isomer. We propose the nomenclature C5H4CCH-I and C5H4CCH-II for the two isomers of ethynyl cyclopentadiene, and that further observations are required to determine the structure of these molecules. We also suggest that future studies in more evolved star forming regions may provide further insight into the formation pathways of these molecules. Our modelling of these emissions also provides the rotational constants for both K.F=0 and K.F=1b transitions in the ground vibrational state, as well as the hyperfine structure constants for 13C and 14N, allowing us to set new lower limits on the zero-point vibrational energy correction in both cases. The software engineering methodology known as Feature-Driven Development (FDD) achieves versatility through a feature framework that facilitates communication among development team members. A group of researchers adapted this approach for their own use, in the process of jointly working on a set of grid computing projects. As a result of this collaboration, a unified grid computing framework was established, providing a framework for problem-solving that could be applied across various domains. Ultimately, this grid computing framework was successfully applied to resolve an emergency medical services (EMS) routing problem, a complex issue that had been previously unaddressed. In contrast to FDD's original purpose, this project shows that a translational method can be an effective way to develop a new technology, allowing problems in application domains to influence the design of the underlying technology. This experience was then used to develop a new technology for supporting the collaborative problem-solving approach, a grid-based virtual design team environment. This new technology, in turn, was successfully applied to solve another EMS routing problem, further demonstrating the value of this approach. In conclusion, this project demonstrates the potential for a translational method to be an effective way to develop a new technology in the computer science field, and this approach should be considered by other researchers in this field. Given the pivotal role that curiosity plays in the learning process, as well as its intricate nature, it is essential to develop precise methods for measuring curiosity dynamics in social contexts. Our novel multimodal framework, designed for the qualitative assessment of curiosity within small group learning settings, addresses this challenge by using a wealth of data, including behavioral, interaction, and self-reported measures from students. By combining these diverse data sources, our method extracts an abundance of intricate features that capture various aspects of curiosity from multiple viewpoints. These features, along with the learning material's features and contextual information, are then integrated into an array of learning scenario features. Our method allows for a thorough, in-depth evaluation of curiosity dynamics in learning scenarios through the use of multiclass support vector machines. By exploring the intricate relationships between curiosity, learning outcomes, and other performance indicators, such as performance and self-efficacy, in learning scenarios of varying levels of curiosity, our method has demonstrated the capacity to generate a wide range of data-driven insights that can inform the design of more engaging and effective learning environments. Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for predicting data on a given domain by employing a specified kernel function to capture the underlying patterns. While common kernel choices provide insight into various data characteristics, their applicability is limited to a few notable features of certain domains. In contrast, Mat\'ern Gaussian functions offer a more general and systematic approach to analyzing and predicting data on any given graph by combining exponential and power terms with a clear and interpretable structure. This paper introduces a novel kernel derived from Mat\'ern Gaussian functions, demonstrating its applicability and effectiveness in predicting data on graphs through a case study involving the estimation of subdifferential sets. Additionally, this paper presents a new antitruncation operator, which facilitates the solution of linear equations with prescribed restrictions on a defined domain. This operator, in turn, enables the extension of Gaussian processes to cover data with a complex structure, thereby enhancing the predictive capabilities of Gaussian processes in various contexts. This research is further illustrated by examples in statistics, mechanics, and image processing, showcasing the broad implications of the antitruncation operator for Gaussian processes. This paper is an extended version of a previous paper presented at the 12th International Conference on Gaussian Processes in Machine Learning. In this expanded version, an alternative derivation of the Mat\'ern Gaussian graph kernel is provided, along with additional experimental comparisons and a more detailed discussion of future research directions. This is particularly demonstrated through additional experiments in signal processing, in addition to the existing examples in statistics, mechanics, and image processing. In this expanded version, an additional section on a related operator and a section on the downloadable software code and model parameters used in this research have also been included. This code is currently available on GitHub under the MIT license. We propose an algorithm to identify the center of a metropolitan area within a city by utilizing the mobility patterns of a group of riders in the area. The algorithm's performance is tested using real-world ride-sharing data from several major cities, and it shows that it can accurately pinpoint the city's core by analyzing the movement of just a few hundred riders. Furthermore, it is observed that increasing the number of riders provides only a minimal increase in precision. To validate our approach, we gather independent data, including GPS tracking and online search data, to measure the effectiveness of our identified central areas in representing the entire city. The algorithm's effectiveness is found to be largely dependent on the availability of high-quality road network data rather than the number of riders used. In addition, we explore various sensing strategies for optimizing the detection of a city's core by selecting the optimal group of riders with the highest detection probability. Utilizing real-world ride-sharing data from several major cities, we develop an algorithm to predict the distribution of riders within the city, and we determine the optimal subset of riders that maximizes the algorithm's accuracy. The proposed algorithm and our experimental results reveal valuable insights for designing and executing urban mobility data collection campaigns. In contrast to traditional methods that focus on gathering data from network centers, we show that a significant proportion of ride-sharing data originates from the city's periphery, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of an unbiased approach that prioritizes data collection in proportion to the density of road networks. Ultimately, our results indicate that approximately 20-30% of ride-sharing data is generated within 2-3 kilometers from the city's core, and we provide a quantitative analysis of the relationship between this data distribution and various urban planning indicators, including population density and network centrality. Furthermore, we investigate the feasibility of detecting a city's core using high-resolution GPS tracking data from a single vehicle over an extended period. Our results show that this approach is viable and can achieve comparable performance to that of ride-sharing data, but with some differences in data distribution. Building on these findings, we examine the potential of using a single vehicle to collect urban mobility data in an optimal manner. Our proposed algorithm determines the optimal route for the vehicle to follow in order to accurately detect the city's core, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach using real-world ride-sharing data from several major cities. Ultimately, our results indicate that there are distinct patterns in the distribution of urban mobility data, and we investigate the feasibility of using these patterns to design an optimal data collection campaign using a single vehicle. We've analyzed several efficient field theories that explain neutrino and dark energy using recent J/ψ decay data from the BESIII collaboration, which shows a significantly lower muon plus photon pair count than expected. This discrepancy, occurring at energies above 2.4 GeV, significantly reduces the number of events by a factor of about 10 at 6.5 GeV. To determine the consequences of these new data for the field theories, we re-examined three prominent theories: Neutrino-Dark-Sector-Eflect (NDSE), Dark-Radiation Model (DRM), Neutrino-Extremely-Sensitive-Dark-Sector (NESDS), and Neutrino-Dark-Sector-Strongly-Coupled (NDSSC). To establish an upper bound on the number of invisible particles in J/ψ decays, we used DRMC and DRM methods, resulting in a 95% confidence level for the number of invisible particles at approximately 5.6·10^6, a value substantially higher than the combination of all other contributing processes. This analysis indicates that in the energy range above 2.4 GeV, the number of invisible particles in J/ψ decays significantly exceeds the predicted count for all other processes, accounting for about 90% of the observed deficit. Furthermore, this analysis indicates that the invisible neutrino and dark energy systems in the six considered theories fail to efficiently describe the J/ψ decay data, with the exception of NDSE and DRM in the energy range above 2.4 GeV. These two theories demonstrate compatibility with the BESIII J/ψ decay data at a 95% confidence level, resulting in an upper bound for the number of invisible particles in J/ψ decays of approximately 5.6·10^6, in contrast to all other contributing processes. In addition, these two theories also efficiently describe the J/ψ decay data in the energy range below 2.4 GeV, resulting in an upper bound for the number of invisible particles in J/ψ decays of approximately 2.4·10^7, in comparison to all other contributing processes. In the energy range above 2.4 GeV, the number of events in the DRMC and DRM branches becomes too small for experimental detection, implying that in the energy range below 2.4 GeV, neutrino and dark energy systems in the six considered theories will also efficiently describe the J/ψ decay data in the DRMC and DRM

The standard second-order difference method in time (SDIMT) is a reliable technique for solving ordinary differential equations (ODEs), but it requires consistent and equal timesteps. However, this constraint can be relaxed for a significant improvement in computational efficiency, without compromising the method's key properties, by employing variable timesteps while maintaining consistency and allowing for backward steps. This research introduces a variable timestep SDIMT (VSDIMT) method that leverages a similar concept to Krylov-Sort, discarding previous smaller steps that have minimal effect on the solution, for an anticipated order of O(Δt^2) accuracy, with a theoretical framework that includes a stability analysis, deriving an explicit coercivity-based consistency correction formula for VSDIMT, and validating the method against various test cases for partial differential equations (PDEs) and differential algebraic equations (DAEs). The results show that VSDIMT can achieve substantial timestep reductions, often exceeding ten-fold, without compromising solution accuracy, and with an added benefit of significantly improved memory requirements compared to its equal-timestep counterpart. The research also explores alternative inconsistency tolerance criteria, such as the residual norm, which can lead to even larger timestep reductions, although these may compromise solution accuracy in some instances. The proposed method is implemented using the finite difference method for two-dimensional Poisson's equation and is made available as an open-source Python package, with supporting information available in the supplementary materials. The research findings suggest that variable timestep SDIMT can be an attractive alternative to its equal-timestep counterpart for solving ODEs and PDEs, providing significant timestep reductions and improved efficiency, while maintaining solution accuracy in most test cases. The research also highlights the method's potential for solving stiff problems involving large systems of equations, such as those arising from the discretization of time-dependent nonlinear PDEs with non-smooth source terms, such as the MHD equations. The research provides a theoretical framework for variable timestep SDIMT, derived timestep error formulas, and stability and consistency analysis for the method, as well as an exploration of alternative inconsistency tolerance criteria. This study introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum evaluation (MFSE), a framework that assesses the singular spectrum of multivariate functional data in high-dimensional spaces. Our approach is adaptable to a wide range of data types and domains, including multivariate functional data, functional time series, panel data with functional observations, and multivariate time series with heavy-tailed errors. We have developed asymptotic theory supporting two primary estimation methods: one for constructing confidence intervals and another for a consistent estimation of the spectral density; both are applicable across various dimensional domains. Our research team is dedicated to exploring extensions and innovations within the MFSE framework. Specifically, we investigate the singular spectrum evaluation for specific multivariate functional processes such as Gaussian processes, long-memory fractals, and their hybrid forms. Furthermore, we have established an alternative asymptotic theory supporting the root-n consistent estimation of the spectral density in a standard multivariate setting with independent observations. This work has been publicly available since 2021 and our research team is open to collaborations and discussions. The MFSE R package is available for download from CRAN, along with a user manual providing detailed guidance on package functionality and an early version of the MFSE framework source code. The latter is currently available on R-Forge due to CRAN's submission guidelines. The package contains essential functions supporting our research, including those related to the Gaussian and long-memory estimators as well as the multivariate long-memory estimator. These functions enable the estimation and simulation of multivariate beta-stable fractal processes, construction of confidence intervals, and the fit of multivariate long-memory fractal processes. The package also includes several data sets derived from real-world applications, including multivariate functional data, functional time series, panel data with functional observations, and multivariate time series with heavy-tailed errors. The MFSE package's functionality is showcased using these data sets in the provided user manual. This research focuses on a one-dimensional stochastic walk subject to a linear drift and irregular boundaries, where barriers become impenetrable upon hitting. Although the walk exhibits persistent behavior within a global framework, its local duration is influenced by the specific starting points and may not prolong the walk beyond a certain period. Consequently, persistent behavior can be guaranteed across the entire domain for finite durations by selecting appropriate local periods that align with the walk's starting points. This selected global domain of persistence is defined by the points from which the walk can last at least a certain number of steps. We synthesize the life stories of four logicians from the 20th century, Alan Turing, Alonzo Church, Kurt Godel, J.B. Rosser, Stephen Kleene, Emil Post, Rudolf Carnap, Alfred Tarski, and Nicolas Bourbaki. Our account is presented in four chapters corresponding to these logicians. Godel's discovery of a fundamental property about first-order logic served as a significant milestone in the development of modern computer science and philosophy of science. After World War II, the Amsterdam Conference saw important contributions from Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Church, among others, though one author, J.B. Rosser, made a crucial advancement in the theory of Turing machines that allowed for unbounded computation resources to be circumvented. Following the Amsterdam Conference, the development of theoretical computer science and related fields continued to evolve, marked by important milestones such as the Kolmogorov complexity theorem and the undecidability theorem, ultimately laying the foundation for Nicolas Bourbaki's constructive topology. Two appendices provide a historical context for the Amsterdam Conference and a formal proof of the unsolvability of the decision problem using Godel's incompleteness theorems, as well as a discussion on the Church-Turing thesis.

In chapter one, we explore the early lives and contributions of Alan Turing, Alonzo Church, Kurt Godel, J.B. Rosser, Stephen Kleene, and Emil Post.

In chapter two, we delve into the pre-war achievements of Rudolf Carnap, Alfred Tarski, and Nicolas Bourbaki, before shifting to the Amsterdam Conference in 1946-1947 and the post-war era.

In chapter three, we examine the life stories of Stephen Kleene and Alan Turing in greater detail, as well as the development of computer science and the philosophy of science in the mid-20th century.

In chapter four, we analyze the discovery of the property about first-order logic by Kurt Godel and the contributions of Kurt Godel, J.B. Rosser, Rudolf Carnap, and Alfred Tarski at the Amsterdam Conference in 1946-1947.

Two appendices are included: one provides a historical context for the Amsterdam Conference in 1946-1947, while the other offers a discussion of the Church-Turing thesis and a formal proof of the undecidability theorem using Godel's incompleteness theorems. This thesis is an extension of Peter J. Taal's undergraduate thesis

Acoustic models that incorporate structural elements are crucial for comprehending how sound interacts with these components. However, many acoustic systems defy identification due to a lack of comprehensive information about their structural underpinnings. This project seeks to address this challenge by assuming some unknown system behaves similarly to an established reference system when it comes to structural properties and sound relationships. This assumption allows us to define a distance metric that measures the similarity between any given system and the reference system, based on how sound evolves within each system. This distance metric becomes a distance metric for the space representing all possible acoustic systems. This way, any system whose sound evolution tracks that of the reference system can be included in the space without additional information. As a result, many unknown systems will be identified within this defined space, even without direct access to their structural details. This finding holds significant implications for enhancing machine learning models by collecting a diverse range of data from various structural configurations and relabeling it as part of a broader space of possible acoustic systems. This strategy is an important advancement in the field, as it demonstrates that learning acoustic systems is inherently easier than learning their structural counterparts. This project also explores the potential of its proposed method by applying it to an example acoustic system involving a guitar string. By showing that the method can successfully identify other systems with similar sound patterns, even within a narrow frequency range, it highlights the challenge of learning structural information in low-frequency ranges. This is because sound in these ranges is less sensitive to changes in structure, making it harder to distinguish between different configurations. To illustrate this concept through a practical application, we focus on converting spoken dialog language into written summary in another language. To tackle this challenge, we leverage neural machine translation models and employ a method called "voice alias" to bypass language barriers. In our experiments, we used the Movie Dialog Test Set, which revealed that our approach delivers performance comparable to models trained on data for the target language, while also demonstrating the ability to perform well on languages with limited training data. Our findings suggest that zero-shot voice interpretation is a feasible achievement, indicating great potential for future advancements in the field. ViDaExpert is a cutting-edge tool that allows for an in-depth exploration of vector-based data, offering an intuitive interface for both a visual and quantitative analysis of complex patterns, and streamlining the process of creating and validating data visualizations for statistical and machine learning models. It provides a comprehensive framework for transforming high-dimensional data into two-dimensional representations, using established methods such as UMAP, and incorporates an exhaustive set of metrics and indicators to facilitate a deeper understanding of data structures and cluster validity. Furthermore, ViDaExpert integrates a customizable dashboard for visual performance assessment and cluster analysis, and its robust architecture supports both local development and seamless deployment on cloud and container platforms. This instrument is designed to accelerate and streamline the data visualization process, making it an invaluable resource for both seasoned professionals and new users of ViDaExpert. It is available under the Apache License 2.0 and is part of the ViDaExpert framework, which can be accessed via its official repository on GitHub. This instrument is currently being used in various applications, including the analysis of software metrics, gene expression data, and multidimensional vectors, among other data sets. This paper provides a thorough overview of the instrument's architecture, its features, and its strengths, which are illustrated through an example data set presented in its accompanying appendix. We assess the computational efficiency of novel methods for calculating Newtonian gravitational potentials on even surfaces, particularly those that are two-dimensional. Compared to the established fast Fourier transform (FFT) technique, we found that one of the novel methods, "grid-tree" (GT), delivers superior performance, with GT requiring roughly 10-20 times less computational time than FFT for the same level of accuracy in our tests involving flat two-dimensional areas and a significant number of point masses. Additionally, the GT technique demonstrates robust accuracy even with highly overlapping point masses, a scenario in which FFT encounters precision limitations due to its sensitivity to the "resolution" parameter, which determines the level of precision in calculating the potential at each grid point. The GT technique achieves this level of performance improvement while employing a comparable number of parameters to FFT and "hierarchical octree" (HO), another novel method we evaluated, yet HO was found to be significantly slower than GT. We explored various configurations of the GT and HO techniques and examined how they handle the trade-off between accuracy and efficiency, including cases where HO can be optimized to perform closer to GT's speed, albeit with a significant increase in parameters, thus further highlighting the GT technique's fundamental processing efficiency. We primarily evaluated the GT technique using a substantial dataset consisting of 512 point masses and demonstrated its applicability to multiple relevant problems involving even surfaces by combining it with an established algorithm for determining particle positions within an octree, which we adapted to guarantee quick root-finding, a crucial step in identifying particles on or near the surface by utilizing a unique method that leverages the properties of two-dimensional Newton interpolation, enabling "early exit" from recursive tree searches and accurately locating all particles with a gravitational impact on the surface, a critical step for both potential and nearest neighbor searches. We observed significant performance improvements, exceeding two orders of magnitude, in all our tests using two-dimensional FFT on an NVIDIA V100 GPU, which we attribute to the unique characteristics of this specific processor, which we found to be more akin to HO than GT in terms of processing behavior. As such, we believe that further research is necessary to fully understand the implications of our findings, which could be influenced by the unique properties of this particular GPU, for potential applications involving the FFT technique on GPUs.
